reports.title: Proclamation No. 1250/2021 — A System for the Determination of the Division of the Federal Subsidy and Joint Revenues
reports.publisher: House of Peoples' Representatives, Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia
reports.description: Resolves this file's own prior dropped note: the import located this proclamation hosted on an actual .gov.et domain (justice.gov.et), and this round independently re-fetched and pdfplumber-extracted the bilingual Federal Negarit Gazette No. 29 PDF directly (not the private-blog copy previously the only locatable source). Confirmed verbatim, Article 2(3) (Definitions): "'Regions' or 'Regional States' shall mean members of the Federation as are recognized under the Constitution of Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia; where appropriate it may include Addis Ababa and Dire Dawa to attain the objective of this proclamation." This is the House of Federation's own governing instrument for determining the federal-subsidy and joint-revenue division formula (the mechanism that produces the itemized figures in et-budget-proclamation-1297-2023's Article 7) — it establishes the FORMULA-SETTING PROCESS (a Coordinating Committee prepares a draft distribution formula, submitted to and determined by the House of Federation, per Arts. covering pages 13276-13290+) rather than fixing a specific percentage in the statute itself; Ethiopia's actual subsidy formula is a periodically-revised administrative output of this process, not a fixed statutory number.
reports.cadence_note: One-off foundational legal instrument (establishes a recurring administrative process; the process's own output formula is revised periodically, not on a fixed schedule stated in this proclamation).

reports.title: Dire Dawa Administration 2015 (E.C.) Fiscal Year Budget Proclamation (Dire Negarit Gazeta No. 41/2015)
reports.description: Resolves this file's own prior dropped note: the import located a genuine Dire-Dawa-self-published budget proclamation, hosted on the Administration's own site (ddacouncil.gov.et) — independently re-fetched and pdfplumber-extracted this round (76-page bilingual PDF, not AI-summarized). Enacted "in accordance with Article 12(1)(b) of the Dire Dawa Administration charter No. 416/2004." Verbatim: "The total revenue of the Administration of the year 2008 E.C. [sic, cites the prior year's actuals in its own preamble] which is made up of Federal subsidy and the administration's revenue is as follows; a) From Federal subsidy; • Government treasury Birr 847,580,000 • External assistance & Loan Birr 3,720,000 • Sustainable Dev.t Goal Birr 139,200,000 b) Ordinary revenue Birr 903,311,414 ... d) From internal revenue Birr 27,572,910 ... Total Sum Birr 2,054,419,826." This is a genuine self-published municipal/city-administration budget document with real, itemized figures — distinct in kind from et-budget-proclamation-1297-2023's federal-side subsidy line item, and the strongest single municipal-tier document found for Ethiopia this round.
reports.cadence_note: Annual Administration budget proclamation; this edition is No. 41/2015 (Ethiopian calendar, approx. Gregorian 2022/23).

dependencies.basis: Both documents independently confirm Addis Ababa and Dire Dawa's distinct federal-chartered status: Proclamation 1365/2025's own Article 9(9) defines 'Region' for its purposes as including 'Addis Ababa and Dire Dawa City Administrations', directly resolving this branch's own open question (af-municipal-batch2.json, et-proc-1365-addis-applicability-unverified) about whether the property-tax law names Addis Ababa specifically — confirmed via direct PDF download and pdftotext (not the third-party legal-summary site the original node was sourced from). Relationship recorded as 'cites' since the two proclamations independently establish the same city-administration structure rather than one being derived from the other.

The federal budget proclamation's itemized Article 7 subsidy figures for each region and for Addis Ababa/Dire Dawa are the administrative OUTPUT of the formula-determination process Proclamation 1250/2021 establishes (Coordinating Committee prepares a draft distribution formula, submitted to and determined by the House of Federation) — the annual budget proclamation applies, rather than independently invents, that process's resulting formula each year.

Dire Dawa's own budget proclamation states its total revenue is 'made up of Federal subsidy and the administration's revenue' and itemizes the federal-subsidy component (Government treasury, External assistance & Loan, Sustainable Development Goal support) — the same three-part structure the federal budget proclamation's own Article 7/8 subsidy lines for Dire Dawa describe, for a different fiscal year.

reports.title: The Kenya Poverty Report 2022
reports.description: KNBS's 2022 poverty report (Sections 2.2.1 "The Food Poverty Line", 2.2.2 "The Overall Poverty Line", p.15; Section 6.1 Conclusion). Quote: "The resulting food poverty lines were KSh 2,668 and KSh 3,521 for rural and urban areas, respectively." / "The overall poverty lines in monthly adult equivalent terms were calculated as KSh 4,358 and KSh 8,006 for rural and urban areas, respectively." / "The national food poverty headcount rate for individuals in 2022 was 31.7 per cent" / "The overall poverty rate increased slightly from 37.3 per cent in 2021 to 39.8 per cent in 2022". NOTE — CORRECTED FIGURE: the underlying research lead (docx) mis-transcribed the urban food poverty line as KSh 3,251; the verified primary figure is KSh 3,521 (digit transposition in the original lead, corrected here). The overall poverty line's non-food component is updated using the non-food Consumer Price Index (CPI); the food component is updated via Kenya Continuous Household Survey (KCHS) unit-value prices, not CPI.

reports.title: 2017/18 Household Budget Survey — Key Indicators Report
reports.description: NBS's 2017/18 Household Budget Survey (HBS) Key Indicators Report, still the most current national poverty line as of this verification round (the 2024-25 Integrated Household Budget Survey remains in pilot stage as of a 27 Jan 2025 Pilot Survey Report; no full results published yet). Quote: "Food Poverty Line: TZS 33,748 per adult equivalent per month" / "Basic Needs Poverty Line: TZS 49,320 per adult equivalent per month". Methodology: "the monetary value of minimum food bundle or basket containing 2,200 kilocalories per adult per day for one month... based on the food consumed by 10 to 50 percent of the population," derived from "251 most common food items." No CPI-indexation language found in this report; poverty lines are updated via periodic HBS re-survey, not an annual CPI-adjustment formula.

reports.title: Ghana Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI) Report, 2024/2025 Q3
reports.description: GSS-authored MPI report (06-2024-2025Q3-MPI-Report, signed, published Jan 2026). Quote: "Ghana has experienced a continuous reduction in its monetary poverty over 25 years from 51.7 percent in 1991/1992 to 23.4 percent in 2016/2017." Multidimensional poverty rate for Q3 2025: 21.9% (~7.2 million people), down from 24.9% in Q4 2024. reports.title: Local Government Act, 2002 (No. 5 of 2002)
reports.description: UPDATE 2026-08-13 (AF/G.23, confirmed s.130's referenced finance law is the Local Government Finance and Audit Act 2004, added verbatim s.130 text): The Gambia's Local Government Act. Directly verified via pdftotext extraction, Part VII (Financial Provisions), Section 128: "(1) The revenue and funds of a Council include all sums of money or funds accruing to a Council. (2) The revenue and funds of a Council shall be applied to the administration, development and welfare of the inhabitants within its Area of jurisdiction. (3) The Central Government shall provide twenty-five per cent of the Council's development budget." Section 131 separately grants Councils independent rating/taxation power (General Rates Act, 1992); Section 130 defers detailed financial regulation to a not-yet-located "Local Government (Finance and Audit)" law, stating in full: "The financial affairs of a Council shall be regulated in accordance with a Local Government (Finance and Audit) law to be enacted by the National Assembly." This referenced law was confirmed this round (AF/G.23) to be the "Local Government Finance and Audit Act, 2004" — cited by name and year in two independent primary Gambian government sources (the National Audit Office's audit report on Kanifing Municipal Council, see gm-nao-audit-kmc-2017-2019, and Kanifing Municipal Council's own budget page, see gm-kmc-budget-2021) — though its full text could not be located online at any government, NGO, or legal-database source despite exhaustive search (NAO's own "Laws & Standards" listing page omits it). No broader equalisation/formula-based revenue-sharing mechanism across the 5 divisions was found beyond this single 25% development-budget clause.
reports.cadence_note: One-off foundational legal instrument.

dependencies.basis: The specific attribution comes from the IMF's own ROSC (Report on the Observance of Standards and Codes) Data Quality Assessment Framework for The Gambia, describing GBoS's practice: "the general framework for compiling the CPI is the ILO CPI compilation manual and COICOP is used in the classification... The classification of COICOP follows Classification of Individual Consumption by Purpose (COICOP) 1999 which is in conformity with international standards." This is IMF-authored (a third-party assessment of GBoS), not GBoS's own methodology note, but is the most specific documented evidence of the actual dependency — GBoS's own CPI release corroborates only the COICOP classification directly (table headers), not the manual name. `cpi-manual` already exists in the corpus (used by 8 other countries including Niger, Algeria, Morocco, Rwanda, Tunisia, Tanzania, Uganda, South Africa) — reused per the branch's node-id discipline.

An AU/StatAfric-authored Peer Review of The Gambia's National Statistical System (August 2025, EU-funded Pan-African Statistics Programme II) states: "the statistical work is guided by the African Charter on Statistics and the UN Fundamental Principles of Official Statistics and other international statistical [standards]" and "The main purpose of the Peer Review was to assess the GBoS's compliance with the African Charter." Third-party (AU/StatAfric), not GBoS-authored, and describes the National Statistical System broadly rather than the CPI specifically — 'cites' rather than 'methodology_depends_on' to reflect that weaker basis. `african-charter-statistics-2009` already exists in the corpus (first reused since the Tanzania precedent in af-synthesis.json).

Guinea-Bissau's Constitution (Lei Constitucional nº1/96, directly verified via FAOLEX), Article 110 §1-2: "As autarquias locais têm património e finanças próprios. O regime das finanças locais, a estabelecer por lei, deverá visar a justa repartição dos recursos públicos pelo Estado e pelas autarquias locais" [Local authorities have their own patrimony and finances; the local finance regime must aim at a fair distribution of public resources between the State and local authorities]. Article 118 grants autarquias a share of direct-tax revenue. IMPORTANT: this fiscal-sharing guarantee applies ONLY to "autarquias locais" (municípios, secções autárquicas, juntas locais, per Art. 106) — a MUNICIPAL tier, not the 9 regiões. Art. 107 defines regiões as purely deconcentrated political-administrative divisions with centrally-appointed governors (Art. 108), i.e. NOT a decentralised fiscal tier at all. Art. 107 §2 defers regional organisation to a separate ordinary law, which could not be located online this round — genuine NOT FOUND for the provincial/regional tier specifically requested.

reports.title: Loi n°2014-020 du 27 septembre 2014 relative aux ressources des Collectivités Territoriales Décentralisées
reports.description: Madagascar's resources law for its three-tier Collectivités Territoriales Décentralisées (Communes, Régions, Provinces), verified via direct download (hosted on the electoral commission CENI's own site, mirroring the full official text). Art. 184 lists commune-eligible fiscal revenue including 'l'impôt synthétique' and both foncier taxes. Art. 180-183 establish the general own-source/shared-revenue framework. KEY FINDING — Art. 194, the Impôt Synthétique repartition formula: "La répartition du produit de l'impôt synthétique... se fait comme suit : - 50% au profit du budget de la Commune ; - 30% au profit du budget de la Région ; - 10% au profit du budget de la Province ; - 10% au profit du Fonds national de péréquation." Further shared-tax formulas: Art. 195 (hydrocarbon royalty): 40% Commune / 30% Région / 10% Province / 20% Fonds national de péréquation; Art. 206 (telecom-mast tax): 50% Communes / 30% Régions / 20% Provinces. Art. 198-204 list commune-exclusive local taxes (civil-protection/dangerous-animal tax, a 'taxe de résidence pour le développement' explicitly earmarked for Fokontany-level development financing, a water/electricity-subscriber tax).
reports.cadence_note: One-off foundational legal instrument.

reports.title: Rapport Technique et Financier 2025 — Fonds National de Péréquation (FNP)
reports.publisher: Ministère de l'Intérieur et de la Décentralisation / Fonds de Développement Local (FDL), Madagascar
reports.description: A ministry/agency-authored annual report on the Fonds National de Péréquation's own funding and disbursement, hosted on the FDL's own site (fdl.mg). Cadrage juridique section confirms the FNP's legal basis: "La loi organique n°2014-018... complétée par la loi organique n°2016-030... en son article 25 dispose que... il est institué un mécanisme dénommé Fonds National de Péréquation, destiné à atténuer les inégalités entre les Collectivités Territoriales Décentralisées." Funding sources per Loi 2014-020 (as amended by Loi 2018-011 and Loi 2021-010): 10% of impôt synthétique proceeds, 20% of hydrocarbon-royalty proceeds, 10% of mining-royalty proceeds, plus advertising- and TV-game-show-tax proceeds. Actual FY2025 figures (Section 3, as at 30 November 2025): total FNP revenue 11,671,932,255.99 Ariary, of which 90% (10,504,739,030.38 Ariary) earmarked for CTD investment spending — but Table 2 records an honest admission of zero execution: "Transfert de Dotation de Péréquation pour Investissement pour les Communes 0.00 ... Il n'y a pas eu de décaissement... suites aux évènements politiques" [no disbursement occurred... due to the political events (beginning 25 September 2025)]. Separately (fdl.mg's 'subventions-fnp' page), the commune-selection formula for a 2025 cohort of 100 new beneficiary communes is based on INSTAT's own poverty index: "la sélection des Communes est basée sur le classement par ordre décroissant de l'IPM (Indice de Pauvreté Multidimensionnelle) de l'issu des données du dernier RGPH 3 de l'INSTAT" — a genuine, newly-documented FDL-to-INSTAT cross-institutional dependency.
reports.cadence_note: Annual technical/financial report; this edition covers through 30 November 2025.

reports.title: Loi n°2015-004 du 21 janvier 2015 relative aux Collectivités Territoriales Décentralisées à statut particulier
reports.description: Madagascar's special-status law for Antananarivo, Nosy Be, and Sainte-Marie, accessed via a FAOLEX mirror (the Assemblée Nationale's own hosted copy returned HTTP 403). Art. 41 splits Commune-tier resources between Antananarivo's Commune Urbaine (CUA) and its subordinate Mairies d'Arrondissement: "Les ressources dévolues aux Communes prévues par le Chapitre II du Titre V de la loi n° 2014-020... sont réparties comme suit : 70% au profit des Mairies d'Arrondissement ; 30% au profit de la Commune Urbaine d'Antananarivo." Art. 40 provides for a separate special subvention to the CUA, amount fixed by Council of Ministers decree. Art. 57-58 give the reciprocal arrangement for Nosy Be and Sainte-Marie: resources normally split between Commune/Région/Province tiers 'profitent intégralement' to these two communes urbaines alone, 'affectées d'office à leur budget.'
reports.cadence_note: One-off foundational legal instrument.

dependencies.basis: The FNP report's own funding-source breakdown (10% of impôt synthétique, 20% of hydrocarbon royalty, 10% of mining royalty) is directly calculated from the percentages Loi 2014-020 assigns to the Fonds national de péréquation in Articles 194-195 (the 10%/20% FNP shares of those same two taxes).

Art. 41 and Art. 57 both explicitly compute Antananarivo/Nosy Be/Sainte-Marie's special-status resource splits FROM 'les ressources dévolues aux Communes prévues par le Chapitre II du Titre V de la loi n° 2014-020' — a direct, named, formula-level dependency on the general communal resources law.

reports.title: Loi Organique n°2014-018
reports.description: Organic law of 12 September 2014 implementing Constitution Article 88(4), per its own Exposé des Motifs. Article 10: "La Province regroupe deux ou plusieurs Régions" [The Province groups together two or more Regions]. reports.description: Malawi's organic local government law, verified via the MalawiLII/Laws.Africa consolidated text (as at 2017-12-31). Sec. 79(1): "In every financial year a rate shall be made and levied by the Council to meet some liabilities falling to be discharged out of the general fund," with Sec. 79(4) allowing the council to differentiate rates "between areas and between classes of property." Sec. 44(1): "The sources of revenue for the Council to finance its operations shall be those stated in the Third Schedule." Sec. 64 gives a fallback flat-levy mechanism where formal property assessment is unavailable. Sec. 46(1) establishes a council general fund into which both own-source revenue and central grants flow. Sec. 44(4): "The distribution of Government grants to the Council shall be done by the Government upon the recommendation of the Local Government Finance Committee" — a direct statutory link to the body now operating as the National Local Government Finance Committee (NLGFC).
reports.cadence_note: One-off foundational legal instrument.

reports.title: Guidebook on the Local Government System in Malawi
reports.publisher: Ministry of Local Government and Rural Development (MLGRD), Government of Malawi
reports.description: MLGRD's own 2013 guidebook, verified via a ReSAKSS-hosted mirror of the government publication. Establishes the General Resource Fund: "The General Resource Fund (GRF) is the unconditional grant that government transfers to local governments," with a stated usage minimum: "Government however expects local governments to use a minimum of 25% of the GRF for service delivery." Names Malawi's equalization-adjacent mechanism, structurally parallel to Mozambique's FCA/Tanzania's LGFA: "The Local Development Fund (LDF) is a nation-wide financing mechanism for local development that has been established by the Malawi Government to support decentralization." States the closest Malawian analogue to a fixed equalization percentage: "The 1998 Decentralisation Policy goes further by specifying that central government will make available to districts at least 5% of national revenues, excluding grants, to be used for the development of districts." CAVEAT: hosted only via a third-party mirror (resakss.org), not an official malawi.gov.mw domain, though the content is a verbatim Government of Malawi publication.
reports.cadence_note: One-off policy/guidance instrument.

reports.title: Lilongwe City Council — March 2024 Financial Report
reports.description: Lilongwe City Council's own official site, publishing a genuine financial report with real figures — a positive exception among the four Malawian city councils checked (Blantyre, Mzuzu, and Zomba's own sites were each confirmed to have no equivalent financial documents). "LCC has a total annual budget of MWK16.766 billion. Out of this MWK7.378 billion is under Central Government Transfers (CGT), and MWK9.387 billion under Locally Generated Revenues (LGR)." Revenue performance to date: "A total of MWK 15 billion has been realized in the year representing a 91% performance against the budget revenues." Forward projection: "Total revenue budget for 2024-25 is at MWK29.7 billion."

reports.title: Loi n°2023-004 du 13 mars 2023 portant Code des Collectivités Territoriales (code en vigueur)
reports.publisher: Conseil National de Transition / Présidence de la Transition du Mali
reports.description: Mali's current, governing collectivités code, verified via the Journal Officiel text (mirrored on ILO's NATLEX). Art. 22(9): communal councils deliberate on "la fixation des taux des impôts et taxes communaux dans le cadre des bases et des maxima fixés par la loi." Art. 155 states the fiscal-legality principle: "Le principe de la légalité de l'impôt implique que la création des impôts et taxes est du domaine de la loi. L'organe délibérant de la Collectivité territoriale, par sa délibération, fixe le taux des impôts et taxes locaux dans la limite du plafond déterminé par la loi." Art. 182 defines collectivité resources: "1. des ressources fiscales qui comprennent: les impôts d'Etat transférés aux Collectivités territoriales; les impôts et taxes locaux directs; les impôts et taxes locaux indirects. 2. des produits par nature...3. des ressources budgétaires qui sont constituées des dotations et subventions spéciales de l'Etat aux Collectivités territoriales." Art. 241 ("De la solidarité et de la coopération entre collectivités territoriales") only cross-references generically: "conformément aux textes en vigueur," without naming a specific fund. Art. 251 explicitly abrogates the predecessor code: "La présente loi abroge la Loi n°2017-051 du..." KEY FINDING: ANICT and FNACT are NOT NAMED by acronym anywhere in this current code (confirmed via full-text grep), and no explicit transfer percentage appears anywhere — unlike the 2017 code it replaced, this code leaves the state→collectivité transfer rate entirely unquantified in statute, delegated to undefined "dotations et subventions spéciales."
reports.cadence_note: One-off foundational legal instrument, currently in force.

reports.title: Loi n°2017-051 du 02 octobre 2017 portant Code des Collectivités Territoriales (ABROGÉE par la Loi n°2023-004)
reports.publisher: Présidence de la République du Mali
reports.description: The predecessor collectivités code, verified via a FAOLEX mirror of the Journal Officiel text (06 October 2017), promulgated by then-President Ibrahim Boubacar Keïta. Art. 28 creates FNACT: "L'Etat garantit et organise le principe de solidarité entre les Collectivités territoriales. Il est créé à cet effet un Fonds national d'Appui aux Collectivités territoriales (FNACT)." Art. 29 sets an explicit numeric transfer floor and a natural-resource retrocession clause: "L'Etat procède annuellement à un transfert des ressources budgétaires aux Collectivités territoriales. Le taux de transfert qui ne peut être inférieur à 30% en 2018...sont définies par la loi de finances. L'Etat rétrocède aux Collectivités territoriales concernées un pourcentage des revenus issus de l'exploitation, sur leur territoire, des ressources naturelles." This is the clearest verbatim primary-source statement found in this branch's Mali research establishing both FNACT's legal creation and a hard minimum transfer rate. It is no longer in force, expressly abrogated by Art. 251 of ml-loi-2023-004-code-collectivites — kept in the corpus as a historical/superseded citation documenting the specificity the current code dropped.
reports.cadence_note: One-off foundational legal instrument, no longer in force (superseded 2023).

reports.title: Loi n°2024-017 du 11 décembre 2024 portant ratification du Traité portant création de la Confédération des États du Sahel (AES)
reports.publisher: Conseil National de Transition / Présidence de la Transition du Mali (Journal Officiel)
reports.description: The Journal Officiel's own text of Mali's ratification of the AES Confederation Treaty, verified directly (Journal Officiel 2024-29). Verbatim: "LOI N°2024-017 DU 11 DECEMBRE 2024 PORTANT RATIFICATION DE L'ORDONNANCE N°2024-015/PT-RM DU 20 SEPTEMBRE 2024 AUTORISANT LA RATIFICATION DU TRAITE PORTANT CREATION DE LA CONFEDERATION DES ETATS DU SAHEL (AES), ADOPTE A NIAMEY (NIGER), LE 06 JUILLET 2024, LORS DU PREMIER SOMMET DES CHEFS D'ETAT DE L'AES," promulgated by "Général d'Armée Assimi GOITA," Bamako, 11 December 2024. reports.title: Rodrigues Regional Assembly Act 2001 (Act No. 39 of 2001)
reports.description: UPDATE 2026-08-13 (AF/G.23, fuller Section 42 quote + alternate primary mirror check): A second primary copy of this Act, hosted on the Rodrigues Regional Assembly's own official domain (assembly-rra.govmu.org/Documents/Legislations/rraAct2017updatedJan2017.pdf, "as updated to January 2017"), confirms the same Section 42 text with the closing clauses not quoted below: "There shall be a Rodrigues Consolidated Fund which shall consist of -- (a) any money standing to the credit of the Rodrigues Consolidated Fund; (b) money appropriated to the Rodrigues Consolidated Fund by the National Assembly; (c) all recurrent revenue of the Regional Assembly; and (d) any other money properly accruing to the Rodrigues Consolidated Fund under any other enactment, but shall not include any deposit referred to in section 8 of the Finance and Audit Act." This RRA-hosted copy is arguably the more directly primary host (the Assembly's own site vs. a Ministry of Education mirror) and is retained here as a citation-worthy alternate URL rather than a URL swap. Mauritius is a small unitary state without provinces in the usual African federal sense; the autonomous island of Rodrigues (under its own Regional Assembly, per the Constitution's Third Schedule) is the closest analogue to a provincial tier. Directly verified via pdftotext extraction. Section 42: "There shall be a Rodrigues Consolidated Fund which shall consist of— (a) any money standing to the credit of the Rodrigues Consolidated Fund; (b) money appropriated to the Rodrigues Consolidated Fund by the National Assembly; (c) all recurrent revenue of the Regional Assembly..." Section 44(4): "Cabinet shall, having regard to the various criteria referred to in section 46, determine the quantum of financial resources to be allocated to Rodrigues." Section 50(c): "all duties and taxes imposed by any revenue law and applicable to Rodrigues shall be collected by the Regional Assembly on behalf of the Government and shall be paid into the Consolidated Fund." Net effect: Rodrigues has its own Consolidated and Capital Funds but fiscal resources are ultimately determined by Cabinet via annual appropriation, and general tax revenue collected in Rodrigues flows to the NATIONAL Consolidated Fund rather than staying local — "limited fiscal autonomy," not independent taxing/spending power.
reports.cadence_note: One-off foundational legal instrument.

COMESA itself publishes a "Harmonized Consumer Price Index" for Mauritius on its opendataforafrica.org portal, but this is COMESA-authored ABOUT Mauritius, not authored BY Statistics Mauritius — does not satisfy the branch's sourcing rule. No Statistics Mauritius document naming COMESA in connection with its CPI was found.

reports.title: Lei n.º 12/2023, de 25 de Agosto — Lei de bases da criação, organização e funcionamento das autarquias locais
reports.description: Mozambique's CURRENT organic municipal law, verified via direct PDF download and pdftotext extraction of the official Boletim da República (I Série, Número 165, Suplemento, 25 August 2023) — supersedes Lei n.º 6/2018 (itself amended/republished by Lei n.º 13/2018), which superseded the original 1997 framework. Art. 16 (Autonomia): "1. As autarquias locais gozam de autonomia administrativa, financeira e patrimonial. ... 3. A autonomia financeira compreende os poderes de: a) elaborar, aprovar, alterar e executar planos de actividades e orçamento; b) elaborar e aprovar as contas de gerência; c) dispor de receitas próprias, ordenar e processar as despesas e arrecadar as receitas que, por lei, forem destinadas às autarquias; ... e) recorrer a empréstimos." Art. 50(1) grants the Municipal Assembly explicit budget powers: "a) aprovar posturas; b) aprovar o orçamento do município e as suas revisões; ... i) estabelecer taxas autárquicas derramas e outras receitas próprias." This 2023 law establishes the powers but does not itself name specific taxes or the compensation-fund formula — those live in the separate finance law, mz-lei-1-2008-regime-financeiro-autarquico.
reports.cadence_note: One-off foundational legal instrument, current as of 2023 (post-dates and repeals Lei 6/2018).

reports.title: Lei n.° 1/2008, de 16 de Janeiro — Regime financeiro, orçamental e patrimonial das autarquias locais e o Sistema Tributário Autárquico
reports.description: Mozambique's municipal finance law, verified via a Wayback Machine capture (2011) of the originating Ministério da Administração Estatal PDF, which is now offline (mae.gov.mz unreachable) — same primary text, accessed via the earliest available archival mirror rather than a dead live host. KEY FINDING — Art. 43(2): "O montante do Fundo de Compensação Autárquica é objecto de uma dotação própria a inscrever no Orçamento do Estado e é constituído por 1,5% das receitas fiscais previstas no respectivo ano económico" [The Fundo de Compensação Autárquica (FCA) amount is set by its own appropriation in the State Budget and consists of 1.5% of the fiscal revenue projected for the relevant economic year]. Art. 43(3): the fund's proceeds are "de afectação livre pelas autarquias beneficiárias" [freely allocable by the recipient municipalities]. Art. 44's distribution formula: "FCAa = NHa/NHT x 75%FCA + Ata/ATT x 25%FCA" — each municipality's share is 75% weighted by its population share (Número de Habitantes) and 25% by its territorial-area share (Área Territorial). Art. 51 lists the municipal tax system: Imposto Pessoal Autárquico, Imposto Predial Autárquico (IPRA), Imposto Autárquico de Veículos, Imposto Autárquico de Sisa, Contribuição de Melhorias, plus fee-based (not tax-based) 'taxas por Licenças Concedidas e por Actividade Económica.'
reports.cadence_note: One-off foundational legal instrument (still in force as of this round; not superseded by Lei 12/2023, which governs institutional structure rather than finance).

reports.title: IPRA — Imposto Predial Autárquico (Conselho Municipal da Cidade de Pemba)

reports.description: A genuine .gov.mz municipal-government-authored page (Pemba, not one of Mozambique's four largest cities but a real, currently-active municipality) publishing actual applied property-tax rates: "O Imposto Predial Autárquico (IPRA) é um tributo municipal anual que incide sobre o valor patrimonial dos prédios urbanos situados no território do município... Habitação: Taxa de 0.4% sobre o valor patrimonial. Comércio/Indústria/Outros: Taxa de 0.7% sobre o valor patrimonial." CAVEAT: the page cites 'Lei n.º 1/2008' Articles 4, 35, 38-40, 44, 54-55 for its valuation/payment-schedule provisions, but cross-checking against the verified Lei 1/2008 text shows its actual Art. 44 is the FCA distribution FORMULA (see mz-lei-1-2008-regime-financeiro-autarquico), not an IPRA calculation provision — the municipal page's article citations appear to be misattributed, likely actually referring to a subordinate Código Tributário Autárquico (candidate: Decreto n.º 63/2008) that could not be independently located/verified this round (404). Use this as evidence IPRA is actively administered with real rates; do not treat its specific article citations as verified.

reports.title: Ordonnance n°2010-54 portant Code Général des Collectivités Territoriales du Niger
reports.description: Niger's general code of territorial collectivités, verified via a Niger-government-authored primary text (hosted on WHO's extranet legal repository, corroborated by an identical copy on UEMOA's own document repository, orfao.uemoa.int). Art. 20: "La commune assure les services publics répondant aux besoins de la population et qui ne relèvent pas...de l'Etat ou de la région. Elle jouit de la personnalité morale et de l'autonomie financière." Art. 30 gives the commune fiscal/budgetary competence: "budgets et comptes; création d'impôts et taxes rémunératoires conformément aux dispositions de la loi des finances; fixation des taux des impôts et taxes communaux dans le cadre des bases et des maxima fixés par la loi des finances." Art. 32: "Le Conseil municipal vote le budget, examine et adopte les comptes de la commune avant leur transmission pour le contrôle de légalité" — establishing state (préfet/tutelle) legality review after council adoption. Art. 79 defines the mayor's role: "préparer et exécuter le budget de la commune dont il est l'ordonnateur; tenir les comptes de la commune; établir les rôles des impôts, taxes et redevances communaux." A 2019 amending law (Loi n°2019-12) exists but was not verified to alter these fiscal articles this round — treat the 2010 text as the base fiscal framework, not confirmed unamended.

reports.title: Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria, 1999 — Section 162 (Federation Account) and Fourth Schedule (Functions of a Local Government Council)
reports.description: The constitutional root of Nigeria's three-tier revenue-sharing system. Verified via direct PDF download from a federal .gov.ng host (National Human Rights Commission). Section 162(3): "Any amount standing to the credit of the Federation Account shall be distributed among the Federal and State Governments and the Local Government Councils in each State on such terms and in such manner as may be prescribed by the National Assembly." Section 162(6): "Each State shall maintain a special account to be called 'State Joint Local Government Account' into which shall be paid all allocations to the Local Government Councils of the State from the Federation Account and from the Government of the State." Section 162(7): "Each State shall pay to Local Government Councils in its area of jurisdiction such proportion of its total revenue on such terms and in such manner as may be prescribed by the National Assembly." This document establishes the mechanism and obligation only — the actual vertical/horizontal percentages are prescribed by the Allocation of Revenue (Federation Account, etc.) Act (ng-allocation-of-revenue-act). CAVEAT: the source PDF has a recurring extraction artifact dropping the first 1-4 characters of many lines (confirmed via both pdftotext -layout and -raw, so likely a font/rendering issue in the source itself); only grammatically-complete lines were quoted.
reports.cadence_note: One-off foundational instrument (constitution).

dependencies.basis: Kano Municipal Council's own 2025 budget spreadsheet lists 'Federal Allocation' as a named revenue line (₦4,586,665,421) — the Federation Account distribution the Allocation of Revenue Act governs. The document names the revenue category but does not itself quote the Act's percentage formula, so 'cites' rather than 'calculated_from'.

The Lagos Auditor-General's report lists 'Statutory Allocation' as a distinct revenue column for each LGA — the State Joint Local Government Account's Federation Account-derived component, which the Allocation of Revenue Act governs the terms of. No formula/percentage is itself quoted in this report, so 'cites' rather than 'calculated_from'.

Section 162(3) directly anticipates the Allocation of Revenue Act by describing distribution 'on such terms and in such manner as may be prescribed by the National Assembly' — the Constitution establishes the obligation, the Act (already in corpus) supplies the actual formula.

reports.title: Nigeria's Value Added Tax (VAT) Revenue-Sharing Formula, effective 1 January 2026
reports.publisher: Federal Government of Nigeria (under the 2025 Tax Reform Acts)
reports.description: THE CURRENT formula, independently verified directly (Nairametrics, 20 July 2026), NOT the formulan import's own unsourced bonus material described as current. Verbatim: "the new formula implemented on January 1, 2026, allocates VAT as follows: Federal Government: 10%, States: 55%, Local Governments: 35%" — replacing a prior formula the same article quotes directly: "Under the previous VAT sharing formula, the Federal Government received 15% of distributable VAT, states received 50%, while local governments got 35%" (this superseded 15/50/35 split is the exact figure the import's bonus material presented as current — a real staleness catch, not a hypothetical one). The horizontal (inter-state) method also changed: "50% based on equality, 20% according to population and 30% using the place of consumption," replacing a system that favoured states with corporate headquarters. The shift moved roughly ₦219.72 billion from federal to state governments in H1 2026 alone.
reports.cadence_note: Standing formula, changed by the 2025 Tax Reform Acts effective 1 January 2026; supersedes the pre-2026 15/50/35 split.

reports.description: UPDATE 2026-08-13 (AF lead-chase round, following AF/G.23's open lead): Lei n.º 16/92's own full text remains unlocated, but its title, date and gazette locator are now confirmed via a government-authored INDEX entry — NOT the law's primary text — hosted on asg-plp.org (Associação dos Secretários-Gerais dos Parlamentos de Língua Portuguesa, a third-party host): São Tomé's own Assembleia Nacional documentation service (Direcção de Serviços de Apoio Parlamentar e Documentação, DSAPD/DDIP), in its September 2007 "Sumário das Legislações Publicadas nos Diários da República: 1975-2007" (section "Impostos"), lists: "Lei n.º16/92, de 31 de Dezembro de 1992, DR. n.º 27. - Lei das Finanças Locais." This confirms Lei 16/92's title is "Lei das Finanças Locais" (Local Finance Law) — a general local-government finance law, distinct from but complementary to this Príncipe-specific statute lineage — and situates it as the capstone of a coordinated December 1992 package: Lei 10/92 (autarquias framework, 9 Set 1992), Lei 11/92 (autarquia-body electoral law, 9 Set 1992), Lei 12/92 (electoral rolls, 9 Out 1992), Lei 15/92 (tax-legislation authorization, 4 Nov 1992), Lei 16/92 (this finance law, 31 Dez 1992), Lei 17/92 (1993 state budget, 31 Dez 1992). Evidentiary tier: this is a government-authored INDEX/summary entry (title + date + gazette locator only), not the statute's own primary legal text, so no separate node is minted for Lei 16/92 from this alone — see the corresponding _dropped no-document entry in st-leadchase-lei16-92.json. Original finding follows. The island of Príncipe has Autonomous Region status with its own elected Regional Government and Regional Assembly (since 1995), a genuinely federal-like fiscal relationship despite the country's small size. Hosted on principe.gov.st (the regional government's own official site). Article 101 ("Transferências orçamentais"): "Em cumprimento do princípio da solidariedade consagrado neste Estatuto e na Lei, o Orçamento Geral do Estado de cada ano inclui verbas a transferir para a Região Autónoma do Príncipe, nos termos estabelecidos na Lei n.º 16/92, de 31 de Dezembro—Lei de Finanças Locais e Regionais" [In compliance with the principle of solidarity enshrined in this Statute and the Law, the General State Budget each year includes funds to be transferred to the Príncipe Autonomous Region, under Law 16/92 of 31 December — Local and Regional Finance Law]. Articles 87 (solidarity principle, cost-sharing) and 89 (financial autonomy via State Budget transfers) corroborate.
reports.cadence_note: One-off foundational legal instrument.

reports.title: Loi n° 2013-10 du 28 décembre 2013 portant Code général des Collectivités locales (Acte 3 de la décentralisation)
reports.publisher: Assemblée Nationale du Sénégal / la Primature
reports.description: Senegal's 2013 decentralization reform code, verified via direct download of the official Primature (Prime Minister's office) PDF, cross-checked against an independent mirror. Art. 185 (own-source revenue): lists direct communal taxes ("taxe sur la valeur des locaux servant à l'exercice d'une profession; taxe d'enlèvement des ordures ménagères; taxe de balayage...") and indirect communal taxes ("taxe sur l'électricité consommée; taxe sur l'eau; taxe sur la publicité;...taxe sur les distributions d'essence, de gas-oil"), with rate-setting delegated to municipal council deliberation within nationally-fixed maxima. Art. 281: "Les ressources nécessaires à l'exercice par les collectivités locales de leurs compétences leur sont dévolues soit par transferts de fiscalité, soit par dotations, ou par les deux à la fois." KEY FINDING — Art. 324 creates the Fonds de Dotation de la Décentralisation (FDD): "Le fonds de dotation de la décentralisation, créé par la loi des finances, reçoit une dotation équivalant à 3,5% de la Taxe sur la Valeur Ajoutée perçue au profit du budget de l'Etat." Art. 328 creates the Fonds d'Équipement des Collectivités locales (FECL): "reçoit une dotation équivalant à 2% de la Taxe sur la Valeur ajoutée...réparti sur la base du principe de la solidarité nationale, chaque année, par arrêté conjoint du Ministre chargé des Finances et du Ministre chargé des Collectivités locales." Both percentages are stated as floors, revisable only upward: "Ce pourcentage est modifié dans le sens d'une hausse progressive, à chaque fois que de besoin."
reports.cadence_note: One-off foundational legal instrument, amended 2019 (this article set confirmed unchanged).

reports.title: Manuel d'opérations du Fonds d'Équipement des Collectivités Territoriales (FECT)
reports.publisher: Agence de Développement Municipal (ADM), under Senegal's Ministère de la Gouvernance territoriale, du Développement et de l'Aménagement des Territoires (MGTDAT), PACASEN programme
reports.description: ADM's own operational manual for the FECL (renamed FECT), verified directly (PDF metadata: created 2021-06-14). Quotes its own governing legal basis directly: "Aux termes de l'article 328 de la loi n° 2013-10...«le Fonds d'équipement des collectivités territoriales est réparti, chaque année, par arrêté conjoint du Ministre chargé des Finances et du Ministre chargé des collectivités territoriales, entre les différents ordres de collectivités territoriales, sur la base de modalités et de critères objectifs et équitables fixés par décret»." Art. 4 of Décret n°2018-1250: the Fund allocates via four named 'guichets' (windows): "Allocation globale d'Équipement," "Allocation spéciale," "Allocation d'inter-territorialité," and "Allocation de Performance." A worked simulation illustrates the split: for a hypothetical 1 billion FCFA, 70% goes to the Allocation globale d'équipement (subdivided 49% Communes/10.5% Villes/10.5% Départements), 15% to Allocation spéciale, 5% to inter-territorialité, 10% to performance — explicitly labeled a simulation, not an actual annual figure. Self-critical finding: "le FECL alloué annuellement représente 1% des recettes fiscales de l'Etat...une bonne partie de ce FECL (2/3 de son montant) est alloué aux agences intervenant pour le compte des CL, seul 1/3 du FECL est mis à la disposition directe des CL." Names Dakar, Guédiawaye, Pikine, Rufisque, and Thiès (as 'villes') and Touba (as 'Touba Mosquée,' a commune in Diourbel region) as designated pilot Collectivités Territoriales under the programme.
reports.cadence_note: Standing operational manual, not a periodic report.

reports.title: Consumer Price Index (CPI)
reports.description: Seychelles's national CPI. NBS's own CPI page describes it as measuring "changes in the price of goods and services actually charged to consumers," classified using UN COICOP ("12 divisions and four sub-group levels"), with a weight base period of 2018 (from the 2018 Household Budget Survey, covering Mahé, Praslin, La Digue) and a price base of 2020=100 introduced January 2021. A July 2024 IMF Technical Assistance mission on Seychelles's CPI (report title: "Report on Consumer Price Index Mission") states its aim was to ensure "the CPI more broadly reflects the standards and best practices described in the 2020 CPI Manual" — independent corroboration of active methodological modernisation, though this is IMF's own document about Seychelles, not NBS's self-published statement. A confirmed 2025/2026 primary NBS release was not directly verified this round (only third-party data-aggregator figures), though the TA mission and existing infrastructure strongly suggest continued monthly publication.
reports.cadence_note: Monthly per NBS's own site description; a specific 2025/2026 primary release was not independently re-verified this round.

_dropped.why: A SADC Secretariat HCPI bulletin (sadc.int/file/3171) lists Seychelles by name among covered member states and separately notes "Seychelles did not participate in the 2005 ICP round hence there is no Household Final Monetary Consumption Expenditure data (HFMCE) which are used as country weights for HCPI compilation" — real, specific evidence that Seychelles IS covered by the SADC HCPI. However: (1) this bulletin's specific URL and date could not be confirmed this round (the document appears undated, possibly a 2013-era edition, distinct from the originally-minted sadc-hcpi-newsletter node's Stage_1_HCPI PDF), and (2) NBS Seychelles's own site links to "SADC HCPI" only as a bare navigation hyperlink with no citing sentence, insufficient to quote. Deferred pending a dated, re-verified source rather than force-linked on an unverified/undated document, matching the caution applied to Mauritius's near-identical near-miss this same wave.
No NBS Seychelles document mentioning COMESA was located this round.

Seychelles is a founding member of the Indian Ocean Commission (COI/IOC), alongside Comoros, Madagascar, and Mauritius — all four founding members have now been researched in this branch and NONE has produced a citable COI/IOC document from their own statistics agency. This corpus's "no country cites the COI/IOC" gap remains open after exhausting the most likely candidates; a future session should consider searching the COI/IOC's OWN site for a document naming its member states' statistical cooperation, rather than continuing to search member states' sites individually.

GENUINE STRUCTURAL ABSENCE, not a search failure: Seychelles has 26 administrative districts with NO independent fiscal tier. Article 167 of the 1993 Constitution states "laws may provide for local government," but per a University of Pretoria academic country report, "this provision has not been fully implemented through new legislation," and "The Local Government Act of 1991 was suspended in 1993 when the current Constitution was promulgated." A Commonwealth Local Government Forum (CLGF) profile independently corroborates: "There is no constitutional provision for, or legislation governing, local government" and "The local administration has no powers to raise revenue and all funds are transferred from central government" (local government expenditure was 0.6% of total government expenditure in 2013/14). Both sources are secondary/academic (not a directly-verified primary Constitution quote — both the gov.sc PDF and constituteproject.org fetches of Article 167 failed or were truncated this round), so no node is minted for an absence; recorded here as a note for corpus completeness.

reports.title: The Local Government Act, 2022
reports.description: Sierra Leone's current local-government law, verified directly via download (hosted on the Ministry of Finance's own site). Its own preamble states the Act's purpose is "to repeal and replace the Local Government Act 2004." Section 49: "A local council shall be financed from (a) its own revenue collections; (b) central government grants for devolved functions; and (c) transfers of services delegated from Government Ministries." Section 49(4) lists own-source revenue categories including "grants (recurrent and capital) for devolved functions from the Government; development grants; grants for devolved services from the MDAs; precepts from local taxes; property tax; licences; fees and charges; share of mining revenues; interests and dividends." Section 50: "Each year a local council shall be paid tied grants (a) for the discharge of the devolved functions; (b) for the development of its locality; (c) towards its administrative cost." Section 53: "Parliament shall appropriate to a Local Council as a tied grant for each devolved service at least the amount necessary to continue the operation and maintenance of that service" — a statutory grant-adequacy floor, comparable in function (though not identical in mechanism) to the FNACT/30%-floor provisions found elsewhere in this branch (e.g. Mali's superseded 2017 code).
reports.cadence_note: One-off foundational legal instrument, currently in force.

reports.title: Local Government Act, 2004 (No. 1)
reports.description:
UPDATE 2026-08-13 (AF/G.20, municipal-tier round 25): This Act is now legally SUPERSEDED by The Local Government Act, 2022 (see sl-local-government-act-2022 in af-sierra-leone-municipal.json), whose own preamble states its purpose is "to repeal and replace the Local Government Act 2004." The 2022 Act carries forward and extends the financing framework described below (its own Sections 49-53), including an explicit grant-adequacy floor (S.53) not present in the 2004 text. Retained below for historical reference and because the 2004 Act's own text remains independently useful evidence of Sierra Leone's earlier fiscal-decentralization framework.

Sierra Leone's (former, 2004-2022) Local Government Act. Verified directly via downloaded PDF + pdftotext extraction. Part VII (Financial Matters): S.45(1) "Local councils shall be financed from their own revenue collections, from central government grants for devolved functions and from transfers for services delegated from Government Ministries"; S.46(1) tied annual grants for devolved functions and administrative costs; S.58 "Revenue raised from local taxes and from mining revenues, other than those collected by the Government, shall be shared between the local councils and the Chiefdom Councils"; S.60 mining-revenue share for local councils "as may be determined by the Ministry." STRUCTURAL CAVEAT: Sierra Leone's four "provinces" (Northern, North West, Southern, Eastern) plus Western Area are purely administrative groupings with no elected government or budget of their own — actual fiscal transfers under this Act flow to the district/city council and Chiefdom Council tier, not to a provincial-level entity. This national law is nonetheless the correct instrument for this corpus's provincial/state tier, since no separate provincial fiscal law exists to find.
reports.cadence_note: One-off foundational legal instrument.

States: "At the regional level, the NSDS is aligned with the IGAD RSDS and EAC RSDS, while at the national level, the Statistics Act guides statistical production and development in the country" and "The government of Somalia has aligned itself very much with the SDGs, Agenda 2063, the Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD) Vision 2050 and the Regional Strategy for the Development of Statistics (RSDS)." At the continental level: "NSDSs respond to the Africa Charter for Statistics and the Strategy for Harmonisation of Statistics in Africa (SHaSA)." Somalia joined the East African Community (EAC) in 2024 — a major, recent development. IMPORTANT: this document names the EAC's and IGAD's general Regional Strategy for the Development of Statistics (RSDS), NOT the EAC's specific harmonised-CPI regulation already in this corpus (`eac-hcpi-regulations`) — the two are different documents, so no edge is drawn to that node. AFRISTAT was searched for and NOT found in this document, SNBS's CPI methodological note, or a 2025 SNBS GDP policy brief.
reports.cadence_note: One-off foundational strategy document (2024-2029 planning horizon).

reports.title: Provisional Constitution of the Federal Republic of Somalia (2012)
reports.description: Somalia's Provisional Constitution, still in force (provisional status unchanged as of 2026). Directly verified via downloaded PDF (pdfplumber extraction, not AI-summarized). Article 50 (Principles of Federalism): "(e) Fair distribution of resources; (f) The responsibility for the raising of revenue shall be given to the level of government where it is likely to be most effectively exercised." Article 54 (Allocation of Powers): "The allocation of powers and resources shall be negotiated and agreed upon by the Federal Government and the Federal Member States (pending the formation of Federal Member States), except in matters concerning: (A) Foreign Affairs; (B) National Defense; (C) Citizenship and Immigration; (D) Monetary Policy, which shall be within the powers and responsibilities of the federal government." Article 51(3) establishes an annual conference of Federal/Member State executives to agree on national socio-economic development and common-market policies. A Somali National Economic Council report ("Building Cooperative Fiscal Federalism in Somalia") corroborates these same articles but is itself policy analysis, not a signed intergovernmental fiscal-federalism agreement — no distinct IGFF agreement document was located this round.
reports.cadence_note: One-off foundational instrument.

reports.title: Transitional Constitution of the Republic of South Sudan, 2011
reports.description: South Sudan's Transitional Constitution. Directly verified via pdftotext extraction of the FAOLEX-hosted official text. Article 168(5),(7),(8) (Guiding Principles): "The sharing and allocation of resources and national wealth shall be based on the premise that all states, localities and communities are entitled to equitable development without discrimination... The National Government shall fulfill its obligations to provide financial transfers to all levels of government, and shall... apportion revenue equitably among the states and local governments... Revenue sharing shall reflect a commitment to devolution of powers and decentralisation of decision-making." Article 176(1) and 177(f) set a specific quantified formula: "at least two percent of net oil and other mineral revenues for each producing state." Article 178(1) establishes the National Revenue Fund ("All revenue collected for or by the National Government shall be pooled in a National Revenue Fund administered by the Ministry of Finance and Economic Planning"), and Article 179(1) establishes the National Fiscal and Financial Allocation and Monitoring Commission ("an independent commission... to ensure transparency and fairness in regard to the allocation of funds collected at the level of the National Government to the states and local governments"). CORRECTION: there is no "National Revenue Authority" named anywhere in this Constitution — the relevant bodies are the National Revenue Fund (a pooled account) and the Fiscal and Financial Allocation and Monitoring Commission (an oversight body), not a revenue-collection authority. South Sudan's internal state structure has been highly unstable (10 states originally, expanded to 32 in 2015, reverted toward 10 states + 3 administrative areas under the 2018 Revitalized Peace Agreement) — the 2018 Agreement's own fiscal-federalism text was not independently located this round (only secondary commentary), flagged for a future session.
reports.cadence_note: One-off foundational instrument.

_dropped.why: South Sudan's own foundational statistics law (the Southern Sudan Centre for Census, Statistics and Evaluation Act, 2011, directly checked) contains no mention of AFRISTAT or the African Charter on Statistics. No NSDS/Master Plan for Statistics Development 2014-2020 reference to either was found. NOTE: a `ss-nbs-cpi -> eac-hcpi-regulations` edge ALREADY EXISTS in this corpus (af-synthesis.json, sourced from the EAC's own overview page naming South Sudan as a Partner State) — this round independently corroborates it further: the EAC's own HCPI Regulations document text itself (checked directly this round for the DR Congo file) lists "Republic of South Sudan" by name among its six explicitly named Partner States, strengthening rather than contradicting the existing edge. A UN Women assessment of NBS additionally notes "NBS is working closely with Member States of the East African Community (EAC) to integrate statistics and harmonize household survey questionnaire content across the States" — general survey-harmonisation corroboration, not itself a new citable edge.

reports.title: FY2026 Emergency Budget Guidelines — Council of Ministers Approval
reports.publisher: Ministry of Finance and Economic Planning (MoFEP), Sudan
reports.description: Sudan's Ministry of Finance and Economic Planning's own site, reporting the Council of Ministers' approval of the FY2026 emergency budget (approved December 2025, following an October 2025 guidelines/objectives approval). Verbatim (Arabic): "وتلتزم الموازنة بتحويل نصيب الولايات حسب قانون قسمة الموارد ووفق التحصيل الفعلي للإيرادات العامة في ظل عدم تحمل أي صرف إضافي" [The budget commits to transferring the states' share according to the Resource-Sharing Law and in accordance with the actual collection of general revenues, without incurring any additional expenditure]. This is MORE SPECIFIC than the aggregate lump-sum 'transfers to states' line already documented in sd-budget-2021-transfers: it names a specific governing law (the 'Resource-Sharing Law', قانون قسمة الموارد) and ties state transfers to actual revenue collection rather than a fixed figure — though the article itself does not quote the Resource-Sharing Law's own text or a formula/percentage. Deepens the national tier per this project's fallback rule (state-level fiscal transparency has collapsed under the war; the national tier is scoured instead).

Negative finding, recorded for future reference rather than as a dropped edge attempt: Sudan has NOT signed or ratified the African Charter on Statistics 2009 (an AU status table lists "48 Sudan - - -" with no signature/ratification dates), unlike many other African countries already wired to AU-level statistical instruments elsewhere in this corpus.

No individual Sudanese state's own budget or fiscal document was locatable this round (extensive search, explicitly failed) — the war has apparently collapsed most state-level online fiscal transparency. Best available substitutes used instead: the Interim National Constitution 2005 Art. 110 (general resource-allocation process, not independently re-verified against primary text this round) and a secondary IGC academic paper describing the National Revenue Fund / FFAMC (Fiscal and Financial Allocation and Monitoring Commission) and the 1971 People's Local Government Act — neither independently verified against primary legal text, so neither minted as a node this round. Flagged for a future session with more research budget to pursue Sudanese state fiscal law directly.

reports.title: Somalia Consumer Price Index (CPI)
reports.description: Somalia's CPI, independently re-fetched and confirmed this round. Verbatim, own methodological note: a "comprehensive modernization of the Consumer Price Index (CPI) system" completed with World Bank technical support, adopting COICOP 2018, expanding "geographic coverage to all Federal Member States and Somaliland," reweighted from the 2022 SIHBS survey. reports.title: African Charter on Statistics
reports.description: The Charter (adopted 2009) is now mintable for the first time: Tanzania's own Statistics Act, Cap. 351 (R.E. 2023), Section 3 (Interpretation), independently re-fetched and confirmed this round, defines "international standards" verbatim as "standards or guidelines for producing statistical information prescribed in the African Charter on Statistics, 2009, the Fundamental Principles of Official Statistics of the United Nations, other standards issued by recognised international organisations and includes international best practices." This is a national statute naming the Charter directly by title and year — the first documented case in this corpus of an AF-branch country's own law citing it, closing G.15's open lead. Parallel checks of South Africa, Kenya, Nigeria, Ghana, Ethiopia and Egypt's statistics acts did not surface an equally clear citation this round (per the import) — not independently re-checked by this session; a real gap, not a confirmed absence for those six.

reports.description: Tanzania's national statute governing Local Government Authority own-source revenue. Verified via direct PDF download and text extraction. Section 6(1)(u) (urban authorities): "all monies derived from the service levy payable by corporate entities or any person conducting business with business licence at the rate not exceeding 0.3 percent of the turnover net of the value added tax and excise duty" (an equivalent clause for district councils appears at Section 7(1)(y)). Section 31A(1): "Notwithstanding the provisions of this Act, the Tanzania Revenue Authority shall have the obligation to evaluate, assess, collect and account for property rate and advertisement fees for billboards, posters and hoarding" — property rate is listed as an LGA revenue category (Sections 6(1)(o)/7(1)(z)) but its evaluation/assessment/collection was statutorily reassigned to the national Tanzania Revenue Authority, meaning LGAs no longer administer this own-source revenue line themselves.
reports.cadence_note: One-off foundational legal instrument (R.E. 2019 = Revised Edition 2019).

reports.title: Rapport du Contrôle des Comptes et de la Gestion de la Commune d'Amou 1, Exercices 2020 à 2023
reports.description: Cour des Comptes control report on Commune d'Amou 1 (chef-lieu Amlamé), verified via direct PDF download and pdftotext extraction; independently confirmed still listed on the Cour des Comptes' own report-listing page (published 7 November 2025). Quantifies FACT dotations directly: "la commune a bénéficié des dotations du FACT d'un montant total de 75 675 903 FCFA pour les travaux d'investissement. Sur la même période, les dépenses d'investissement effectuées en termes d'émissions de mandats s'élèvent à 70 902 144 F CFA et en termes de payement à 18 065 837 F CFA, soit un taux de payement de 25,48 %" — i.e. of 75.68 million FCFA in state investment dotations received, only 25.48% was actually disbursed as payment, a real gap between transfer and execution. Confirms the budget-adoption procedure: "Le budget de la commune d'Amou 1 est élaboré par le Maire, adopté par le conseil, soumis au contrôle de légalité du Préfet et approuvé par le Ministre de tutelle." The report itself quotes Articles 82, 83 and 84 of Togo's decentralization law on compétences propres/partagées/transférées (Art. 7 of loi n°2019-006 modifiant la loi n°2007-011): "les collectivités territoriales ont pour mission la conception, la programmation et l'exécution des actions de développement d'intérêt local... Ces missions sont accomplies dans la limite des compétences définies aux articles 82, 83 et 84 de la même loi et réparties respectivement en compétences propres, compétences partagées et compétences transférées."
reports.cadence_note: One-off multi-year control report (exercices 2020-2023), part of the Cour des Comptes' ongoing series of per-commune audits (51 published as of November 2025).

reports.title: Rapport du contrôle des comptes et de la gestion de la Commune de Blitta 1, exercices 2020-2021
reports.description: Cour des Comptes control report on Commune de Blitta 1, verified via direct PDF download and pdftotext extraction; independently confirmed still listed on the Cour des Comptes' own report-listing page (published 2 October 2024). Confirms a second, independent FACT-funded investment: a mandat for "Paiement du 1er acompte de 30% des travaux de construction d'un dalot 1.00x0.80 à Blitta-Gare dans le cadre du FACT (2 992 777 F x 30%)" = 897,833 FCFA, corroborating the FACT dotation mechanism named in the glossary as "Fonds d'Appui aux Collectivités Territoriales". Lists commune investment-resource sources per Article 336 of the 2019 decentralization law: "les subventions, les dotations d'investissement et d'équipement allouées par l'Etat... les emprunts... les dons et legs" among others, and the report's own analysis concludes "la commune de Blitta 1 dispose d'une faible capacité d'investissement" — a weak capacity to mobilize investment resources despite the legal framework.

reports.title: Loi n°2019-006 du 26 juin 2019 portant modification de la loi n°2007-011 du 13 mars 2007 relative à la décentralisation et aux libertés locales
reports.description: Togo's current decentralization law, hosted on Togo's own Assemblée Nationale site and verified directly. Article 82: "Les compétences ci-après sont des compétences propres de la commune: Développement local et aménagement du territoire..." (enumerating urbanisme, infrastructure, energy, sanitation, commerce, health, and sports competencies). Article 83: "Les compétences ci-après sont partagées entre l'Etat et la commune: Développement local et aménagement du territoire..." (shared State-commune competencies across the same sectors plus education and culture). Articles 7 (communes' general development mission) and 84 (compétences transférées) and Article 336 (commune investment resources) are quoted verbatim within the two Cour des Comptes reports above (tg-cour-comptes-amou1-2020-2023, tg-cour-comptes-blitta1-2020-2021) but were not independently re-located within this consolidated text this session — the consolidated PDF fetched here confirmed Articles 82-83 directly.
reports.cadence_note: One-off foundational legal instrument, currently in force (as amended).

dependencies.basis: The audit report directly quotes Article 7 of loi n°2019-006 (via its modification of loi n°2007-011) on communes' development mission, and names Articles 82, 83 and 84 of the same law as the source of the commune's compétences propres/partagées/transférées framework.

The audit report directly quotes Article 336 of "la loi de 2019 sur la décentralisation" (loi n°2019-006) as the legal basis for the enumerated list of commune investment resources (subventions, dotations d'investissement, emprunts, dons et legs, etc.).

reports.title: Loi organique n° 2018-29 du 9 mai 2018, relative au Code des Collectivités Locales
reports.publisher: Assemblée des Représentants du Peuple, Tunisie
reports.description: Tunisia's foundational municipal/regional finance code, verified directly via full-text download. Art. 131: "L'Etat s'engage, à travers les lois de finances, les lois fiscales et les lois relatives aux biens, à ce que, progressivement, les ressources propres représentent la part déterminante des ressources de chaque collectivité locale." Art. 132 enumerates ressources propres: local taxes (per Art. 65 of the Constitution), shared/transferred tax product, shares of impôts partagés, penalties, redevances, non-fiscal revenue, and "la quote-part des collectivités locales au titre de la régularisation, de la péréquation et de la solidarité". Art. 61 creates the Haute Instance des Finances Locales (HIFL) under the tutelle of the Haut Conseil des collectivités locales, tasked to "promouvoir l'autonomie financière des collectivités locales et de réduire les disparités entre elles", propose transfer-allocation criteria to the State budget, and issue opinions on local-finance questions.
reports.cadence_note: One-off foundational legal instrument, currently in force.

reports.title: Résumé exécutif du deuxième rapport annuel de la Haute Instance des Finances Locales (2020)
reports.publisher: Haute Instance des Finances Locales (HIFL), Tunisie
reports.description: HIFL's own second annual report (covering 2017-2020), verified directly. Quantifies the national transfer-to-own-resources ratio: "لم تتجاوز نسبة التحويلات للجماعات المحلية من إجمالي الموارد الذاتية لميزانية الدولة منذ عدة سنوات، عتبة 3%" [The share of transfers to local governments out of the state budget's own total resources has not exceeded a 3% threshold for several years]. Reports two of its own composite indices for 2020: "بلغ مؤشر الاستقلالية لكافة الجماعات المحلية % 37,3 خلال سنة 2020" [the autonomy index for all local governments reached 37.3% in 2020] and "تراجع مؤشر اللامركزية لكافة الجماعات المحلية ليبلغ % 4 سنة 2020" [the decentralization index for all local governments fell to 4% in 2020]. Also notes local-government expenditure as a declining share of state-budget expenditure (excluding debt service), down to 4.9% by 2020.
reports.cadence_note: Annual report; this is the second edition, covering results for 2017-2020.

reports.title: Rapport de mission — Accompagnement des communes en difficultés financières: Commune Ezzouhour, Gouvernorat de Kasserine

reports.description: A named-commune fiscal-distress diagnostic hosted on Tunisia's own official local-government portal, verified directly. Quantifies the commune's structural dependency: "تمثل تحويلات الدولة أكثر من 92% من موارد العنوان الأول فيما لا تتجاوز الموارد الذاتية 7,27%" [State transfers represent more than 92% of Title I (operating) resources, while own resources do not exceed 7.27%]. reports.title: Bilans comparés au 31 décembre 2024 — Caisse des Prêts et de Soutien des Collectivités Locales (CPSCL)
reports.publisher: Caisse des Prêts et de Soutien des Collectivités Locales (CPSCL), Ministère de l'Intérieur, Tunisia
reports.description: CPSCL's own comparative balance sheet, verified directly (a downloaded financial-statement PDF, in French, hosted on CPSCL's own site). Confirms CPSCL's active lending role to Tunisian local governments with real figures: "Prêts en cours de réalisation" (loans being disbursed) 18,083,815 TND (2024) vs. 23,507,195 TND (2023); "Prêts en cours de remboursement" (loans being repaid) 293,342,332 TND (2024) vs. 307,684,982 TND (2023); "Fonds de dotation" (endowment fund) held constant at 86,161,054 TND both years; "Immobilisations financières" (financial fixed assets) 311,788,558 TND (2024) vs. 331,617,692 TND (2023). CPSCL separately publishes its own annual procurement plans (marchés publics) approved by its Conseil d'Administration, confirming ongoing institutional operation into 2025.
reports.cadence_note: Annual comparative balance sheet.

dependencies.basis: HIFL is itself created by Article 61 of the Code des Collectivités Locales ("Il est créé, sous la tutelle du Haut Conseil des collectivités locales, une Haute Instance des finances locales..."), and its own annual report is the institutional product of that statutory mandate.

Zambia — 22nd-highest-population country. `zm-zamstats-cpi` and `zm-social-cash-transfer-factsheet` already cover CPI/social protection; this round adds the council fiscal tier and the Local Government Equalisation Fund (LGEF). Important correction to a common assumption entering this round: the LGEF is NOT fixed at a specific percentage of national revenue by the Constitution — it is an annually-appropriated discretionary fund (Parliament decides the amount each year), with only its CAPITAL-EXPENDITURE portion (20%) fixed by statute.

reports.title: The Local Government Act, 2019 (No. 2 of 2019)
reports.description: Zambia's current local government law, verified via direct PDF download from parliament.gov.zm and pdftotext extraction. Sec. 25(1): a local authority "may make by-laws to impose a levy on" property owners/occupiers, businesses, or commodity sales within its area, with proceeds accruing to the authority (Sec. 25(3)). Sec. 27(1): power to impose fees/charges for licences, services, or goods supplied, subject to Ministerial approval for owners' rates and personal levy (Sec. 27(3)). Sec. 48: borrowing authority, subject to the Public Finance Management Act, 2018. Sec. 2 defines the "Equalisation Fund" as "the Local Government Equalisation Fund established under the Constitution" — a direct statutory cross-reference to the constitutional instrument. Sec. 47(1)-(4): the Minister of Finance may make regulations governing the Fund's administration; "A local authority shall use at least twenty percent of the funds received by a local authority from the Equalisation Fund, in any financial year, to finance capital expenditure"; an annual report on the Fund's operations must be laid before the National Assembly.
reports.cadence_note: One-off foundational legal instrument.

reports.title: Constitution of Zambia (Amendment) Act, No. 2 of 2016 — Article 163 (Local Government Equalisation Fund)
reports.description: Verified via direct PDF download. Art. 163(1): "There is established the Local Government Equalisation Fund." Art. 163(2): "Parliament shall annually appropriate monies to the Local Government Equalisation Fund which shall be disbursed by the Ministry responsible for finance to local authorities." Art. 163(3): "The Government may provide additional funds and grants to a local authority, as prescribed." IMPORTANT FINDING: this constitutional text does NOT fix the LGEF at 5% (or any fixed percentage) of national revenue — extensive search (this Constitution's full text, the repealed Local Government Act Cap. 281 which predates the LGEF entirely, and a 2016-vintage constitution mirror) found no primary Zambian legal text stating a fixed percentage currently in force. The Fund is discretionary annual parliamentary appropriation; only its capital-expenditure USE (20%, per zm-local-government-act-2019 Sec. 47(2)) is fixed by statute, not the total AMOUNT appropriated to it.
reports.cadence_note: One-off foundational legal instrument (constitutional amendment).

reports.title: Report of the Committee on Local Government Accounts on the Report of the Auditor General on the Audit of Accounts of Local Authorities for the Financial Year Ended 31st December 2023
reports.publisher: National Assembly of Zambia (Committee on Local Government Accounts, drawing on Office of the Auditor General audits)
reports.description: The single strongest finding of this round — a national parliamentary committee reporting named, itemized, quantitative figures for individual city councils, verified via direct PDF download and pdftotext. Kitwe City Council (§28): over-collection of local revenue "K2,582,86[6]" broken down by category — "local taxes (K1,778,575), licenses (K249,834), levies (K2,360,958), permits (K1,071,577)" — and full utilization of its LGEF capital component: "Utilisation of Local Government Equalisation Fund – K4,663,674...the entire 20% capital component was spent on eligible projects including road maintenance, street lighting, and procurement of refuse equipment." Ndola City Council (§34): "the Council budgeted to receive funds amounting to K141,259,842 but only received K121,498,667, resulting in a funding shortfall of K19,761,175...total funds available stood at K138,577,713. Of this, K127,216,278 was expended, leaving a balance of K11,361,435 unspent." Lusaka City Council (§67): "budgeted to generate funds...totalling K443,059,301 against which amounts totalling K377,728,897, were received...an adverse variance of K65,330,404," and "Failure to Collect Property Rates K150,684,093...from 63,049 properties...with a ratable value of K75,386,465,135." National aggregate (§13, Treasury submission): "LAs had budgeted to receive grants from the MLGRD and to generate revenue from various sources, amounting to K3,765,372,879. However, the actual funds received and generated totaled K3,429,740,801." One council (Chiengi Town Council, §51) reported that a project "stalled due to the abolishment of the 20% capital component of the Equalisation Fund" — an internal tension with the still-in-force statutory 20% rule (Kitwe's own entry in the SAME report discusses full utilization of that same 20% component for the same fiscal year) — recorded as a documented ambiguity, not resolved.
reports.cadence_note: Annual parliamentary committee report on the Auditor-General's local-authority audit; this is the FY2023 edition.

dependencies.basis: The Act's own definitions section states directly: "'Equalisation Fund' means the Local Government Equalisation Fund established under the Constitution" (Sec. 2) — an explicit textual cross-reference from the statute to the constitutional instrument that creates the fund.

Kitwe City Council's own submission, as recorded in this report, directly invokes the statutory 20%-capital-expenditure rule: "the entire 20% capital component was spent on eligible projects" — the exact mechanism Sec. 47(2) of the Local Government Act, 2019 establishes.

The report repeatedly discusses named councils' receipt and use of the "Local Government Equalisation Fund (LGEF)" — the fund Article 163 of the Constitution establishes — including the Treasury's own submission committing to "continue to support LAs with the Local Government Equalisation Fund (LGEF)."

reports.title: Constitution of Zimbabwe (Amendment No. 20) Act, 2013 — Chapter 17, Section 301 (Allocation of revenues between provincial and local tiers of government)
reports.description: Zimbabwe's constitutional devolution mandate, verified via direct PDF download and pdftotext extraction (text-layer copy; a separate ILO NATLEX-hosted copy of the same Constitution is a non-OCR'd scan and could not independently confirm this quote). reports.title: Urban Councils Act [Chapter 29:15], Zimbabwe
reports.description: Zimbabwe's organic law governing urban local authorities, verified via direct PDF download and pdftotext extraction. Sec. 272(1): "as often as it considers necessary in respect of each financial year or part thereof, a council may fix and levy a general rate upon all rateable property in the council area." Sec. 273(1): a council may "fix and levy a special rate upon all rateable property in that portion of its area which derives benefit" from specific works, to recover the cost of those works.
