reports.title: Population and Housing Census
reports.description: Decennial population and housing census. 2022 census recorded 878,674 persons (up 17.6% from 2012), reversing prior decline; projections approach ~950k+ by mid-decade.
reports._notes: Foundational demographic product. Documents the demographic turnaround coincident with the oil boom and rising foreign-born share.

reports.title: Labour Force Survey
reports.description: Periodic household labour-force survey producing participation, employment and unemployment rates. Recent rounds show improving indicators but large gender gaps.
reports._notes: Core labour-market product. Male participation and employment substantially exceed female rates; women’s unemployment is roughly double men’s in recent readings.

reports.title: Natural Resource Fund (NRF)
reports.publisher: Government of Guyana / Ministry of Finance
reports.description: Sovereign wealth fund that receives and manages oil revenues under the Natural Resource Fund Act. Central fiscal institution of the oil era; balance reached multi-billion USD levels; withdrawal rules amended to accelerate public investment.
reports._notes: Core fiscal-governance node of the oil boom. Continuously cited in budget, sustainability and intergenerational-equity analysis. Withdrawals now finance a large share of public investment and current spending.
reports._url_evidence: Ministry of Finance publications section for the Natural Resource Fund; page lists the NRF Act 2019/2021, the Operational Agreement and the NRF monthly and quarterly reports.

reports.title: Oil production (Stabroek / Liza and subsequent FPSOs)
reports.description: Offshore crude-oil production from the Stabroek Block and subsequent developments. Production has risen from zero (pre-2019) to the high-hundreds of thousands of barrels per day, driving extreme GDP growth.
reports._notes: Transformative production node. Output growth is the direct driver of the multi-year double-digit real GDP expansion and of NRF inflows. Continuously cited as the structural break in Guyana’s economic history.
reports._url_evidence: Data Centre of the Ministry of Natural Resources' Petroleum Management Programme; lists official oil production, oil price, gas produced/flared and per-field production data series.

reports.title: National Accounts / GDP
reports.publisher: Bureau of Statistics / Bank of Guyana
reports.description: System of national accounts producing GDP by production and expenditure. Extreme oil-driven growth has lifted nominal GDP into the mid-to-high tens of billions of USD and per-capita GDP into upper-middle / near high-income territory on paper.
reports._notes: Core macroeconomic product. Growth rates in the mid-to-high teens (and higher in peak years) are almost entirely oil-driven; non-oil GDP grows more moderately and is itself partly stimulated by oil-financed public spending.

reports.title: Georgetown / Region Four (Demerara-Mahaica)
reports.description: Capital city and the most populous administrative region. Primary urban and commercial domain; absorbs a large share of construction and service activity linked to the oil boom.
reports._notes: Lived urban core of the transformation. Census and construction indicators show rapid housing and building growth concentrated here.

reports.title: Poverty measurement (historical and residual)
reports.publisher: Bureau of Statistics / World Bank / independent
reports.description: Poverty headcount and related indicators. Pre-oil poverty was among the highest in South America; recent official poverty series are sparse, limiting assessment of how the boom has translated into broad-based welfare gains.
reports._notes: Critical social-gap node. Pre-oil poverty headcount was very high (~40%+ in older readings). Lack of recent comprehensive poverty data is a recognised constraint on evaluating the inclusiveness of the oil-driven expansion.

reports.title: FPSO fleet (Liza Destiny, Liza Unity, Prosperity, ONE Guyana)
reports.description: Floating Production, Storage and Offloading vessels that constitute current production capacity. Four vessels online; further FPSOs (Uaru/Errea Wittu and beyond) scheduled to push capacity toward 1.3 mbd.
reports._notes: Physical production platform. Each successive FPSO has driven step-changes in output and in NRF inflows. Continuously cited in production and revenue tracking.
reports._url_evidence: Official petroleum ministry data chart of production by the Liza, Unity Gold and Payara Gold streams (the Destiny/Unity/Prosperity FPSOs) from 20 Dec 2019 to 30 Jun 2026; no official page exists for the 'FPSO fleet' as such, and ONE Guyana is not yet broken out.

reports.title: NRF inflows and withdrawals
reports.publisher: Bank of Guyana / Ministry of Finance
reports.description: Periodic reporting of deposits into and withdrawals from the Natural Resource Fund (profit oil, royalties, signature bonuses; approved budget transfers).
reports._notes: Operational fiscal pulse of the oil era. Cumulative deposits multi-billion USD; withdrawals finance a large and rising share of the national budget. Balance tracked in the low-to-mid single-digit billions of USD.

reports.title: Non-oil GDP
reports.publisher: Bureau of Statistics / Bank of Guyana
reports.description: GDP excluding crude-oil extraction. Grows more moderately than headline GDP but is itself stimulated by oil-financed public investment and local-content activity.
reports._notes: Key analytical distinction. Non-oil growth in the high-single to low-double digits is frequently cited as evidence of spillovers; critics note that much of it is still oil-money circulating through construction and public services.

reports.title: National Budget
reports.description: Annual national budget. Increasingly financed by NRF withdrawals; supports large public investment, cash transfers, wages and social programmes.
reports._notes: Operational spending framework of the boom. NRF transfers now cover a material share (order of 30%+) of a rapidly expanding budget.
reports._url_evidence: Ministry of Finance budget landing page listing the annual Budget Speech, Budget At A Glance and Budget Estimates volumes for 2026, 2025 and earlier years.

reports.title: Consumer Price Index / Inflation
reports.publisher: Bureau of Statistics / Bank of Guyana
reports.description: Urban consumer price index and inflation measures. Inflation has remained relatively contained compared with regional peers, with food prices the main driver.
reports._notes: Price-stability node. Average inflation in the low-to-mid single digits in recent years; food inflation higher and more relevant for poorer households.

reports.title: Balance of Payments / External accounts
reports.description: Balance of payments and external-sector statistics. Large current-account surpluses driven by oil exports; capital account reflects FPSO and related investment imports.
reports._notes: External counterpart of the oil boom. Current-account surplus remains large even as import bills for FPSOs and investment goods spike in delivery years.

reports.title: Local Content Act / local-content regime
reports.description: Legal and regulatory framework requiring and monitoring local participation in the oil and gas value chain. Intended channel for non-oil employment and enterprise development.
reports._notes: Spillover-policy node. Continuously cited as the main institutional attempt to convert oil activity into broader domestic employment and firm growth.
reports._url_evidence: Official Local Content Register of the Ministry of Natural Resources / Local Content Secretariat, hosting the full text of the Local Content Act 2021.

reports.title: Cash transfers and social grants
reports.description: Expanding set of cash grants, vouchers and social transfers financed in part by NRF withdrawals. Visible instrument of oil-revenue redistribution.
reports._notes: Lived redistribution node. Budget documents and independent commentary track the growth of cash grants and related transfers as a primary way households feel the oil boom.
reports._url_evidence: Government of Guyana official cash grant portal (coat of arms, 'Powered by OPM NDMA') for registration, identity verification and bank payment of the $100,000 cash grant.

reports.title: Public debt
reports.publisher: Ministry of Finance / Bank of Guyana
reports.description: Stock of public debt relative to GDP. Remains moderate by regional standards despite rapid spending growth, supported by oil-revenue inflows.
reports._notes: Sustainability indicator. Debt-to-GDP has risen modestly with domestic issuance but stays well below levels typical of stressed regional peers.
reports._url_evidence: Ministry of Finance Public Debt Reports section listing the Public Debt Annual Report series (2015-2018, 2020).

reports.title: Region 4 (Demerara-Mahaica) — coastal demographic core
reports.description: Most populous administrative region (~40% of national population). Contains Georgetown and the densest coastal settlement.
reports._notes: Demographic and economic core. Continuously cited as the primary concentration of population, formal activity and oil-boom construction.

reports.title: Hinterland regions (1, 7, 8, 9)
reports.publisher: Bureau of Statistics / Ministry of Amerindian Affairs
reports.description: Interior regions that hold the large majority of national land area but a small share of population. Highest Indigenous population shares and historically highest poverty rates.
reports._notes: Structural geographic contrast. ~12–13% of population on two-thirds of the land; poverty and service gaps have historically been several times higher than on the coast.

reports.title: Amerindian / Indigenous population and villages
reports.publisher: Bureau of Statistics / Ministry of Amerindian Affairs
reports.description: Indigenous (Amerindian) population statistics and the system of titled and untitled villages. Fourth-largest ethnic group nationally; majority population in hinterland regions 1, 8 and 9.
reports._notes: Core identity and territorial node. Continuously cited in land-rights, poverty and service-delivery analysis; titled Amerindian lands cover a material share of national territory.

reports.title: Education system — coverage, grants and feeding
reports.description: Education-sector statistics and programmes: school infrastructure, Because We Care cash grant, uniform grant, school-feeding programme, and exam-fee support. Large and rising budget allocation financed in part by oil revenues.
reports._notes: Primary human-capital and redistribution channel. Because We Care and school feeding are the most visible household-level education supports; hinterland and riverain schools receive targeted hot-meal and infrastructure attention.

reports.title: Because We Care cash grant
reports.publisher: Ministry of Education / Government of Guyana
reports.description: Per-child cash grant paid to families of schoolchildren (public and private). Flagship education-linked transfer expanded under the oil-revenue budget.
reports._notes: Lived cash-transfer node. Continuously cited as the main direct financial support reaching most school-age children; amount has been raised in successive budgets.
reports._url_evidence: Ministry of Education landing page for the 'Because We Care' government cash grant, describing the per-child grant, uniform voucher and grant increases.

reports.title: National School Feeding Programme
reports.description: School-meal programme providing breakfast and hot meals, with particular emphasis on hinterland and riverain schools.
reports._notes: Complementary in-kind support. Explicitly prioritises hinterland attendance and nutrition; also creates local catering livelihoods.
reports._url_evidence: Ministry of Education department page describing the National School Feeding Programme: targets all nursery and Grade 1-2 primary schools, regions covered, with Regions 7, 8 and 9 targeted separately; no dedicated programme landing page exists.

reports.title: Health system — access and hinterland gaps
reports.publisher: Ministry of Health / Bureau of Statistics
reports.description: Public health-system statistics and outcomes. National indicators have improved but remain below regional averages; access and quality gaps are largest in the hinterland.
reports._notes: Human-capital counterpart to education. Continuously cited for interior service-delivery challenges and for the need to convert oil revenues into better health outcomes outside the coastal strip.
reports._url_evidence: Bureau of Statistics data table 'Number of Health Institutions by Type and by Region, Guyana: 2024' (391 facilities across the 10 regions), sourced from the Ministry of Health statistical unit.

reports.title: Gold production and exports
reports.publisher: Guyana Gold Board / Bureau of Statistics
reports.description: Gold production and export statistics. Long-standing non-oil extractive sector, important in hinterland livelihoods and as a residual export earner.
reports._notes: Primary non-oil extractive node. Continues to matter for hinterland employment and for export diversification even as oil dominates the aggregate accounts.
reports._url_evidence: Guyana Gold Board documents repository listing Annual Reports (2013-2022), financial statements, Gold Exports 2020-2023 and GGB & Dealer Declarations 2020-2023.

reports.title: Rice and sugar — traditional agriculture
reports.publisher: Bureau of Statistics / Guyana Sugar Corporation / GRDB
reports.description: Rice and sugar production and export statistics. Historic coastal agricultural pillars that remain relevant for employment and rural livelihoods even as their relative economic weight has declined.
reports._notes: Traditional coastal agro-export nodes. Continuously cited in non-oil sector analysis and in discussions of rural employment outside the oil and construction boom.

reports.title: Bauxite production
reports.description: Bauxite production and export statistics. Historic extractive sector, mainly in Region 10 and related areas; residual non-oil industrial activity.
reports._notes: Legacy industrial-extractive node. Completes the non-oil primary-sector set alongside gold, rice and sugar.

reports.title: Guyana Power and Light (GPL)
reports.description: State-owned vertically integrated electricity utility. Serves the large majority of grid-connected customers; peak demand has roughly doubled with the oil-driven construction and commercial boom.
reports._notes: Core power-system node. Customer base and peak demand have risen sharply (peak demand from ~120 MW in 2020 toward 200+ MW); capacity additions and the forthcoming gas-to-energy project are the main responses.
reports._url_evidence: Guyana Power and Light Inc.'s own site, Publications > Annual Reports listing (2009-2012); the item is a utility rather than a publication, so this is its official report series page.

reports.title: Gas-to-Energy project (Wales)
reports.description: Associated-gas pipeline and combined-cycle power plant project intended to bring offshore gas ashore for domestic power generation and to lower electricity costs.
reports._notes: Strategic energy-transition node. Continuously cited as the main near-term solution to high-cost, fuel-oil-based generation and as a link between the oil sector and domestic industrial potential.
reports._url_evidence: Gas to Energy section of the Ministry of Natural Resources' Petroleum Management Programme, carrying the Public Notice of GTE Project Approval and links to GTE project documents.

reports.title: Housing programme / housing development
reports.publisher: Ministry of Housing / Government of Guyana
reports.description: Large-scale public housing and house-lot allocation programme. One of the most visible uses of oil-financed public investment on the coast.
reports._notes: Lived boom indicator. Budget allocations for housing are among the largest functional lines; new schemes and construction are transforming the coastal landscape around Georgetown and secondary towns.
reports._url_evidence: Retrieved and read: the Central Housing and Planning Authority's Home Construction Assistance Programme page, which sets out the programme's actual terms - three house types with government-set prices (two-bedroom flat house G$7,000,000; three-bedroom flat bungalow G$9,000,000; three-bedroom elevated house G$12,000,000) plus eligibility, household-income and land-tenure documentation requirements. This is a substantive programme page, not a homepage. The slug found in the first pass (/home-construction-assistance-programme/ and /home-subsidy-programme/) is a stub or 404; the '-2' variant is the live page.
reports._url_route: sitemap - chpa.gov.gy/sitemap_index.xml -> page-sitemap.xml

reports.title: Roads, bridges and transport infrastructure
reports.description: National programme of road, bridge and corridor investment (coastal highways, Linden–Lethem, hinterland roads, river transport). Major oil-financed capital expenditure.
reports._notes: Physical integration node. Continuously cited as the attempt to link hinterland and coastal markets and to support the construction and logistics boom.
reports._url_evidence: Ministry of Public Works projects page listing current road, bridge and port works (Soesdyke-Linden Highway, East Bank Public Road, Mackenzie-Wismar Bridge, Parika port).

reports.title: Public investment programme
reports.description: Overall public capital expenditure financed increasingly by NRF withdrawals. Encompasses energy, transport, housing, health and education infrastructure.
reports._notes: Aggregate fiscal-impulse node. Budget size has multiplied since the start of oil production; capital spending is the primary channel through which oil revenue enters the domestic economy.
reports._url_evidence: Retrieved and read: Guyana Ministry of Finance Mid-Year Report 2025, which reports the Public Sector Investment Programme explicitly - 'At the end of the first half of this year, PSIP expenditure totalled $247 billion, 51.6 percent higher when compared with the same period in 2024', with the domestic portfolio at $215 billion, $7.6 billion of foreign-funded projects, and the full-year PSIP revised up to $784.2 billion from $737.7 billion. This is the Ministry's recurring PSIP reporting product, listed at https://finance.gov.gy/mid-year-reports/.
reports._url_route: publisher's own publications index (finance.gov.gy/publications -> mid-year-reports)

reports.title: EITI / extractive-sector transparency
reports.description: Extractive Industries Transparency Initiative reporting and related disclosure of oil, gas and mining revenues and payments.
reports._notes: Governance counterpart to the NRF. Continuously cited in discussions of revenue transparency and accountability in the oil era.
reports._url_evidence: GYEITI's official site, Country Report archive listing the seven Guyana EITI country reports from FY2017 through FY2023.

reports.title: Foreign direct investment statistics
reports.publisher: Bank of Guyana / Bureau of Statistics
reports.description: FDI flows and stocks. Dominated by oil-sector investment (ExxonMobil consortium and related service companies); non-oil FDI is smaller but rising with construction and services.
reports._notes: External-investment counterpart of the production boom. Continuously cited in balance-of-payments and growth analysis.

reports.title: Region 10 (Upper Demerara-Berbice) — Linden industrial/mining
reports.description: Interior region centred on Linden. Historic bauxite and industrial centre; gateway corridor toward the deeper hinterland (Linden–Lethem).
reports._notes: Secondary industrial and transport node. Completes the set of major regions beyond the pure coastal core and the deep hinterland.

reports.title: Water and sanitation access
reports.publisher: Guyana Water Inc. / Bureau of Statistics
reports.description: Household access to improved water and sanitation. Coastal coverage is higher; hinterland and riverain gaps remain material.
reports._notes: Basic-services node. Continuously cited alongside electricity as a constraint on living standards outside the best-served coastal areas.
reports._url_evidence: Retrieved and read: Guyana Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey 2019-2020, Survey Findings Report (Government of Guyana and UNICEF), published in the Bureau of Statistics publications catalogue. Chapter 10 ('Live in a safe and clean environment') carries the water and sanitation access statistics - drinking-water source and service level, sanitation facilities and handwashing - with tables disaggregated by region and population group. This is the official household-survey source for water and sanitation coverage; Guyana Water Inc. publishes only service descriptions and water-quality tests.
reports._url_route: publisher's own publications catalogue (statisticsguyana.gov.gy/publications/)

reports.title: Amaila Falls hydropower (project)
reports.description: Long-planned large hydropower project in the interior. Intended long-run renewable complement to gas-to-energy and thermal generation.
reports._notes: Long-horizon energy node. Continuously cited as the major renewable option for eventual surplus power and industrialisation; implementation has faced repeated delays.
reports._url_evidence: Guyana Energy Agency hydropower page describing the Amaila Falls project (developer, licences, completed feasibility study and EIA, ~103 MW run-of-river scheme); it is a project rather than a publication and the page content is dated.

_slice: City of Calgary — municipal template replication
_note: From the 2026-07-31 import research handoff (archive/research-input/research-handoff-2026-07-31/), verified edge-by-edge against primary sources and converted to the live schema 2026-08-07. Per-edge verdicts in the handoff merge session. From the 2026-07-31 import handoff, verified against primary sources 2026-08-07. The Grande Prairie six-document template replicates cleanly on Calgary with two corrections. (1) The handoff's ab-dip-requisition report duplicates the live node of the same id — not re-emitted here; the edge is wired into the existing node. (2) The handoff's calgary-municipal-census node is wrong: Calgary discontinued its civic census (last conducted 2019; the handoff URL 404s) and the 2026 budget sources population from the City's own Corporate Economics projections and Statistics Canada instead — the census node is dropped and replaced by calgary-economic-outlook, which the budget names verbatim. Three of the five handoff edges verified against Bylaw 9M2026, the council report C2026-0172 and the 2025 Annual Financial Report; one remapped, one dropped. Four additional verbatim-documented edges added wiring Calgary into existing provincial/institutional nodes (ab-education-property-tax-requisition, psab-psas, ab-tbf-fiscal-plan) and the statements into the budget, matching the Grande Prairie pattern.

reports.title: Property Tax Bylaw (Rates of Taxation)
reports.description: Annual bylaw setting the tax rate for each assessment class, passed under section 353 of the Municipal Government Act. Recites the estimated municipal expenditure excess it must raise, the taxable assessment on the assessment roll it levies against, the provincial education requisition it collects on the province's behalf, and the ministerially set designated industrial property requisition rate. The 2026 instance is Bylaw 9M2026, passed 31 March 2026.

release_schedule.rule: Before approving the final tax rates, Council must receive the provincial budget to determine what funding will be made available to The City and how much property tax revenue the province is requesting. This is done in the spring, typically March.
release_schedule.note: The City passes a new Property Tax Bylaw each year in spring (typically March), after Council receives the provincial budget. The current bylaw is Property Tax Bylaw 9M2026 (2026 rates); prior years' bylaws (e.g. 14M2024) were similarly numbered and passed in spring of their respective years. LiveWire Calgary reporting shows final rates were set around March 20, 2024 and around late March 2026 (article published April 1, 2026), consistent with the stated 'typically March' timing. The next bylaw covering 2027 rates would be expected in spring (March) 2027.

reports.title: Property Assessment Roll
reports.description: Annual valuation of every assessable property in the city under the Municipal Government Act, with a valuation date of 1 July of the prior year; assessment notices are mailed in early January. Bylaw 9M2026 records the 2026 roll at $450.8 billion total assessment. The base against which every property tax rate in the city is levied, and published in machine-readable form annually on data.calgary.ca.

entries.covers: 2027 property assessment notices (projected, based on historical January mailing pattern)

release_schedule.note: Calgary's annual property assessment roll notices are mailed to property owners in early-to-mid January each year (2024: Jan 3; 2025: Jan 10; 2026: Jan 14), opening the Customer Review Period. No published multi-year calendar or statutory fixed date was found; exact day varies year to year within January, so the projected 2027 entry uses month-level precision.

reports.title: Service Plans and Budgets
reports.description: Multi-year operating and capital budget adopted by Council (the 2023-2026 cycle, adjusted annually — the 2026 Budget Adjustments were approved December 2025 as C2025-0901). Sets the municipal tax revenue requirement the Property Tax Bylaw is then calibrated to raise, and names its population and inflation sources.

entries.covers: 2027-2030 Business Plans and Budgets (first year of the next four-year Service Plans and Budgets cycle)
entries.note: Calgary runs a rolling four-year Service Plans and Budgets cycle with annual adjustments approved by Council each Nov/Dec: original 2023-2026 Service Plans and Budgets deliberated by Council in November 2022; 2024 budget adjustments approved November 2023; 2025 budget approved Nov 22, 2024; 2026 budget approved Dec 3, 2025 (matches corpus's current url). The City is now running the 2027-2030 Business Plans and Budgets process (community engagement in early-mid 2026, base budget to Council in May 2026, early review in July 2026), with the newsroom explicitly stating Council 'will develop and approve the 2027-2030 Business Plans and Budgets in November' 2026, continuing the same annual Nov/Dec pattern. No published calendar gives an exact date yet.

reports.title: Annual Financial Report (Consolidated Audited Financial Statements)
reports.description: Annual audited consolidated financial statements required of every Alberta municipality by the Municipal Government Act, prepared in accordance with Canadian Public Sector Accounting Standards. Reports actuals beside the Council-approved budget throughout, and discloses the provincial property taxes The City collects on the Government of Alberta's behalf. The 2025 report was released in spring 2026.

entries.covers: 2024 Annual Financial Report (FY2024), presented to Audit Committee Apr 17 2025 then Council later in April 2025
2025 Annual Financial Report (FY2025) -- CFO sign-off dated Apr 28, 2026; this is the report on file
2026 Annual Financial Report (FY2026) -- next expected edition, projected from the observed April pattern

release_schedule.note: Alberta's Municipal Government Act sets a statutory deadline of May 1 each year for municipalities to submit audited annual financial statements to the province (https://www.alberta.ca/annual-financial-reporting-for-municipalities), but Calgary's own practice runs slightly ahead of that: the report covering the prior fiscal year is presented to the Audit Committee in mid-to-late April, then goes to Council later that same month, and is posted to calgary.ca/our-finances/annual-reports.html around the same time. Confirmed data points: the FY2024 report went to Audit Committee on Thu Apr 17, 2025 and to Council 'later this month' (CBC, corrected Apr 21, 2025); the FY2025 report (the one currently on file, 2025-Annual-Financial-Report.pdf) was signed off by the CFO on Apr 28, 2026. A prior-year Audit Committee filing for the FY2023 report is numbered 'AC2024-0438', consistent with an April 2024 Audit Committee date. Naming convention note: 'YYYY Annual Financial Report' refers to the report covering fiscal year YYYY (ended Dec 31, YYYY), released in the spring of YYYY+1 -- so the file already on record (2025-Annual-Financial-Report.pdf) is the most current edition and does not need correcting. Next expected edition is the FY2026 Annual Financial Report, expected around April 2027.

reports.title: Calgary and Region Economic Outlook (incl. Calgary and Region Population Projections)
reports.description: Semi-annual economic forecast by The City's Corporate Economics division, comprising the Calgary and Region Population Projections/Outlook and forecast tables for inflation, housing starts and other indicators. The population and inflation assumptions named in the City budget are drawn from it. Replaces the municipal census in Calgary's budget process — the civic census was last conducted in 2019 and has been discontinued.
reports.cadence_note: Spring and fall editions, with interim updates to the forecast tables and population projections (the 2026 budget cites a January 2025 update).

entries.covers: Fall 2026 Calgary and Region Economic Outlook

release_schedule.note: City of Calgary Corporate Economics maintains an 'Economics Release Dates' page listing Calgary & Region Economic Outlook releases by reference period and release month (only month-level precision given, no specific day). Spring 2026 edition was released April 2026 (already past); Fall 2026 edition is listed with Release Date: October 2026. The page states dates are tentative and subject to change. Population Outlook / population projections are published within the Spring edition of the Economic Outlook report (updated annually in January, published each Spring), consistent with releases_per_year=2 on file.

reports.title: Business Register
reports.description: Statistics Canada's continuously maintained central repository of baseline information on businesses and institutions operating in Canada (IMDB record 1105). It is the sampling frame from which most of the agency's economic surveys draw their populations, and every establishment on it carries a NAICS industry code.
reports.cadence_note: The register is maintained continuously; published outputs from it (business counts) are released twice per year.

release_schedule.rule: The Canadian business counts (the public release product of the Business Register, SDDS 1105) are produced semi-annually for each June and December reference period, and the data are released in August and February.
release_schedule.note: StatCan's Business Register (SDDS 1105) itself is a continuously-updated internal database, but its public release product 'Canadian business counts' is published twice a year, matching the corpus's releases_per_year=2. Confirmed releases: June 2025 data released 2025-08-15, December 2025 data released 2026-02-13. The official StatCan release schedule (cal2-eng.htm) lists 'Canadian business counts, June 2026' as upcoming on 2026-08-14. The following release (December 2026 data) is projected via the stated semi-annual pattern and is not yet on the published calendar.

release_schedule.note: Confirmed via both the 'Next release' statement on the June 2026 Daily article (released 2026-08-04, stating July data due 2026-09-03) and StatCan's official 2026-2027 Major Economic Releases calendar PDF, which lists monthly dates through early 2027. reports.title: Discharge Abstract Database (DAD)
reports.description: CIHI's database of administrative, clinical and demographic information on hospital discharges (and some day surgery) across Canada, released annually. It is the primary vehicle for ICD-10-CA and CCI coded hospital data.

entries.covers: Hospital stays in Canada, 2021–2022 (DAD-based annual report)
Hospital stays in Canada, 2025–2026 (projected next annual DAD-based release)

release_schedule.note: CIHI's DAD metadata page and 'Submission deadlines and refresh dates' page (https://www.cihi.ca/en/submit-data-and-view-standards/submission-deadlines-and-refresh-dates) list quarterly facility submission deadlines for DAD (with Q4/year-end final deadline June 30) but explicitly mark public 'Data refreshed' dates as 'Not applicable' for DAD, i.e., no published release calendar exists for the raw database. However, CIHI publishes an annual public-facing report/analysis built on the newly closed fiscal year's DAD data, 'Hospital stays in Canada' (formerly similar quick-stats/analysis products), consistently in mid-to-late February each year (Feb 23 2023, Feb 22 2024, Feb 20 2025, Feb 19 2026), roughly 11 months after the covered fiscal year (Apr-Mar) ends. This is used as the best available proxy for the DAD's one-release-per-year cadence given no explicit calendar for the raw data asset itself.

reports.title: Harmonized Commodity Description and Coding System (HS)
reports.description: The multipurpose international product nomenclature developed by the World Customs Organization: more than 5,000 commodity groups, each identified by a six-digit code. The commodity-side counterpart to the industry classifications already in this corpus — national trade statistics, including Canada's, are coded to it, with countries adding digits beyond six for tariff and statistical detail.
reports.cadence_note: The WCO's Harmonized System Committee 'prepares amendments updating the HS every 5 – 6 years' — editions 2002, 2007, 2012, 2017, 2022. Not an annual release; releases_per_year is nominal.

release_schedule.rule: The WCO prepares amendments updating the HS nomenclature every 5-6 years through the Review Sub-Committee and HS Committee; the HS Convention provides a two-and-one-half-year implementation period after adoption before a new edition enters into force (six months for reservations, two years for correlation tables/translation/legislative updates). The HS2022 edition entered into force 1 January 2022; the next edition, originally planned as HS2027, was pushed back one year due to COVID-19-related delays and will be HS2028, entering into force 1 January 2028.
release_schedule.note: This is a periodic amendment/nomenclature update, not a recurring data report with dated calendar entries. The WCO's own site frames it as a 5-6 year revision cycle governed by the HS Convention's implementation timeline rather than a fixed calendar. A further, more fundamental revision (HS2033) is already being planned as a follow-on cycle.

reports.title: ICD-10-CA and the Canadian Classification of Health Interventions (CCI)
reports.description: The companion Canadian clinical classifications maintained and published by CIHI: ICD-10-CA (the Canadian enhancement of the WHO's ICD-10 for diseases and health problems) and CCI (health interventions). Published together as versioned classification releases with accompanying Canadian Coding Standards, they are the coding standard for hospital data submissions.
reports.cadence_note: Versioned releases roughly every three years — v2015, v2018, v2022, with v2025/v2027 enhancement cycles under way — with coding-standard updates in between. releases_per_year is nominal.

entries.covers: Next CCI / Canadian Coding Standards version (fiscal year 2027-2028); ICD-10-CA itself remains frozen at its 2022 version with no further updates planned

release_schedule.rule: CIHI is postponing implementation of new versions of CCI and the Canadian Coding Standards until fiscal year 2027-2028. Separately, CIHI will no longer be updating ICD-10-CA at all, aligning with WHO's 2019 halt of ICD-10 updates as the international community moves toward ICD-11.
release_schedule.note: This report bundles ICD-10-CA and CCI, but the two now have divergent status: ICD-10-CA is permanently frozen (CIHI stated it 'will no longer be updating ICD-10-CA'), so only the CCI component will see a future release. CIHI's most recent bulletin (as of mid-2026) postpones the next CCI/Canadian Coding Standards version to fiscal year 2027-2028 (Apr 1, 2027 - Mar 31, 2028) without a specific date yet announced. Prior versions were labeled 'Version 2018' and 'Version 2022,' and the 2025-2026 Classification Tables (an interim update, not a full new version) were released October 2024.

reports.description: The annual provincial and territorial counterpart of the national income and expenditure accounts (IMDB record 1902), producing GDP by income and by expenditure, household income and consumption, and government sector accounts for each province and territory. SOR/2007-303 adopts its definitions by name in the DIVISION 1 interpretation section that governs the all-provinces Equalization formula, which is what makes this the highest-value node in the equalization cluster. Table number added 2026-09-06 under §7a's table-number ruling. Resolved at www150.statcan.gc.ca/t1/tbl1/en/tv.action?pid=3610022201, which returns 'Gross domestic product, expenditure-based, provincial and territorial, annual' — the expenditure-based half of this node's accounts. reports.cadence_note: Annual, released as part of the provincial and territorial economic accounts cycle (typically November for the preceding reference year).

reports.title: Canadian Government Finance Statistics (CGFS)
reports.description: Statistics of revenue, expense, assets and liabilities for the federal, provincial, territorial and local governments and the Canada and Quebec pension plans (IMDB record 5174), compiled under the IMF's Government Finance Statistics accounting framework. Named in SOR/2007-303's DIVISION 1 revenue base at s. 5(b)(ii) and in the Territorial Formula Financing part at s. 19(1)(b)(ii), and it completes a chain from a statutory transfer formula through a national statistical programme to the imf-gfsm standard already in the corpus.
reports.cadence_note: Quarterly per IMDB record 5174; the equalization and TFF calculations draw on the annual consolidated figures.

release_schedule.note: Statistics Canada publishes CGFS quarterly via 'The Daily'; each release explicitly states the date of the next quarterly release. The June 26, 2026 release (Q1 2026 data) states: 'Data on the Canadian government finance statistics for the second quarter of 2026 will be released on September 25, 2026.' Past releases confirm the quarterly cadence: Q4 2025 released 2026-03-30, Q3 2025 released 2026-01-09, Q2 2025 released 2025-09-26, Q1 2025 released 2025-06-27.

reports.title: Annual Oil and Gas Extraction Survey (OGEX)
reports.description: The annual survey of companies engaged in oil and gas exploration, development and production in Canada (IMDB record 2178), collecting financial and operating statistics including the volume and value of marketable production. SOR/2007-303's Nova Scotia division names it in seven provisions of s. 8 — more than any other survey in the section — as the determination of oil, heavy oil, mined oil and natural gas volumes and values, the same physical production the corpus's Alberta energy-royalty cluster values through NYMEX WTI, ICE Brent and Argus.

release_schedule.note: Statistics Canada's IMDB survey page (SDDS 2178) confirms the survey is Annual, with data collection running 'April to September' each year (2024 reference year collection ran April 22 to September 5, 2025), and the 2024 reference-year results were released via The Daily on September 29, 2025 (https://www150.statcan.gc.ca/n1/daily-quotidien/250929/dq250929c-eng.htm). Based on the stated annual collection window (through September) and the confirmed September 29 release for the prior cycle, the next release for 2025 reference-year data is projected for approximately September-October 2026.

Projected next annual edition (Volume III / Canadian and International coverage)

release_schedule.note: R.L. Polk & Co. no longer publishes this title. Polk's vehicle-registration-manual business (including the title once called 'Foreign Vehicle Registration Manual', renamed 'Volume III' in 1990 — the successor of the 'Canadian and International Registration Manual') was sold to World Data Corporation in 2012; Polk itself was absorbed into IHS in 2013 and later S&P Global. World Data Corp's press release (PRNewswire, Feb 16 2016) states the '2016 Motor Vehicle Registration Manuals Volumes I, II and III' were 'Released in mid-January [2016]', comparing page-count revisions against the 2015 edition -- indicating a recurring annual (mid-January) release cycle for the whole three-volume set. A dealer-facing 'World Data Corp (Polk Book) Quick Reference Guide' dated March 2025 confirms the product line (still informally called the 'Polk Book') was still active in 2025. No dated release calendar or exact-day rule was found, only this observed annual mid-January cadence, so this is marked observed-pattern rather than published-calendar or stated-rule. The corpus's existing releases_per_year=1 is consistent with this.

reports.title: CMHC Rental Market Survey / Rental Market Report (average and median market rents)
reports.description: CMHC's annual survey of the primary rental market (privately initiated rental structures with three or more units), conducted each October and published as the Rental Market Report with accompanying data tables. It produces both average market rent (AMR) and median market rent (MMR) series by unit size and rental market area, which provincial residual housing-benefit formulas name as their rent benchmark — Ontario and Nova Scotia use the average, Manitoba the median.
reports.cadence_note: Survey conducted each October; the Rental Market Report and data tables are published in the following months (recent editions in December-January).

entries.covers: 2026 Rental Market Report (average and median market rents)

release_schedule.note: CMHC's official Reports Calendar page lists the Rental Market Report as last published December 11, 2025, with the next edition scheduled for December 2026 (exact day not yet specified). The page states release dates are subject to change. Note CMHC also publishes a separate 'Mid-Year Rental Market Update' around July each year, but that is a distinct, smaller-scope product from the main annual Rental Market Report covered by this corpus entry.

reports.title: Ontario portable housing benefit framework (O. Reg. 367/11 under the Housing Services Act, 2011, Schedule 4.1)
reports.publisher: Government of Ontario (Ministry of Municipal Affairs and Housing)
reports.description: The consolidated general regulation under the Housing Services Act, 2011. Schedule 4.1 sets the framework for portable housing benefits paid by service managers, including the monthly benefit formula 80% AMR - [(AFNI x 0.30)/12], where AMR is CMHC average market rent data posted on the Ministry's website and AFNI is adjusted family net income. This residual design is the statutory template for Ontario's National Housing Strategy portable benefit programs, including the Canada-Ontario Housing Benefit.
reports.cadence_note: A consolidated regulation amended periodically rather than issued in dated editions; the AMR input it names is refreshed annually with CMHC data posted on the Ministry website. Filed as annual for the same reason other standing legal instruments in this corpus are.

release_schedule.note: O. Reg. 367/11 (Schedule 4.1, portable housing benefit / municipal housing allowance provisions) is a consolidated regulation amended periodically by the Ontario government rather than reissued on a fixed calendar. The e-Laws consolidation page (ontario.ca/laws/regulation/110367) requires JavaScript and does not expose a dated release/amendment calendar via fetch. Corroborating third-party service-manager documents (e.g. DNSSAB, Ontario Aboriginal Housing Services, City of Toronto affordable housing pages) confirm the Average Market Rent (AMR) data referenced by the benefit calculation is 'updated annually' using CMHC Rental Market Survey data, but none state a fixed month/day on which the Ministry posts the refreshed AMR figures or amends the regulation, so no computable next date exists. This supports the existing cadence_note's characterization of the item as a standing legal instrument treated as annual by convention rather than on a genuine fixed schedule.

reports.title: Manitoba Rent Assist benefit rates (80% of Median Market Rent schedule)
reports.description: The benefit schedule for Manitoba Rent Assist, the province's portable rent supplement. For non-EIA recipients the benefit is the difference between 80% of Median Market Rent (by household size) and 30% of net household income; Median Market Rent is established by the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation. Rates are republished as the MMR benchmark is updated.
reports.cadence_note: Benefit tables are refreshed as the CMHC-based Median Market Rent benchmark is updated, normally annually in July.

entries.covers: Annual Rent Assist benefit rate update (contingent on a rise in the CMHC Median Market Rent benchmark)

release_schedule.rule: Each July, Rent Assist benefits will go up if there has been an increase in the median market rent.
release_schedule.note: The Manitoba Families Rent Assist fact sheet states benefit tables are reviewed each July and increased only if median market rent has risen, so an update is not guaranteed every year but the review point is annual in July. The most recent July (2026) cycle has already passed as of the reference date (2026-08-11), so the next stated-rule occurrence is July 2027. No dated release calendar was found on the program page, fact sheet, or EIA manual chapter 19 (shelter/utilities/fuel) beyond this general July rule.

reports.title: Canada-Nova Scotia Targeted Housing Benefit (rent supplement rates and eligibility parameters)
reports.publisher: Province of Nova Scotia (Department of Growth and Development / Nova Scotia Provincial Housing Agency)
reports.description: The portable rent supplement cost-shared under the National Housing Strategy. Since the August 2024 redesign the benefit equals the applicant's actual rent, capped at the average monthly rent for the area, minus 30% of total household income; eligibility requires spending 40% or more of household income on rent. The province implements CMHC's household income levels and average market rents for determining eligibility and supports.
reports.cadence_note: Program parameters are updated as CMHC's annual household income levels and average market rents are adopted; the current formula dates from the August 2024 program change.

release_schedule.note: No published release calendar and no fixed-date rule. NSPHA's eligibility page states "Household Income Limits are established and updated annually by the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation," but the table on that page is still marked "*Effective September 1, 2024" as of August 2026 (nearly two years later) — i.e., the province has not mechanically re-adopted CMHC's figures on a fixed annual date. In practice, the program's rates/eligibility parameters have changed at irregular, policy-driven intervals (e.g., the August 2024 overhaul described in the province's news release, plus earlier ad hoc formula/eligibility changes in 2023 reported by CBC), not on a predictable calendar. This matches the existing cadence_note's framing (parameters updated "as CMHC's annual household income levels and average market rents are adopted") but there is no evidence of an actual fixed adoption date, so no computable next occurrence can be given.

reports.title: Règlement sur les conditions de location des logements à loyer modique (CQLR c. S-8, r. 3)
reports.publisher: Gouvernement du Québec (Société d'habitation du Québec)
reports.description: The consolidated regulation under the Act respecting the Société d'habitation du Québec that fixes rent in low-rental (HLM) and rent-supplement housing. Section 6 sets basic rent at 25% of the total monthly income of the household's first two occupants, and indexes the regulation's dollar parameters annually on 1 March to the Statistics Canada Consumer Price Index for rented accommodation for Ville de Montréal.
reports.cadence_note: A consolidated regulation amended periodically; its dollar amounts move once a year, on 1 March, by the CPI indexation rule in section 6.

entries.covers: Annual indexation of low-rent housing (HLM) contribution/rent amounts effective March 1, 2027, based on December 2026 CPI for rented housing (Montreal)

release_schedule.rule: Article 6: "Les sommes mentionnées au paragraphe 2 du deuxième alinéa et au cinquième alinéa sont ajustées au 1er mars de chaque année selon l'indice des prix à la consommation pour les logements en location établi, pour le mois de décembre précédent, par Statistique Canada pour la Ville de Montréal." The Société d'habitation du Québec must inform the public of the result via a notice published in the Gazette officielle du Québec (and by other means it considers appropriate).
release_schedule.note: The regulation itself (S-8, r. 3) is a codified legal text amended irregularly by government decree, not on a fixed publication schedule. However, it contains a built-in annual indexation mechanism (art. 6, and similarly art. 8/11/12 for other amounts) requiring the Société d'habitation du Québec to adjust certain dollar amounts every March 1 and publish notice of the new figures in the Gazette officielle du Québec. The March 1, 2026 adjustment has already occurred as of today (2026-08-11), so the next occurrence is March 1, 2027.

reports.title: Programme de supplément au loyer du Québec (PSLQ) — rent-calculation rules
reports.description: Quebec's rent supplement program, under which participating tenants pay rent equal to 25% of their total income for the preceding calendar year, calculated under the Règlement sur les conditions de location des logements à loyer modique (CQLR c. S-8, r. 3), with the program paying the difference to the landlord. Quebec's 25% residual is lower than the 30% used by the other provincial residual benefits in this slice.
reports.cadence_note: Tenant rent is recalculated annually against prior-year income; the governing parameters sit in the leasing regulation and move with its 1 March indexation.

entries.covers: Annual March 1 indexation of PSLQ/HLM rent-calculation parameters (tenant contribution calculated against prior-year income)

release_schedule.rule: "Les paramètres seront indexés au 1er mars de chaque année. Une nouvelle version de ce fichier, comprenant les paramètres indexés, sera produite annuellement." (Parameters used in the rent-calculation file governing low-rent/rent-supplement housing — including PSLQ — are indexed on March 1 each year, and a new version of the calculation file is produced annually.)
release_schedule.note: The March 1, 2026 indexation has already occurred (today is 2026-08-11); next occurrence is March 1, 2027. This confirms the existing cadence_note on file: the governing calculation file (Guide explicatif — Fichier relatif au Règlement sur les conditions de location des logements à loyer modique, applicable to HLM/PSLQ rent-geared-to-income calculations) is reissued annually with parameters indexed as of March 1. Note this is a different regulation from the 'Règlement sur les critères de fixation de loyer' (private market rent-setting, reformed effective Jan 1 2026) — that reform does not appear to apply to PSLQ.

_dropped.why: Handoff claimed: SAFER Regulation s. 5 rent gap = lesser of rent or maximum rent minus 30% of income, benefit 90% of gap (or sliding percentage), base income tied to OAS+GIS+provincial supplement. The formula is real — verified verbatim in the archived bclaws consolidation of B.C. Reg. 298/77 (s. 5(1) '90 - (adjusted income - base income) x 55 / ((maximum rent / 0.3) - base income)'; s. 5(6) base income 'equal to the maximum amount of old age security plus the maximum amount of guaranteed income supplement payable... for the July immediately preceding') — but bclaws marks the regulation 'REPEALED BY 2015-23-50(b), EFFECTIVE APRIL 1, 2015'. SAFER continues as an administrative BC Housing program, so no consolidated statute anchors the current formula, the proposed edge had no target, and the OAS/GIS base-income linkage would need an OAS/GIS benefit-rates node that does not exist in the corpus. Node and edge both dropped; revisit if an OAS/GIS rates node is built and a current BC Housing SAFER rate-table document is adopted as a node.

Handoff included the BC Rental Assistance Program (RAP) as an isolated node ('30% of gross household income residual against maximum rent ceilings') with no proposed dependency and no evidence document. Like SAFER, RAP is an administrative BC Housing program without a current statutory formula instrument located; with no edge to anchor and no verified recurrently-published document, the node was dropped rather than kept isolated.

Handoff claimed: 'Loyers médians du marché adjusted jointly by SHQ and SCHL from SCHL survey data.' The cited Québec.ca PSLQ page confirms the 25% residual and the governing regulation but never mentions SCHL/CMHC or median market rents; the SHQ page on loyers médians du marché (habitation.gouv.qc.ca) returned 403 to all fetch attempts, so the SHQ-SCHL linkage could not be documented. The LMM series belongs to the AccèsLogis rent-setting regime, not the PSLQ residual formula, so the claim may also be wrong-target. Replaced by two verified edges: qc-pslq -> qc-loyer-modique-regulation and qc-loyer-modique-regulation -> statcan-cpi. Revisit the SHQ LMM document if it becomes fetchable.

Handoff claimed: Alberta Rent Assistance Benefit residual based on 30% of total household income including AISH effective October 2025, previously calculated from household income and local market rent. The cited alberta.ca/rent-assistance page says only that the RAB 'amount is calculated based on household income and local market rent' — no 30% figure, no AISH statement, and no named external report (CMHC is not mentioned), so there is nothing to wire an edge to and no external target existed in the proposal. Node dropped as well: no recurrently published formula or rate-schedule document was located, only a program page. Revisit if the Alberta rent assistance program guide (which may name CMHC market rent) is located and fetchable.

Handoff claimed: New Brunswick Rent Supplement Program reduces tenant rent to 30% of adjusted household income, program funds the difference to market rent. Self-contained residual formula with no external report named and no target proposed, so there is no edge to verify; the only anchor is a gnb.ca program page (whose handoff URL contains a typo, 'rent-suppplement'), not a recurrently published formula or rate document. Node and non-edge both dropped.

Handoff claimed: Saskatchewan Housing Benefit pays fixed monthly amounts by household size where shelter costs are 35-45% or >45% of before-tax income, citing 'Saskatchewan Housing Corporation fact sheets (2026 rates)' with no URL. No evidence document could be fetched, no external report is named in the claim, and no target was proposed. Three others (wto-trade-monitoring, imf-article-iv, oecd-economic-surveys) were re-checked directly and remain open — cadence and authorship for the WTO/OECD/UNCTAD joint report are now confirmed (previously inferred from the handoff), but the specific data-source or StatCan-citation quotes needed to mint them were not retrieved this session (robots/403 walls, or fetches that returned only page navigation). The 57 `note` entries (organisation nodes, meeting/summit series, financing line-items, and their off-model edges) were reviewed as a set and found to be deliberate, well-reasoned design exclusions from the original triage, not unexamined leads — none were re-opened. reports.title: World Economic Outlook (WEO)
reports.description: The IMF's twice-yearly flagship survey of global macroeconomic prospects, with a country-level database of output, inflation, fiscal and external indicators. Historical data and projections are compiled by IMF country desk officers from information gathered in missions to member countries.
reports.cadence_note: Full editions in April and October, with shorter WEO Updates in January and July.

entries.covers: World Economic Outlook, April 2026: Global Economy in the Shadow of War
World Economic Outlook, October 2026 (full edition, expected around the IMF/World Bank Annual Meetings, Oct 12-18, 2026 in Bangkok)

release_schedule.note: IMF's own WEO landing page states the report is 'usually published twice a year, with updates in between' (full editions in April and October; interim Updates in January and July). The April 2026 full edition was released April 14, 2026 and the July 2026 Update on July 8, 2026 (both already past as of 2026-08-11). No dated release calendar for the October 2026 full edition was found on imf.org as of this research; the projection to October 2026 is based on the twice-yearly pattern and the confirmed Oct 12-18, 2026 Annual Meetings dates in Bangkok, Thailand, where the October WEO is traditionally unveiled.

reports.title: Fiscal Monitor
reports.description: One of the IMF's flagship trilogy, surveying public finance developments and projecting fiscal balances and government debt across the membership. Fiscal data follow GFSM 2014 (or SNA 2008 / ESA 2010 based national methodologies) and country projections are drawn from the WEO database.
reports.cadence_note: Published twice yearly alongside the WEO, in April and October.

release_schedule.note: IMF's own Fiscal Monitor landing page states the report is 'prepared twice a year' but does not give explicit months. Confirmed by recent editions: April 2026 edition published 2026-04-15 (imf.org/-/media/files/publications/fiscal-monitor/2026/april/english/text.pdf), October 2025 edition tied to a press briefing dated 2025-10-15, consistent with the on-file cadence_note (April/October, alongside WEO and Spring/Annual Meetings). The 2026 Annual Meetings run 2026-10-12 to 2026-10-18 in Bangkok, so the October 2026 Fiscal Monitor is expected within that window, but the IMF has not yet posted an exact release date, hence month-level precision.

reports.title: OECD Economic Outlook
reports.description: The OECD's twice-yearly analysis of major global economic trends and prospects for the next two years, with projections for output, employment, prices, fiscal and current balances. The underlying database draws historical data from national statistical agencies and OECD statistical databases, on SNA 2008 / ESA 2010 and BPM6 concepts.
reports.cadence_note: Two full editions per year (roughly June and November/December), plus Interim Economic Outlook updates.

entries.covers: OECD Economic Outlook, Volume 2026 Issue 2 (full twice-yearly edition)
OECD Economic Outlook, Volume 2027 Issue 1 (full twice-yearly edition)

release_schedule.note: The OECD publications landing page (oecd.org) and OECD-iLibrary render dynamically via JS and did not expose a dated release calendar to fetch tools. Confirmed via news coverage of actual editions: full twice-yearly editions were released 2025-12-02 (OECD raises UK growth forecast for 2026 on budget impact) and 2026-06-03 (OECD cuts global growth outlook...), consistent with the existing cadence_note (~June and ~November/December). Separately, Interim Economic Outlook updates were observed on 2025-09-23 and 2026-03-26, confirming the interim cadence too, but those are not counted toward this report's releases_per_year=2. Next full edition is therefore projected for early December 2026 based on this observed pattern; no official calendar with an exact day was found.

reports.title: Global Financial Stability Report (GFSR)
reports.description: The third of the IMF's flagship trilogy alongside the World Economic Outlook and the Fiscal Monitor, assessing risks to global financial stability. Minted 2026-08-09 (sweep session, Tier-3 item, h1-international-reports.json) closing a `no-document` lead that had correctly identified this as a genuine recurrent flagship but lacked a verified report-to-report dependency at the time it was triaged.
reports.cadence_note: Published twice yearly alongside the WEO and Fiscal Monitor, in April and October — confirmed by the October 2025 edition's own cross-references to 'the April 2025 Global Financial Stability Report'.

release_schedule.note: No published GFSR release calendar exists. The report is released twice yearly (April and October) timed to the IMF/World Bank Spring and Annual Meetings, alongside the WEO and Fiscal Monitor. Confirmed: April 2026 GFSR was published with a press briefing on April 15, 2026 (transcript: imf.org/en/news/articles/2026/04/15/tr-04142026-press-briefing-transcript-global-financial-stability-report-spring-meetings-2026), and October 2025 GFSR was published October 14, 2025. The 2026 Annual Meetings are confirmed for October 12-18, 2026 in Bangkok, Thailand (imf.org/en/news/seminars/campaigns/2026/10/thailand-2026), so the October 2026 GFSR is expected during that week, most likely mid-week (Tue Oct 13, by analogy with the Oct 14, 2025 Tuesday release and the Apr 14-15, 2026 release), but no exact date has been officially announced yet as of 2026-08-11.

reports.title: Règlement sur le régime de péréquation (Regulation respecting the equalization scheme)
reports.description: Consolidated regulation (CQLR c. F-2.1, r. 11) under the Act respecting municipal taxation establishing Quebec's municipal equalization scheme. Standardized property wealth is established under s. 9 'conformément à la section I du chapitre XVIII.1 de la Loi' from the municipal property assessment roll, and population under s. 8 is 'la plus élevée entre celle relative à cet exercice et celle relative à l'un ou l'autre des 3 exercices précédant l'exercice de référence'. The regulation names no external statistical agency for its inputs, which is why this node is isolated: its inputs are municipal rolls and decree-based population figures, not published statistical releases.
reports.cadence_note: A consolidated regulation, reprinted on amendment rather than published on a schedule; allocations under it run annually.

entries.covers: Annual equalization payment deadline for the 2027 fiscal year

release_schedule.rule: Le ministre verse le montant de péréquation déterminé pour un exercice financier... au plus tard le 30 juin de l'exercice courant (Règlement sur le régime de péréquation, F-2.1, r. 11, art. 33)
release_schedule.note: The regulation text itself (F-2.1, r. 11) is a consolidated document on LégisQuébec that is reprinted on amendment, not published on a fixed schedule — this matches the existing cadence_note. However, the regime it establishes has a stated annual deadline: Article 33 requires the Minister to pay the equalization amount no later than June 30 of the current fiscal year. That deadline for fiscal year 2026 (June 30, 2026) has already passed relative to today (2026-08-11), so the next occurrence is June 30, 2027. Article 15 also sets a September 1 cutoff for municipal financial summaries to be counted, and municipalities must submit summaries by May 1.

reports.title: Règlement sur la répartition entre les municipalités du montant représentant la croissance d'une partie de la taxe de vente du Québec
reports.description: Consolidated regulation (CQLR c. M-22.1, r. 1.2) apportioning among municipalities the amount established under s. 21.26 of the Act respecting the Ministère des Affaires municipales, des Régions et de l'Occupation du territoire, representing the growth of a portion of Quebec sales tax (QST) revenue. Distribution runs through two components (90% / 10% from fiscal 2030 onward), and the second component apportions by an economic vitality index whose source the regulation names outright.
reports.cadence_note: A consolidated regulation, reprinted on amendment rather than published on a schedule; the apportionment it governs runs annually.

release_schedule.note: Confirmed via LegisQuebec consolidated text (adopted 31 Oct 2024, last amended 5 Dec 2025, current version effective 1 Apr 2026): this is a consolidated regulation reprinted whenever amended, with no stated periodicity for amendments and no publication calendar. The regulation's own text contains no deadline/versement provision for this document itself (searched for '31 mai', 'versement', 'paiement' — none found in the regulation). Note: the annual apportionment amounts it governs ARE announced via a separate government news release each November (e.g. Nov 13, 2024 and Nov 18, 2024 articles announcing 2025 amounts, with 'versement...au plus tard le 31 mai 2025'), but that November/May cadence belongs to the annual decree/announcement process, not to this regulation document, which remains genuinely irregular in its own reprint/amendment schedule. This confirms rather than contradicts the existing cadence_note.

_slice: Health funding chain: Canada Health Transfer to Alberta institutions
_note: This slice traces the money for health care from the federal statute that sizes it down to the institution that spends it, and it turns out to be one of the best-documented chains in the whole graph because almost every link is written into legislation rather than administrative practice. The Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements Act does two separate things to the Canada Health Transfer and it uses two different Statistics Canada products to do them. Section 24.1(1)(a)(v) sizes the national pot: the previous year's cash contribution times the greater of 1.03 and one plus the three-year moving average of nominal GDP growth, determined by the Minister at least three months before the fiscal year begins. Section 24.21 then splits that pot strictly by population share. Crucially, the population is not the Census: section 2 of the Canada Health Transfer, Canada Social Transfer and Wait Times Reduction Transfer Regulations prescribes 'Statistics Canada's official estimate of the population of the province on ... July 1 of that fiscal year' (changed from June 1 for fiscal years beginning after March 31, 2024), which is the postcensal Quarterly Demographic Estimates programme, not the census count. That distinction mattered enough that the graph needed a new node for it: the postcensal estimates are themselves derived from the census adjusted for net undercoverage plus births, deaths and migration, so the census sits one hop further back than it looks. Statistics Canada confirms the relationship from its own side, describing the estimates as playing 'a vital role under the Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements and Federal Post-Secondary Education and Health Contributions Act ... in determining the amounts of federal-provincial-territorial transfers.' Equalization runs on the identical population definition under section 11 of the Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements Regulations, 2007, with the Chief Statistician certifying the numbers to the Minister by December 1 each year. Downstream, Alberta's Fiscal Plan books the CHT and CST as named revenue lines and explains movements in them by revisions to Alberta's share of national population, which makes the population estimate the single quantity that appears at both ends of the chain. At the institutional end, Alberta Health Services' business plan states outright that its annual budget is built 'based on the Government of Alberta's budget and fiscal plan', and its consolidated financial statements are prepared under PSAS with the government transfer standard applied to the $15.1 billion of Alberta Health transfers that make up the bulk of its revenue. The one thing that has become harder to trace since 2024 is the Alberta delivery layer itself: the Provincial Health Agencies Act split AHS into four sector agencies with AHS surviving as a provincial health corporation accountable to Acute Care Alberta, and the ministry that approves the AHS budget has changed name twice in two years, so the institutional nodes here are less stable than the federal ones above them.

reports.title: Canada Health Transfer
reports.description: The largest major federal transfer to provinces and territories, providing federal cash support for health care and backing the criteria of the Canada Health Act. The national cash contribution is set in statute at section 24.1 of the Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements Act and escalates each year by a three-year moving average of nominal GDP growth subject to a 3 per cent floor; the national amount is then divided among provinces on an equal per capita basis under section 24.21. Finance Canada publishes provincial and territorial entitlement amounts each year before the start of the fiscal year.
reports.cadence_note: The escalator must be determined by the Minister of Finance not later than three months before the beginning of the fiscal year, i.e. by the end of December for the fiscal year starting the following April 1. Entitlements are re-estimated several times during and after the year under the CHT/CST Regulations, but there is one authoritative annual determination.

release_schedule.note: Finance Canada does not publish a formal release calendar or statutory publication deadline for CHT allocation announcements. However, a consistent annual pattern exists: the Minister/Deputy PM issues a news release in mid-to-late December each year announcing preliminary major federal transfer amounts (including CHT) for the fiscal year beginning the following April. Confirmed instances: Dec 2021 (for 2022-23), Dec 2022 (for 2023-24), Dec 15 2023 (for 2024-25), Dec 23 2024 (for 2025-26), and the major-federal-transfers.html table was updated Dec 11 2025 showing 2026-27 amounts (consistent with a Dec 2025 announcement). Separately, 'final' (as opposed to preliminary) CHT amounts for a fiscal year are determined about 6 months after that fiscal year ends (e.g., final 2025-26 amounts determined September 2026), per the same page's note, but this appears to be a data-finalization step rather than a public announcement event.

reports.title: Canada Social Transfer
reports.description: Federal block transfer supporting provincial post-secondary education, social assistance and social services, and early learning and child care. Unlike the Canada Health Transfer its national amount grows by a fixed 3 per cent legislated escalator rather than a GDP-linked one, but like the CHT it is allocated among provinces strictly on an equal per capita basis. Set out at sections 24.3 to 24.51 of the Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements Act.
