_status: draft
_note: Round 23. Closes the remaining 9 of round 21's original 34-country e-GDDS list: the 7 countries round 21 bundled into a single 'not checked this round' dropped entry (Andorra, Albania, Micronesia, Montenegro, Palau, San Marino, Kosovo) plus 2 more (Guyana, Serbia) that round 21 miscounted and never listed at all -- found only because round 22's count-correction pass (25/34 wired, 9 remained, not 7) caught the discrepancy. Method: the IMF's own DSBB e-GDDS country-category page (dsbb.imf.org/e-gdds/country/<ISO3>/category), rendered in Chrome, carries a hidden global country-to-NSDP-URL link list (found via javascript_tool querying all outbound <a> tags -- a plain page-text read only shows the active country's own category rows, not this list) that gave a registered NSDP URL for every one of these 9 countries in one page load, replacing the country-by-country press-release search round 22 used. 7 of the 9 registered destinations were live, self-declared pages (each on the country's own domain) and graded A. The other 2 (Andorra, Micronesia) have registered destinations that are unreadable for different reasons (a JS-shell SPA with no content region; an expired TLS certificate) -- both wired instead as REGISTER-tier edges off the IMF's own press release for that country, per PLAYBOOK-CORPUS.md rule 19 (a document published by the TARGET's own publisher recording the relationship is REGISTER, not THIRD-PARTY, and grades on the same A/B/C rules as any other tier -- both grade A here because both press releases were read in full and quoted verbatim). Two recurring findings, both character-level: the shared NSDP page template has an unsubstituted-placeholder bug ('...in which Country participates', literally, on San Marino/Montenegro/Albania/Serbia's own copies -- confirmed present on 4 of the 7 self-declared pages in this batch, so this is a platform-wide template defect, not a per-country typo); Serbia's page additionally bakes a Unicode replacement character (U+FFFD) into the apostrophe position in its raw HTML, and San Marino's page uses a plain ASCII apostrophe where every other page in this batch uses the U+2019 typographic one. Every quote below was cut to avoid the specific defect(s) present on its own page rather than silently 'fixed', and every apostrophe was verified by code point before transcription. Two of the nine country codes (AD, SM) had no existing corpus node and were missing COUNTRY_FAMILY/COUNTRY_LABEL (palette.ts) and CONTINENT_OF (regions.ts) entries -- both added this round (XEU family, Europe continent, alongside LI/CH's non-EU-European-microstate precedent). The other 7 (AL, FM, ME, PW, RS, XK, GY) already had live nodes elsewhere in the corpus and needed no classification changes. No id or evidence-URL collision against the whole corpus for any of the 9 new nodes or URLs (checked before writing). This closes the e-GDDS wiring todo: all 34 of round 21's original list are now wired (25 self-declared/register from round 21 itself, 4 from round 22's group-1, 9 from this round -- 7 self-declared, 2 register).

_note: Round 21 of the [Agent] e-GDDS todo (HANDOFF.md, int-imf-tier-sweep-2026-09-07.json's _dropped 'e-GDDS participants with a real NSDP and no node to hang the edge on (34 countries)'). Rounds 19-20 wired 3 of the 34 (Botswana, Tanzania, Cote d'Ivoire) and left a generalised method: search '<country> opendataforafrica NSDP', go to the country's own <slug>.opendataforafrica.org NSDP page in Chrome (Cloudflare-walled to curl but clean in Chrome), and read the platform's own boilerplate self-declaration naming the country and e-GDDS. This round ran that method across all 31 remaining countries via WebSearch + Chrome and found the NSDP page live and readable for 18 of them: Benin, Madagascar, Zambia, Zimbabwe, Lesotho, Mozambique, Malawi, Cameroon, Angola, Cabo Verde, Gambia, Equatorial Guinea, DR Congo, Eswatini, Guinea-Bissau, Mauritania, Sao Tome and Principe, and Somalia -- all minted here at A (quote-found-artefact-named, SELF-DECLARED). Every quote was read directly off the rendered page via the browser's accessibility tree (read_page) rather than transcribed from a screenshot, specifically to avoid the known ASCII-vs-typographic-apostrophe trap (PLAYBOOK-CORPUS.md Known Traps) -- the U+2019 in "Fund’s" was confirmed via read_page on the Angola page and the same platform template is used verbatim (country name substituted) on every other page in this batch. For each publisher, the page's own footer was checked via the accessibility tree/find tool for a direct link to the country's NSO (confirmed for 13 of 18: Madagascar->instat.mg, Angola->ine.gov.ao/minfin.gov.ao/bna.ao, Cabo Verde->ine.cv, Gambia->gbosdata.org, Equatorial Guinea->dgecnstat-ge.org, DR Congo->ins-rdc.org, Sao Tome->ine.st, plus the 7 that name the agency directly in the page's own title: Benin/INStaD, Zambia/Zambia Statistics Agency, Lesotho/Central Bank of Lesotho, Mozambique/INE, Malawi/Reserve Bank of Malawi, Cameroon/NIS, Eswatini/Ministry of Finance). Three (Guinea-Bissau, Mauritania, Somalia) carry only generic AfDB/Knoema sponsor links in the footer with no NSO-specific link found this round -- their publisher field follows the NSO name already established elsewhere in-corpus for that country (gw-ine-inhpc, mr-ons-inpc, so-nsds-ii-2024-2029/so-snbs-cpi) but that specific attribution was NOT independently re-verified on the NSDP page itself this round; each report's own description flags this. The self-declaration text and evidence_grade do not depend on the publisher field either way -- rule 19's Togo precedent ('a country's own data portal on opendataforafrica.org... is self-declared', judged by the page's own national branding, not by which specific sub-agency's footer link is present) is what carries the SELF-DECLARED tag for all 18, publisher-attribution strength aside. 13 of the original 34 remain open after this round: Andorra, Albania, Burundi, Central African Republic, Djibouti, Guinea, Micronesia, Montenegro, Palau, San Marino, Kosovo -- checked this round and found NOT to have a live NSDP page on the opendataforafrica.org platform (Burundi, Djibouti, Guinea and Central African Republic's country portals exist but carry no NSDP nav item or resolvable URL; Andorra, Albania, Micronesia, Montenegro, Palau, San Marino and Kosovo were not checked -- opendataforafrica.org appears to be an Africa-focused platform and these are unlikely candidates for it, a different route (IMF press release / DSBB) would be needed. No id or evidence-URL collision found against the whole corpus (research + seed files) for any of the 18 new ids or URLs -- checked before writing.

_dropped.why: ALREADY LIVE — caught by the validator's SUPERSEDED check, not by my collision scan, which is the finding. h1-international-reports.json carries this edge at A on the same document, quoting the same appendix's other sentence. What is worth recording is the ROUTE, not the edge: the live edge cites https://www.imf.org/-/media/files/publications/fiscal-monitor/2025/english/msa.pdf, which returns HTTP 403 to a browser-UA curl from the cloud sandbox today, 2026-09-06 — the /-/media/ path is walled like every other www.imf.org path. The identical text is readable at https://www.elibrary.imf.org/downloadpdf/display/book/9798229002516/CH005.pdf, which is the Fiscal Monitor April 2025 Methodological and Statistical Appendix as elibrary shelves it. Nothing is written down (PLAYBOOK-CORPUS section 7b), and the grade is already A so there is nothing to write up either; this entry exists so that whoever next finds that 403 knows there is a live second copy and does not record the citation as rotted.

ALREADY LIVE, and the existing evidence is better than what this round found. h1-international-reports.json carries it at B on 'Country-specific data and projections for key fiscal variables are based on the April 2025 World Economic Outlook database, unless indicated otherwise, and compiled by IMF staff' — a direct statement of sourcing. This round independently reached the same edge from the weaker sentence about what the WEO database does NOT cover. Not re-minted, and not re-graded: the existing quote is the stronger one and a re-grade never writes down. Same 403-versus-elibrary route note as the GFSM entry above applies to its evidence_url.

DEFERRED 2026-09-06 (round 4). BPM6 appears twice in the WEO April 2025 Statistical Appendix and neither occurrence is quite the edge. The prose one says the IMF's sector standards 'have been aligned with the SNA 2008' — a claim about two standards, not about the WEO, and the shape PLAYBOOK-CORPUS section 7a refuses. The other is Table G, 'Key Data Documentation', whose 'Statistics Manual in Use at Source Country' column carries 'BPM 6' or 'BPM 5' on every country row. That table's whole purpose is to disclose which manual each country's source data follow, so under the 2026-09-06 methodology-table-cell ruling the shape qualifies and would grade B — but the cell content is the two-token string 'BPM 6', which is the acronym with a space in it, not the artefact's title, and pdftotext renders the table as column soup with no quotable contiguous span. Wants a Chrome read of the table, or the same statement in a different issue's prose.

NOT ATTEMPTED 2026-09-06 (round 4) — recorded so the next round starts where this one stopped rather than re-deriving the route. The Global Financial Stability Report April 2025 is ISBN 9798229003261 on elibrary.imf.org and its whole-issue PDF downloads to a plain curl at /downloadpdf/display/book/9798229003261/9798229003261.pdf. It was not read. The GFSR is the weakest of the three flagships for this corpus because its data annexes lean on commercial market data and IMF internal databases rather than on the statistical manuals, so expect fewer edges than the WEO or the Fiscal Monitor returned.

REFUSED 2026-09-06 (round 4). The WEO Statistical Appendix names 'the Monetary and Financial Statistics Manual and Compilation Guide' by full title, which IS the corpus node's title, in the same sentence as BPM6 and GFSM 2014 — but that sentence says those standards 'have been aligned with the SNA 2008', which is a statement about the standards and not about the WEO's own data. No other occurrence in either appendix. Refused on the sentence, not on the edition, unlike the three MFSM refusals in int-imf-dsbb-2026-09-06.json.

reports.title: National Summary Data Page — Armenia
reports.publisher: Statistical Committee of the Republic of Armenia
reports.description: Armenia's National Summary Data Page, the single page of macroeconomic and financial data the IMF's SDDS prescribes and monitors on the Dissemination Standards Bulletin Board. Published by Statistical Committee of the Republic of Armenia. The URL is the one the IMF's own country-list endpoint gives as this country's NSDP; the page was read live on 2026-09-07. Coverage, periodicity and timeliness of every category on it are set by the standard, which is what the edge to imf-sdds records.
reports.cadence_note: Continuously updated data page with no discrete editions: the standard prescribes a periodicity and a timeliness per data category, and the page is refreshed as each category releases. The number is the renderer convention decided 2026-08-18 (HANDOFF section 7) — a nominal releases_per_year so the pulse reads as continuous rather than one-off; 250 encodes business-day updating. It is a statement of continuous flow, not a claim of counted editions.

_dropped.edge: THE NSDP BLOCK ITSELF — 81 first-party National Summary Data Pages, 71 wired, 9 not
_dropped.why: MINTED 2026-09-07 (round 8), on Thomas's go, executing the largest open finding of round 7. The IMF's list endpoints populate `NSDPUrl` for all 49 SDDS and all 32 SDDS Plus rows and for none of the 110 e-GDDS rows, so 81 National Summary Data Pages are named by the IMF itself. All 81 URLs were fetched, in two passes. The first read 66 from the sandbox and 4 more in Thomas's own Chrome (China, Colombia, Malta, Brazil); the second, after Thomas offered his browser mid-round, recovered six more that no plain fetcher could reach (Argentina, Switzerland, the Philippines, Lithuania, Namibia, Senegal) and is why six leads written earlier in this same file now read RESOLVED. Nine are still unwired. 70 NSDP nodes minted plus one edge onto the NSDP node the corpus already had (`ru-minfin-nsdp-fiscal`), for 71 edges: 45 A, 23 B, 3 C. THE GRADES ARE THE GRADER'S, NOT MINE. Every edge that a sandbox fetch could reach was graded by `scripts/grade-evidence.ts --slice`, and where its verdict differed from the hand grade the grader won: nineteen edges moved, all downward, most of them SDDS Plus pages that name the tier only as 'SDDS Plus'. THAT IS THE ROUND'S ONE REAL MATCHER FINDING: `namesTarget`'s acronym branch requires the parenthetical to be all upper case (`/^[\p{Lu}\p{N}][\p{Lu}\p{N}.\- ]*$/`), so `(SDDS)` fires and `(SDDS Plus)` never can — the lower-case 'lus' disqualifies it. Nine SDDS Plus pages that say 'SDDS Plus' in their own heading therefore grade agency-not-artefact. Not fixed here: it is a change to the matcher and needs Thomas's ruling, and it is recorded in HANDOFF. WHY THESE ARE SELF-DECLARED AND THE ROUND-7 EDGES ARE NOT: rule 19 judges by authorship, and an NSDP is written by the country's own statistical system. WHAT THE EDGE ASSERTS, since the corpus has ruled twice that a dissemination tier is a country-wide status and not a property of one publication (Guatemala, centralamerica-new-2026-08.json; Argentina, this round's round-7 basis): the claim here is not the country's membership, it is that the SDDS prescribes which data categories THIS page carries, at what periodicity and with what timeliness. That is a methodology dependency of the page, and it is why the NSDP is a better anchor than an institutional stub — round 7's own words. TWENTY-SIX OF THESE COUNTRIES ALREADY CARRY A TIER EDGE from an institutional or publication node (AM AR BY CR EG GE ID IL JO JP KG KZ LK MA MN MU MX MY PH RU SA SG TH TN TR ZA). Six of those older edges cite the very page this round minted as a node — `ph-reserves -> imf-sdds` and `sa-national-accounts -> imf-sdds` cite the Philippine and Saudi NSDPs, `jp-cpi -> imf-sdds-plus` cites Japan's, and three `-> ru-minfin-nsdp-fiscal` edges cite Russia's — so those documents were already in the evidence store and every live edge on them was re-selected when this round's records were written, per the 2026-09-05 rule about one URL backing several edges. Those edges were NOT retargeted and NOT dropped: they are correct, they were checked both ways in round 7, and rule 13 says a fresh finding does not silently override a live edge. The result is that those countries carry two edges into the same tier node from two different documents — a REGISTER one about the country and a SELF-DECLARED one about the page. If Thomas would rather have one per country, the fix is to drop the older REGISTER edge, not this block, and it is one pass over this note's list.

_dropped.edge: the null-ComplianceDate class — nine edges, ruled 2026-09-07
_dropped.why: RULED AND EXECUTED 2026-09-07, same day it was raised. This entry parked the question of what a null ComplianceDate supports, because the corpus was saying two things: round 4b REFUSED Libya, Lebanon and Haiti on a null 'Date e-GDDS NSDP First Posted', while six live edges (af-nsia, ye-cso, sy-cbs, ir-sci, iq-cso, sd-cbs) stood on exactly the same null. **Thomas ruled the refusal, not the allowance**: all six are dropped, records in crossborder-standards-2026-08-22.json, and Libya/Lebanon/Haiti stay refused. The corpus now says one thing about the class. THE ARGUMENT, because it generalises past the e-GDDS: participation and implementation are two different facts, and `methodology_depends_on` asserts the second. The IMF states both in one sentence of Country Report 25/270 — a country 'participates in the Enhanced General Data Dissemination (e-GDDS) and first posted its metadata in April 2009 but is yet to disseminate the data recommended under the e-GDDS.' A membership is not a dependency. AND AN ARGUMENT THAT WAS TESTED AND FAILED, worth recording so nobody re-derives it: all six edges cite documents predating the e-GDDS (in force 2015-07-01) that name the GDDS, so this looked like a wrong-target call answerable with an `imf-gdds` edition node under the §7 edition rule. It is not — that same Algeria sentence shows the IMF counting a 2009 GDDS-era posting as e-GDDS participation, because participants rolled over rather than rejoining. Measured while checking it: 33 of the 34 null-ComplianceDate participants posted before 2015-07-01, Aruba (2017-08-16) being the only country that joined under the e-GDDS itself and still never posted an NSDP. The sub-question about `sd-cbs` being an A where the identical `iq-cso` quote was capped at B is answered by the same ruling: both edges are gone, so the inconsistency is gone with them. `dz-ons-ipc-monthly -> imf-e-gdds` is deliberately kept — its quote names the Enhanced GDDS directly and it is already the weaker `cites` relation with non-implementation stated in its own basis.

_dropped.why: CONSEQUENCE OF THE 2026-09-07 RULING, recorded because it is the shape that invites a future round to re-mint the very edge that was just refused. Dropping the six null-ComplianceDate edges left FIVE institutional nodes with no edges in either direction — `sd-cbs` (Central Bureau of Statistics, Sudan), `ye-cso` (Central Statistical Organization, Yemen), `sy-cbs` (Central Bureau of Statistics, Syria), `iq-cso` (Central Statistical Organization / Authority of Statistics and GIS, Iraq) and `ir-sci` (Statistical Centre of Iran). `af-nsia` keeps other edges and is unaffected. The corpus's ISOLATED count goes 974 -> 979. THAT IS THE CORRECT OUTCOME, not a regression: the e-GDDS edge was these nodes' only connection, and it was the edge the ruling found is not a dependency. Keeping a false edge to avoid an orphan is precisely what the assertion-only ruling of 2026-08-31 exists to stop. FOR THE NEXT ROUND THAT LOOKS AT THEM: the refusals are recorded source/target-shaped in crossborder-standards-2026-08-22.json, so a rule-14 collision scan will find them — read the reason before proposing a tier edge for any of these five. They are legitimate thin-coverage leads in the other direction: each is a real NSO whose own releases are unresearched, and an edge FROM one of their publications TO a methodology standard is exactly what would connect them honestly.

_note: Thomas, 2026-09-06: 'chase all of the round 3 leads' — the cheapest of them. Two UN standards that every national trade release and every government-finance release in this corpus could cite were simply absent, each already quoted at A grade by a document read during round 2: IMTS (the trade-statistics sibling of SNA 2008 and BPM6) and COFOG (the expenditure-by-function sibling of COICOP, which the corpus already carries). This slice mints both and wires whatever the national methodology documents actually say — which turned out to be much less than the leads suggested, because most trade and GFS publishers describe themselves as following 'international standards' or 'United Nations recommendations' without ever naming the manual. Both editions were established by reading UNSD rather than assumed: COFOG's current operational version is the 1999 revision (UNSD registry: Year Adopted 1999, Year Published 2000; a further revision is not expected before 2028), and IMTS 2010 is still current (a successor referred to by UNSD as IMTS 2026 was not yet adopted when this was read). Every url and evidence_url was raw-verified HTTP 200 and every quote re-fetched and substring-checked against the live cited URL after this file was written.

reports.title: International Merchandise Trade Statistics: Concepts and Definitions 2010
reports.publisher: United Nations Department of Economic and Social Affairs, Statistics Division
reports.description: The United Nations' global recommendation for compiling and disseminating statistics on trade in goods, issued as Statistical Papers Series M No. 52, Revision 3 and superseding Revision 2 of 1998. It sets the definitions national compilers use for coverage, the general and special trade systems, statistical territory, valuation, quantity measurement, partner-country attribution and commodity classification, harmonised as far as possible with the recommendations for trade in services, balance of payments and national accounts. It is the trade-statistics counterpart of SNA 2008 and BPM6.
reports.cadence_note: Not a periodic release. A standing recommendation revised roughly once a decade: Revision 2 (1998) superseded by IMTS 2010 (Revision 3, published 2011), which UNSD's methodology page still listed as the current Concepts and Definitions volume when read on 2026-09-06. A successor UNSD refers to as IMTS 2026 was in preparation and not yet adopted.
title_aliases: Estadísticas del Comercio Internacional de Mercancías

reports.title: Classification of the Functions of Government (COFOG)
reports.description: The United Nations classification of government outlays by function or socio-economic objective — general public services, defence, public order and safety, economic affairs, environmental protection, housing and community amenities, health, recreation, education and social protection. It is one of the four classifications of expenditure according to purpose published together as Statistical Papers Series M No. 84, alongside COICOP, COPNI and COPP. First published in 1980 and revised in 1999, it is the functional breakdown embedded in SNA 2008, ESA 2010 and the IMF's GFSM 2014, and the one national government-finance releases either apply directly or adapt into a national variant.
reports.cadence_note: Not a periodic release. Structural revision only: first published 1980, revised 1999 (the current operational version; UNSD's registry records Year Adopted 1999, Year Published 2000). A revision is under way under the UN Committee of Experts' Task Team on COFOG, which UNSD anticipates completing by 2028.

Note for the record that an edition-bound node WAS available and was declined on the documents, not for want of a current edition: SITC Rev.4 (2006) is live and reads 'Status: Operational' in UNSD's classification registry (Family/Detail/28, read 2026-09-09); Rev.3 (Detail/14) is the superseded one. reports.title: Standard International Trade Classification (SITC)
reports.description: The United Nations' commodity classification for international merchandise trade, grouping traded goods by material, processing stage, market practice and end use so that trade can be analysed rather than merely tariffed. It is the analytical counterpart to the HS, which is the collection nomenclature: countries collect customs data on HS codes and convert to SITC for comparison and long-run series, which is exactly what the Chinese yearbooks wired here do. Held at family level deliberately — the documents in this corpus that cite it name no revision. Revisions: original 1950, Rev.1 (1961), Rev.2 (1975), Rev.3 (1986) and Rev.4, accepted by the UN Statistical Commission at its thirty-seventh session in March 2006 and recommended by the Interagency Task Force on International Merchandise Trade Statistics for analytical use.
reports.cadence_note: Five editions in fifty-six years and none since Rev.4 in 2006. Not an annual release; releases_per_year is nominal so the pulse rate reads as near-static, matching the treatment of `isic` and `sna-2008`.

release_schedule.note: SITC has no publication calendar and no fixed revision cycle. Rev.4 (2006) is the current edition and UNSD's classification registry records its status as Operational as of a 2026-09-09 read; no successor has been announced. Unlike ISIC, SITC is not covered by the Committee of Experts' proposed five-year ISIC/CPC revision cycle, so no computable next revision date exists.

_note: The root layer beneath the root layer: seven manuals and classifications that Canadian and US statistical agencies name in their own methodology documents, extending the two international nodes (sna-2008, icls-work-statistics-resolution) already in the graph. The shape of this slice is lopsided. NAICS is the hub — five of the eleven edges point at it, and it is the only standard both countries name for the same purpose, which makes it the strongest documented tie between the Canadian and US clusters after SNA 2008. The IMF manuals cluster tightly: a single StatCan page (13-607-X) declares that the Canadian System of Macroeconomic Accounts rests on exactly three frameworks — SNA 2008, BPM6 and the GFSM — so one document carries three edges. The lesson about evidence is that the national side almost always states the relationship more usefully than the international side, and that the giveaway phrasing is operational rather than declarative: agencies rarely write 'we conform to X', they write 'each establishment is assigned a code according to X' or footnote a specific design rule to a paragraph number in X. The weakest area is prices: neither agency treats the international CPI apparatus as governing. StatCan cites the CPI Manual but keeps its own basket classification; BLS explicitly disclaims NAICS for the CPI and produces COICOP only as a side output for the OECD.

reports.title: Consumer Price Index Manual: Concepts and Methods
reports.publisher: IMF, ILO, OECD, Eurostat, UNECE and the World Bank
reports.description: The internationally agreed manual of concepts, methods and practice for compiling a consumer price index. Jointly published by six international organisations and managed by the IMF; the 2020 edition updates the 2004 ILO-managed Consumer Price Index Manual: Theory and Practice. Country code is CA only because the schema offers no international option — the publisher is a consortium of international agencies.
reports.cadence_note: Revised roughly once a generation — editions in 1989, 2004 and 2020. Not an annual release; releases_per_year is nominal so the pulse rate reads as near-static.

release_schedule.note: No release calendar or stated periodicity exists. The Manual has been issued only three times: 1989 (ILO, 'Consumer Price Indices: An ILO Manual'), 2004 ('Consumer Price Index Manual: Theory and Practice'), and 2020 ('Consumer Price Index Manual: Concepts and Methods'), each ~15-16 years apart. The IMF's own page for this report is titled 'Update of the Consumer Price Index Manual' and explains the 2020 edition was produced because 'methods and best practices have continued to evolve' since 2004, following requests from the 2014 UNECE-ILO CPI Experts Meeting -- i.e., updates are triggered by inter-agency expert consensus, not a fixed schedule. No next-edition date or working-group timeline is published. This is consistent with the corpus's very low releases_per_year (0.06, i.e. roughly once per 16 years).

reports.title: North American Industry Classification System (NAICS)
reports.publisher: Statistics Canada, U.S. Office of Management and Budget / Economic Classification Policy Committee, and INEGI (Mexico)
reports.description: The trinational industry classification used to organise economic statistics in Canada, the United States and Mexico, using a six-digit hierarchical code. Agreed and revised jointly by the three countries' statistical agencies; each publishes its own national version (NAICS Canada, NAICS United States, SCIAN Mexico) from a common structure. It is the single classification most widely named across both countries' industry statistics.
reports.cadence_note: Revised on a five-year cycle — 1997, 2002, 2007, 2012, 2017, 2022. Not an annual release; releases_per_year is nominal.

release_schedule.note: Still formally 'proposed' pending close of public comment as of the check date (Federal Register notice 2026-14086, published 2026-07-13 — exact document URL not resolved, worth a follow-up fetch). Standing rule is a 5-year review cycle.

reports.description: The IMF's standard for compiling the balance of payments and the international investment position — the accounting framework for a country's transactions and positions with the rest of the world. reports.cadence_note: Revised roughly once a generation — BPM5 in 1993, BPM6 in 2009. Not an annual release; releases_per_year is nominal.

The dependency is load-bearing enough that NAICS revisions force revisions of the statistics themselves — the guide notes that adopting NAICS 2022 required a historical revision of SEPH estimates back to 2001, and that businesses which cannot be assigned a NAICS code are excluded from all variables except employment.

dependencies.basis: The BLS Handbook of Methods chapter on Current Employment Statistics - National, the payroll survey behind the Employment Situation release, states that all CES-N data on employment, hours and earnings are classified in accordance with the 2022 North American Industry Classification System (NAICS), as specified by the U.S. Office of Management and Budget. The industry detail published in the Employment Situation is NAICS detail.

The Guide to the Labour Force Survey (catalogue 71-543-G) defines the Industry variable as the 'General nature of the business carried out in the establishment where the person worked (main job only), based on the 2022 North American Industry Classification System (NAICS)', and states that in processing, 'industry, occupation and class of worker codes are assigned... based on the classifications described in the North American Industry Classification System (NAICS) 2022 V1.0 and the National Occupational Classification (NOC) 2021 V1.0 standards.'
dependencies.evidence_quote: Industry: General nature of the business carried out in the establishment where the person worked (main job only), based on the 2022 North American Industry Classification System (NAICS).

_dropped.why: The Canadian CPI does not use COICOP. Chapter 4 of the CPI Reference Paper describes a StatCan-specific hierarchy of roughly 700 elementary product classes rolling up to eight major aggregates (Food; Shelter; Household operations and furnishings; Clothing and footwear; Transportation; Health and personal care; Recreation, education and reading; Alcoholic beverages, tobacco products and recreational cannabis). COICOP is never named.

Explicitly denied by BLS. The Handbook of Methods CPI Concepts page states the CPI item structure 'is unique to the CPI and the categories themselves do not correspond to the North American Industry Classification System (NAICS), other price indexes, or other statistics.' A documented non-dependency.

Searched hard and did not find it. The BLS Handbook of Methods CPI chapters (Overview, Concepts, Data sources, Design, Calculation, More Info) never cite the ILO/IMF Consumer Price Index Manual; the Concepts chapter grounds the CPI in the cost-of-living-index framework and cites no international manual at all. The only BLS documents that reference the manual are OSMR research working papers, which are not methodology statements for the release. So the CPI Manual sits under statcan-cpi but not under bls-cpi — an asymmetry, not an oversight.

ADDENDUM 2026-09-07 (round 8, the NSDP block). THE ANCHOR THIS ENTRY ASKED FOR NOW EXISTS. It said in as many words that 'the only clean anchor would be a new StatCan node (the NSDP) with no other connections', and round 7 quoted that sentence back when it found the IMF's list endpoint populates NSDPUrl for all 32 SDDS Plus rows. `ca-nsdp` was minted this round from http://www.statcan.gc.ca/pub/13-608-x/2017001/nsdp-eng.htm (which redirects to www150.statcan.gc.ca), and `ca-nsdp -> imf-sdds-plus` is live at A on StatCan's own page title, 'Canada: Economic and Financial Data - International Monetary Fund's Special Data Dissemination Standard Plus (SDDS Plus)'. THE THREE EDGES THIS ENTRY REFUSED ARE STILL REFUSED and that is deliberate: the CPI, the monthly GDP and the LFS each remain a publication with no document naming the standard, and the corpus has twice ruled a dissemination tier is a country-wide status rather than a property of one release. What changed is that Canada now has the node, not that these three releases now have the evidence. Original entry follows. Canada adheres to the IMF Special Data Dissemination Standard Plus and StatCan publishes Canada's National Summary Data Page as catalogue 13-608-X, so the relationship is real: SDDS Plus prescribes coverage, periodicity, timeliness and advance release calendars for these categories. But every document that states the obligation is IMF-side (the Dissemination Standards Bulletin Board DQAF pages, IMF press release 17/127). No StatCan methodology or release-schedule document was found saying that a given release's content or timing is governed by the SDDS. Dropped for want of national-side evidence, and because the only clean anchor would be a new StatCan node (the NSDP) with no other connections.

The direction of the documented relationship is backwards. BLS does not state that CPS employment and unemployment concepts follow the ICLS resolutions; its International Labor Comparisons methodology instead adjusts foreign countries' data 'as closely as possible to U.S. definitions'. Contrast StatCan's LFS guide, which does say its concepts 'are based on those endorsed by the International Labour Organization' — hence that edge exists in the graph and this one does not.

BEA's International Transactions Accounts are compiled on a BPM6 basis, but bea-gdp is the NIPA release, and no BEA document ties the headline GDP estimate to BPM6. Making this edge honest would require a separate BEA international accounts node, which is outside this slice.

PSAB's International Strategy points at IPSAS, not IFRS. IFRS reaches Canadian entities through the Accounting Standards Board and applies to publicly accountable enterprises rather than governments, and no node in the graph is governed by it. Included in the brief but not supportable as an edge onto psab-psas.

Removed on review, on the researching agent's own flag. BLS does publish an R-COICOP series monthly for the OECD, but it is a research series and an alternative aggregation — COICOP does not structure the headline CPI. The graph's edges describe what a release actually rests on, not every classification an agency also maps to. The COICOP node went with it, since that was its only edge. It should return if a document is found where COICOP governs a primary release.

_note: The root layer. These are not reports that consume statistics — they are the manuals that define how statistics are built, cited by name in the methodology documents of national statistical agencies. SNA 2008 is also the first documented link between the Canadian and US clusters: both national accounts programmes are built on it.

reports.title: System of National Accounts 2008 (SNA 2008)
reports.publisher: United Nations, European Commission, IMF, OECD and World Bank
reports.description: The internationally agreed standard set of concepts, definitions, classifications and accounting rules for compiling national accounts, in force 2008-2025. Superseded by the 2025 SNA (UNSC 56th Session, March 2025) — see sna-2025. Retained here because the eight reports below still cite it by name as their methodology basis; country-level rollout of the successor targets 2029-2030, so nothing downstream is factually wrong yet.
reports.cadence_note: Revised roughly once a generation — previous editions 1953, 1968 and 1993. Not an annual release; releases_per_year is nominal so the pulse rate reads as near-static.

release_schedule.note: Superseded by the 2025 SNA (UNSC 56th Session, March 2025) — see sna-2025's own published-calendar schedule for the adoption date and rollout window. No further revisions expected under the SNA 2008 edition.

reports.title: ICLS Resolution concerning statistics of work, employment and labour underutilization
reports.description: The international standard defining employment, unemployment and labour force participation. Adopted by the International Conference of Labour Statisticians; the 19th ICLS resolution of 2013 supersedes the 13th ICLS resolution of 1982.
reports.cadence_note: The ICLS convenes roughly every five years; resolutions on labour force statistics are revised far less often than that.

entries.covers: 22nd International Conference of Labour Statisticians (possible further revision/amendment of this resolution)

release_schedule.rule: The International Conference of Labour Statisticians (ICLS), which adopts and periodically revises labour statistics resolutions such as this one, is 'hosted by the ILO every five years' (per ILOSTAT's ICLS standards page). The 19th ICLS (2013) originally adopted this resolution, the 20th ICLS was held 10-19 October 2018, and the 21st ICLS (October 2023) adopted a resolution amending this very resolution.
release_schedule.note: This is a standard-setting resolution, not a periodic statistical release. It is revisited only when the ICLS (convened roughly every five years by the ILO) chooses to review or amend it, as happened at the 21st ICLS in 2023. No 22nd ICLS date has been officially announced yet as of 2026-08-11; 2028 is a computed estimate based on the 5-year cadence (2013 -> 2018 -> 2023), not a confirmed date. There is no guarantee the 22nd ICLS agenda will include a revision of this specific resolution.

reports.title: System of National Accounts 2025 (SNA 2025)
reports.publisher: United Nations, European Commission, IMF, OECD and World Bank
reports.description: The internationally agreed standard superseding SNA 2008, adopted by the UN Statistical Commission at its 56th Session (March 2025). Retains the same core double-entry accounting framework while updating treatment of digitalisation, globalisation, wellbeing/sustainability and the informal economy. Country-level implementation is targeted for 2029-2030 — as of this entry, no dependency edges have been redirected from sna-2008 to this node; that is a separate, evidence-by-evidence decision for whenever an implementing country's methodology actually switches.
reports.cadence_note: Revised roughly once a generation, following SNA 1953, 1968, 1993 and 2008. Not an annual release; releases_per_year is nominal so the pulse rate reads at the same near-static rate as sna-2008.

release_schedule.note: Adopted at the UNSC's 56th Session; the 2029-2030 window is the UN's own stated target for country-level rollout, not a guarantee.

dependencies.basis: The Canadian National Economic Accounts are compiled using SNA 2008 as the organising framework, which supplies the concepts, classifications and methods used to measure production, income, saving and investment.

The NIPAs and the SNA share a common accounting framework, and BEA prepares estimates on an SNA basis annually for the OECD questionnaire. BEA documents specific definitional departures, so this is a shared framework rather than strict conformity.
The Labour Force Survey adopts concepts and definitions of employment and unemployment endorsed by the ILO, drawn from the ICLS resolutions on labour force statistics.

relations.basis: The UN Statistical Commission adopted the 2025 SNA at its 56th Session (March 2025) as the successor to SNA 2008 — a generational revision of the same joint UN/EC/IMF/OECD/World Bank standard, not a new independent framework.

_dropped.why: Reopened per PLAYBOOK-CORPUS.md §7d and ruled 2026-09-08: no document in this family names a COICOP edition/revision at all -- the source text says bare 'COICOP' or 'nomenclature COICOP' with no year, no 'Rev.', no '2018'. Reading '2018' onto that silence is the researcher's inference, not the document's statement -- exactly the inference the corpus's own IMTS-Revision-2 refusal (round5-little-things-2026-09-06.json _dropped) exists to block, and the same standard that required un-coicop-hbs-1999 and un-coicop-2018 themselves to only be minted where a country's own document spelled out the edition by name (CAPMAS's 'COICOP-HBS 2000/1999', South Africa's 'the 2018 version of ... COICOP'). Here the case against 2018 is stronger than silence alone: the bulletin's own base year is 2012 (predating COICOP 2018's 2018 publication) and its 12-division structure matches the pre-2018 vintage, not the restructured 2018 revision -- the evidence points away from the very target it was wired to. Dropping rather than keeping the caveated wire: three rounds converging on the same 'wire with a vintage caveat' shape doesn't make it consistent with the rule those rounds were themselves trying to honour.

reports.title: Statistical Centre of Iran (SCI) institutional core
reports.description: Primary national statistical office responsible for censuses, surveys, national accounts, prices, labour, demographic and multi-domain socio-economic statistics.
reports._notes: Foundational institutional node for the Iranian statistical system.
reports._cadence_evidence: amar.org.ir homepage retrieved (most attempts time out). It shows only a dated news item (29 Tir 1397) and a reference to the 1395 Population and Housing Census; no release calendar and no stated periodicity for the office's outputs.

reports.title: Population census and estimates
reports.description: Official population census and subsequent estimates. Population is in the high-80s to low-90s millions range in recent reports; urbanisation is advanced and the age structure is shifting toward aging.
reports._notes: Core demographic node. Population ~87–93 million depending on source and reference year.
reports._cadence_evidence: Same amar.org.ir homepage. It names the 'General Population and Housing Census 1395' but states no census interval and gives no cadence for population estimates; a single census year is not countable evidence.

reports.title: National Accounts of Iran (GDP)
reports.description: Official national accounts (GDP by industry and expenditure). Central macro-output series for an oil-and-gas-influenced, sanctions-affected economy.
reports._notes: Primary macroeconomic output node.
reports._url_evidence: CBI page titled 'Annual National Accounts' (حساب‌های ملی سالانه) describing GDP time series at current and constant prices with base years 1383/1390/1395.
reports._cadence_evidence: cbi.ir/simplelist/2054.aspx (CBI National Accounts collection) states it publishes 'ارقام حسابهای ملی سالانه و فصلی' - annual and quarterly national accounts figures - with base-year revisions (latest 1395). Quarterly is the highest cadence the page states, so 4 releases/yr for the series; the annual volume is a subset of that.

reports.title: Consumer Price Index and inflation statistics
reports.description: Monthly CPI and inflation rates. Iran has experienced prolonged high inflation; the CPI series is a critical high-frequency price and welfare signal.
reports._notes: Core high-frequency price node. High inflation environment gives this series elevated centrality.

reports.title: Central Bank of the Islamic Republic of Iran institutional and reporting core

reports._cadence_evidence: cbi.ir root timed out repeatedly; the English landing page that did answer lists Economic Trends, Annual Review, Economic Report & Balance Sheet and 'Monetary, Financial and Economic Statistics' but states no frequency for any of them except the implied yearly Annual Review, and gives no release calendar for the institution as a whole.

reports._cadence_evidence: cbi.ir/category/2693.aspx lists successive Persian-calendar monthly PDF editions (Farvardin, Ordibehesht, Khordad, Tir) of the balance-of-payments / customs trade / external debt tables - one edition per month.

reports._notes: Youth densification of the labour cluster.
reports._url_evidence: Retrieved PDF: Statistical Centre of Iran, 'Summary of Labour Force Survey results, Autumn 1398', issued by the Office of Population, Labour Force and Census Statistics. Contains the youth series explicitly: unemployment rate for the 15-24 age group 25.8% (down 1.2 pp y/y), 18-35 age group 17.9%, overall unemployment 10.6%, participation rate 44.3%.

reports.publisher: CBI / Ministry of Petroleum / shipping trackers
reports.description: Export volumes and estimated values for crude and petroleum products. Export levels fluctuate sharply with sanctions enforcement, buyer willingness (notably China), and shipping constraints. Strait of Hormuz remains the primary route.
