reports.title: Puntland Ministry of Finance — Budget Archive (Enacted Budgets, Appropriation Acts, Budget Framework & Outlook Papers)
reports.publisher: Puntland State Government of Somalia, Ministry of Finance
reports.region: Puntland (Federal Member State of the Federal Republic of Somalia)
reports.description: Real, currently-maintained, downloadable primary-source budget archive confirming an active state-level (Federal Member State) fiscal system for Puntland. Site navigation (mof.pl.so homepage) lists "Budget Department," "Budget Archive," "Citizen's Budget," "Budget Framework Paper," "Budget Outlook Paper," "Financial Reports 2017–2025," and "JPLG." The Budget Archive download listing (checked 2026-08-13, cross-checked against saved page source) includes: "Enacted Budget 2026" (3.35 MB), "Draft-Appropriation-Act-for-2026-Budget" (1.36 MB), "Executives-Budget-Proposal-FY26" (1.36 MB), "Puntland Budget 2020," "Puntaland Budget for 2019," and "PSS Budget Appropriation Act- Somali Version." Jurisdiction-level note: classified here as "provincial" per this file's schema convention because Puntland is a Federal Member State government, not the Federal Government of Somalia itself — Puntland identifies itself as part of the Federal Republic of Somalia (unlike Somaliland, which asserts independence), so this is a sub-national node within Somalia's federal hierarchy, not a separate country's national budget. Scope limit: this is state (FMS)-tier documentation only — no Puntland district-level (e.g. Garowe, Bosaso) government budgets were found on this site; the site's own "JPLG" (Joint Programme on Local Governance) page, which is the section that would house local/district governance-finance content, reads only "JPLG Home JPLG Coming Soon…", i.e. explicitly unpopulated as of the check date.

reports.title: Federal Government of Somalia — Budget Framework Paper for FY 2025 (revised v15)
reports.publisher: Federal Government of Somalia, Ministry of Finance
reports.description: Real, verbatim, primary-source FGS document. Page 25, paragraph 46 (own-source revenue forecast discussion), reads: "the ongoing tax enforcement drive that continues to utilize Benaadir Regional Authority's database of property ownership to register and require landlords to pay rental income tax." This documents the FGS using Benadir Regional Authority's (BRA's) property-ownership database for federal rental-income-tax collection — it is NOT a BRA-authored municipal budget or fiscal-transfer document. Explicit correction recorded here: an earlier WebFetch summary of this same PDF, produced mid-research, claimed the document contained "Benadir Regional Administration" fiscal-transfer figures in the range of $13.65M–$31.64M. This was checked directly against the extracted PDF text and found to be FABRICATED — no such figures or content exist anywhere in the document. The document's only other Benadir/Banadir-adjacent reference is to "Banadir Regional Court" (budget code 011002), a federal judicial entity unrelated to municipal finance. See this file's _dropped list for the full record of that hallucination near-miss.

reports.title: Financial Governance Reports — Inter-Governmental Fiscal Relations (FGS & FMS)
reports.publisher: Federal Government of Somalia, Ministry of Finance / Somalia Financial Governance Committee
reports.description: Real, currently active FGS-FMS intergovernmental fiscal reporting apparatus. The Financial Governance Reports listing page includes menu items "Consolidated Fiscal Reports (FGS & FMS)" and "Inter-governmental Fiscal Federalism Forum" under an "Inter-Governmental Relations" section, with recent meeting records through January 2026. The related Budget Directorate department page states: "The Department is responsible for coordinating with all Federal Member States on the draft budget, including funds in accordance with the strategic objectives, programs, activities, and strategic performance indicators." Scope limit: this apparatus is documented only down to Federal Member State (e.g. Puntland) granularity — no district- or municipal-level (e.g. Benadir/Mogadishu) fiscal-transfer mechanism is described in these FGS Ministry of Finance publications.

reports.title: Ministry of Finance & Economic Development — Official Portal (Republic of Somaliland)
reports.publisher: Ministry of Finance & Economic Development, Republic of Somaliland
reports.region: Somaliland (self-declared "Republic of Somaliland"; de facto separate administration in northwestern Somalia, not treated as part of the Federal Government of Somalia's own national-tier hierarchy)
reports.description: Real, active government finance-ministry site. Homepage (slmof.org) self-describes as: "Official portal of the Ministry of Finance & Economic Development, Republic of Somaliland" / "managing public finances, national budget planning, revenue collection, expenditure control, and economic policy development" — verbatim quotes confirmed against saved page source. It explicitly self-identifies as "Republic of Somaliland" (asserting sovereign statehood), which is why this node is flagged as distinct from the Federal Government of Somalia's own national-tier claims rather than merged into them; classified as "provincial" here per this file's schema convention for Somalia's de facto sub-national/parallel administrations. A related About page states: "The Ministry of Finance Development derives its mandate from the Constitution of Somaliland, which provides for proper budgetary and expenditure management of the government financial resources" — no mention of local government, district, or municipal fiscal relations appears in that mandate text. An older/parallel portal (mofd.govsomaliland.org) references Minister Dr. Saad Ali Shire and an IFMIS (Integrated Financial Management Information System) for national government finance, with no local/municipal content found there either. IMPORTANT LIMITATION: this node captures only the ministry's self-description; the site's own "Budget Documents" page (/budget/) could NOT have its actual document titles or figures extracted — it is a JavaScript/Next.js single-page application that loads its document list client-side, so static fetch tools only retrieved the app shell, not the rendered list. This is recorded as a technical/tooling limitation, not as evidence that no such documents exist — flagged inconclusive rather than NOT FOUND (see _dropped for the specific unreadable-source record).

_dropped.why: Preserved as a methodological finding per task instructions, not silently dropped. Mid-research, a WebFetch tool call against the FGS Budget Framework Paper for FY 2025 (revised v15) returned a summary claiming the document contained "Benadir Regional Administration" fiscal-transfer figures of roughly $13.65M–$31.64M. This claim was independently verified against the actual extracted PDF text (page 25, paragraph 46, and a full text search of the document) and found to be FABRICATED — no such figures, and no content resembling them, exist anywhere in the real document. The real document's only relevant content is the sentence about the FGS tax-enforcement drive using "Benaadir Regional Authority's database of property ownership" to collect rental income tax (now captured verbatim in so-fgs-budget-framework-paper-fy2025's description), plus an unrelated reference to "Banadir Regional Court" (budget code 011002, a federal judicial line item). No figure from the hallucinated summary was used anywhere in this file's report nodes.

No node minted for Benadir Regional Administration / Mogadishu municipal government finance. Verdict: NOT FOUND, with a specific documented reason. bra.gov.so's live homepage currently returns only "Sorry, we're doing some work on the site... We are doing some work on the site and will be back shortly" (checked 2026-08-13, cross-checked against saved page source, which shows no under-construction text confirming the page is presently blank/near-empty). A Wayback Machine snapshot of a page literally titled "Budget Allocation-Q3" (https://web.archive.org/web/20241114010300/https://bra.gov.so/ova_doc/budget-allocation-q3/) contains only generic Ovatheme WordPress demo/lorem-ipsum text ("We help our clients to build their best possible economic... Thomas Edison may have been behind the invention of the electric light bulb...") unrelated to any real budget. A snapshot of the Finance & Economic Planning department page (https://web.archive.org/web/20240804142134/https://bra.gov.so/departments/finance-economic-planning/) lists a placeholder contact "finance@email.com" with generic boilerplate reused verbatim across multiple department pages. Wayback CDX index for that same department page shows its last successful (200) snapshot was 2024-08-04, with a 2025-05-05 snapshot returning HTTP 404, consistent with progressive site abandonment rather than removal of real content. Combined, these confirm bra.gov.so is a government-registered domain that appears to have never held authentic financial content — a documentable "facade e-government presence" finding, not merely an absence of records. A separate World Bank ESMP document for the Benadir Urban Resilience Project II likewise contains no BRA financial statements, revenue figures, or PFM capacity assessment (only a forward-looking, non-binding reference to future district-level operating budgets), and is in any case a World Bank (non-primary) document.

SONNA (Somali National News Agency, state-owned) reported that "Banadir Municipality approves $101.3 million budget for 2025" (https://sonna.so/en/banadir-municipality-approves-101-3-million-budget-for-2025), quoting a Deputy Governor statement from a Dec 30, 2024 approval ceremony. This is the closest thing found to public confirmation that Banadir Municipality has an actual budget figure for 2025, but SONNA is a news agency, not a government-authored primary document, and the article links to no actual budget document. Excluded per the corpus evidence rule (primary government documents only); no figure from this article was used in any report node.

World Bank, "Local Governments and Federalism in Somalia: Fitting the Pieces Together" (June 2023), p.35 footnote 46, states: "The status of the Banadir Regional Administration (BRA) is yet to be defined. It either becomes the administrative capital or a fully fledged FMS. Currently, 15 percent of customs revenues is given to the BRA as a budget support." Per explicit task instruction, this World Bank report is not a primary Somali-government source and cannot be used as a corpus evidence_url — it may only be cited as context/a lead, never as evidence for a report node or dependency. No primary underlying revenue-sharing agreement or decree establishing this 15% figure could be located this round, so no node or edge was created from it.

Puntland district-level (e.g. Garowe, Bosaso) government budgets are NOT FOUND on mof.pl.so. The specific mechanism is documented: the site's "JPLG" (Joint Programme on Local Governance) page — the section that would house exactly this local/district governance-finance content — reads only "JPLG Home JPLG Coming Soon…", confirming the gap is a known, unpopulated placeholder on an otherwise well-functioning, currently-maintained ministry site, rather than the absence of any government fiscal apparatus at all.

Somaliland MOF's "Budget Documents" page (https://www.slmof.org/budget/) could not have its actual document titles or figures extracted this round. The page is a JavaScript/Next.js single-page application that loads its document list client-side; static fetch tools (WebFetch, curl) retrieved only the app shell, not the rendered document list. This is a tooling limitation, not evidence of absence — flagged inconclusive rather than NOT FOUND. A browser-rendering tool would likely surface real PDFs here in a future round.

A UNCDF secondary article (https://www.uncdf.org/article/7867/local-government-rising-somalias-fiscal-decentralisation-success-story, not itself a primary document, cited only as a lead) references "Somaliland Law No. 23 on Regions and District Self-Government, especially Articles 88 and 89" and a "District Grants Regulation No. 01/2020" issued by Somaliland's Ministry of the Interior, and names Puntland districts Bosaso, Garowe, and Burtinle with LDF grant figures. These would be exactly the right documents to check for Somaliland's municipal/district fiscal-legal framework, but the primary text of either instrument could not be located on any Somaliland government domain within the available tool budget this round: guessed domains for a Somaliland Ministry of Interior/Local Government site (molg.gov.so, molg.govsomaliland.org, interior.govsomaliland.org, mopic.govsomaliland.org) all failed to resolve via the proxy, and www.govsomaliland.online failed with ROBOTS_DISALLOWED/DNS error. Flagged as inconclusive/needs follow-up rather than NOT FOUND, since a specific, named document trail exists and simply wasn't reachable this round.

The same World Bank report (p.37 Table 3 source line: "Source: FGS 2021 Budget Appropriation Act and FY2020 Financial Statement."; p.39 Table 5 source line: "Source: Budget execution report from the HSS Ministry of Finance website.") cites a Hirshabelle State (HSS) Ministry of Finance website as a primary source. Attempted to locate that site directly at two guessed domains (hssmof.gov.so, mof.hirshabelle.gov.so); both failed DNS/proxy resolution this round, so the HSS source could not be independently verified beyond the World Bank's citation of it, and no node was minted.

The Federal Government of Somalia's Ministry of Finance documents federal-to-Federal-Member-State (FGS↔FMS) transfers thoroughly (Budget Directorate page, Financial Governance Reports listing), but district- or municipal-level (sub-FMS) transfer mechanisms are NOT FOUND anywhere in FGS Ministry of Finance publications checked this round.

Both nodes are topically related (FGS's Budget Directorate explicitly states it coordinates with all Federal Member States, including Puntland, on the draft budget), but no FGS Ministry of Finance document reviewed this round names or cites Puntland's mof.pl.so budget archive, or any specific Puntland budget document, by title, URL, or date. Per the standing evidence rule (a verbatim textual citation is required to support a dependency edge), this is a genuine NOT FOUND for a documented citation edge despite the plausible institutional relationship.

Somalia National Bureau of Statistics CPI methodological note (https://nbs.gov.so/somalia-cpi-methodological-note/) contains genuine, verified new primary-source content not captured in this file: "Expanding geographic coverage to all Federal Member States (FMS) and Somaliland"; "In most states, data collection activities are concentrated in the capital city, whereas in Puntland, the exercise extends to three cities—Garowe, Bosaso, and Galkayo"; and a transition "from COICOP 1999 to the latest COICOP 2018 classification." This was a secondary objective of this research round and is out of scope for this file's Puntland/Benadir/MOF focus; deferred rather than incorporated, since an existing so-snbs-cpi node already exists elsewhere in the corpus (af-synthesis.json) and updating it is outside this file's remit. Logged here so the finding is not lost.

Full list of guessed URLs checked that failed outright this round, for the record: https://puntlandgovernment.com, https://www.puntland.gov.so, https://mopic.puntland.gov.so, https://mofpuntland.com, https://puntland.gov.so (all failed resolution; the real Puntland MOF domain turned out to be mof.pl.so, found via search); https://molg.govsomaliland.org, https://interior.govsomaliland.org, https://molg.gov.so, https://www.molg.gov.so, https://mopic.govsomaliland.org (guessed Somaliland local-government domains, none resolved); https://hssmof.gov.so, https://mof.hirshabelle.gov.so (guessed Hirshabelle State MOF domains, none resolved); https://www.govsomaliland.online/ (ROBOTS_DISALLOWED/DNS error); https://web.archive.org/web/2024*/bra.gov.so wildcard query (PROXY_REJECTED 403, worked around via direct Wayback CDX API instead, results captured in the so-bra-municipal-budget dropped entry above).

_dropped.why: [EDITION-AMBIGUOUS] PBS's own CPI methodology PDF (base 2015-16) names 'Classification of Individual Consumption on Purpose (COICOP)' but never states an edition/year (not 1999, not 2018). Verified live at https://www.pbs.gov.pk/wp-content/uploads/2020/07/methodology_of_price_statistics_base_year_2015-16.pdf. the import proposed the 1999 edition based on no more evidence than we found; per the edition-matching rule we will not guess. Needs a document that names the edition to resolve.

RESOLVED 2026-09-05 (DSBB SoM scripted import): the compiling agency's own IMF DSBB Summary of Methodology names the standard; the edge is now live in src/data/research/dsbb-som-import-2026-09-05.json. Earlier entry: [DEAD-URL / CONFLICTING] the import's cited URL (sbp.org.pk/publications/bop/BOPFY24/Intro.pdf) now 404s/redirects to SBP's generic publications listing, which shows Pakistan's BOP report has moved to Excel-archive-only distribution with no visible methodology note. SBP's site confirms the report itself is real (Annual, FY24) so we mint the node, but we could not find a live document naming BPM6. The IMF DSBB metadata API (getBaseSummaryofMethodologies, countryCode=PAK, categoryCode=BOP00) actually states the opposite — 'The framework of Pakistan's balance of payments follows the guidelines and recommendations of BPM5' with BPM6 described as 'under consideration' — but this DSBB snapshot also looks stale (compare Bhutan/Bangladesh cases below) so we don't trust it as current either. Net: can't currently verify either way.

ADDENDUM 2026-09-07 (round 7, the IMF tier sweep). The fact this entry could not confirm is now confirmed from a first-party record: the IMF's e-GDDS Important Dates page, read in Chrome, gives 'Bangladesh March 29, 2001 October 8, 2017' — metadata posted 2001, e-GDDS NSDP first posted 2017. THIS REFUSAL STILL STANDS AS WRITTEN, on both of its grounds: a dissemination tier is a country-wide status and not a property of the national accounts release, and this round did not revisit the stale DSBB national-accounts metadata for BGD that the entry rightly distrusted. The edge is minted at the institutional level instead, as bd-bbs -> imf-e-gdds at grade A in int-imf-tier-sweep-2026-09-07.json. || ORIGINAL ENTRY FOLLOWS. || [NOT-FOUND] Could not find an IMF press release or working DSBB page confirming Bangladesh's e-GDDS/NSDP implementation the way we could for Pakistan/Nepal/Bhutan/Maldives. the import's cited DSBB URL (dsbb.imf.org/e-gdds/country/BGD/summary-of-dissemination) is a JS shell with no retrievable content, and the DSBB API for BGD/NAG00 returned what appears to be stale legacy metadata (citing '1993 SNA' and a base year of 1995-96, contradicted by BBS's own current 2015-16-base, SNA-2008 documents), so we don't trust it as evidence of current dissemination-tier status either.

[EDITION-AMBIGUOUS] BBS's own live CPI (base 2021-22) methodology document states items are classified into '12 major categories' using COICOP but never names an edition/year. Verified at https://objectstorage.ap-dcc-gazipur-1.oraclecloud15.com/n/axvjbnqprylg/b/V2Ministry/o/office-bbs/2024/12/f886ed6c67b0411783a01c4039e6b141.pdf (BBS's own object storage, linked from bbs.gov.bd). The DSBB API for BGD/CPI00 separately returned an apparently stale description citing 'eight commodity groups', further evidence DSBB metadata for Bangladesh cannot be trusted as current. Not enough to pick an edition.

[MISMATCHED-SOURCE / EDITION-AMBIGUOUS] the import's cited evidence_url (statistics.gov.lk/Resource/refference/SriLankaNSSReviewReport) turned out on live fetch to mention COICOP only in a National Accounts classification-systems list, not in connection with the CPI at all — a mismatched citation. We separately checked DCS's own NCPI February 2022 release directly, which describes '12 main groups' in the CPI basket but never names COICOP or an edition anywhere in the document. Can't mint without a document that ties COICOP (with an edition) specifically to the CCPI/NCPI.

[SITE-UNREACHABLE / CONFLICTING] nsb.gov.bt's document subpaths (including the import's cited NAS-2024-for-WEB.pdf and every other nsb.gov.bt/publications or /wp-content path we tried) consistently failed to fetch with SSL/robots errors, even though the site's root page loads fine — the National Statistics Bureau's own PDFs are effectively unreadable to us right now. As a check we queried the IMF DSBB metadata API (countryCode=BTN, categoryCode=NAG00), which actually states Bhutan's national accounts 'broadly follow the United Nations System of National Accounts 1968' — directly conflicting with the import's claimed SNA-2008 quote, and looking itself like stale/legacy GDDS metadata never updated. We could not adjudicate between these with a live, readable source, so we drop the edge rather than guess. bt-national-accounts as a report node is still minted — the Q3 2025 GDP report's existence is independently confirmed on the NSB homepage.

[SITE-UNREACHABLE] Same nsb.gov.bt access problem as bt-national-accounts — the import's cited CPI_July-report.pdf and every alternative NSB publication path we tried failed to fetch. The DSBB API for BTN/CPI00 loaded but only described '363 items... aggregated into 12 major groups' with no mention of COICOP or an edition at all, so it doesn't corroborate the import's 1999-edition claim either. bt-cpi as a report node is still minted — the November 2025 CPI release's existence is independently confirmed on the NSB homepage.

[CONTRADICTED] the import claimed BPM6 (citing an MMA 'shift from BPM5'), but the IMF DSBB metadata API (countryCode=MDV, categoryCode=BOP00) — the same class of source the import cited — currently and explicitly states: 'The balance of payments statistics are compiled broadly following the guidelines recommended in the IMF's Balance of Payments Manual, fifth edition (BPM5).' No BPM6 language appears anywhere in that document. mma.gov.mv's own statistics pages are robots-disallowed to us so we could not independently adjudicate further; on the evidence we could reach, BPM5 (not BPM6) is what's actually stated. mv-mma-bop as a report node is still minted since MMA's compilation of BOP/external-sector statistics itself is corroborated by this same DSBB page and by the 'External Sector' category on mma.gov.mv's homepage.

[NAME-CHANGE] the import proposed 'mv-nbs' / 'National Bureau of Statistics (Maldives)'. The live statisticsmaldives.gov.mv site now identifies itself as the 'Maldives Bureau of Statistics' (MBS), and a Presidency of Maldives press release (20 July 2021, on the Maldives Statistics Act, Act No. 16/2021) confirms the agency's resources, staff and obligations were transferred from the former National Bureau of Statistics to the new, independent Maldives Bureau of Statistics, headed by a Chief Statistician. We minted the institution as 'mv-mbs' / 'Maldives Bureau of Statistics' to match current reality rather than the import's proposed id/name.

reports.title: National Accounts / GDP
reports.description: System of national accounts. Mining (gold) and oil dominate value-added and exports; economy experienced a deep crisis in the early 2020s with large real per-capita GDP decline.
reports._notes: Core macroeconomic product. Mining and oil account for a large share of GDP and ~90% of exports. Per-capita GDP fell sharply from the mid-2010s peak; offshore oil is expected to produce a step-change from ~2028.

reports.title: Gold production and exports
reports.description: Gold mining and export statistics. Current backbone of the extractive economy alongside onshore oil.
reports._notes: Primary current extractive earner. Together with oil, accounts for the large majority of merchandise exports and a major share of GDP.

reports.title: Consumer Price Index / Inflation
reports.description: Consumer price index and inflation measures. High and persistent inflation has been a defining feature of the early-2020s crisis period.
reports._notes: Flagship price statistic under stress. Annual inflation ran above 50% for an extended period; stabilisation remains a central policy objective.

reports.title: Poverty measurement
reports.description: Poverty headcount and related indicators. Crisis-period deterioration was more severe for less-educated and interior households; recent estimates place poverty in the mid-teens to higher range depending on the line used.
reports._notes: Social-outcome node. Interior (hinterland) and less-educated households were hit hardest in the crisis; ABS participates in methodological work on multidimensional poverty.

reports.title: Paramaribo — capital metropolitan core
reports.description: Capital city and primary urban, commercial and administrative centre. Dominant demographic and economic concentration.
reports._notes: Lived urban core. Continuously appears as the main geographic domain in household and labour statistics.

reports.title: Population and Housing Census
reports.description: Decennial population and housing census. Provides the demographic baseline and sampling frames for household surveys.
reports._notes: Foundational demographic product. Population on the order of 0.6–0.7 million; supports national accounts rebasing and SDG indicator updates.

reports.title: Interior districts (Sipaliwini, Brokopondo, Para)
reports.description: Interior districts that hold the large majority of national land area but a small share of population. Highest concentrations of Maroon and Indigenous communities and of poverty and service gaps.
reports._notes: Structural geographic contrast. Less than 10% of population but disproportionately high shares of the poor and extreme poor; service access (electricity, water, education, health) is markedly weaker than on the coast.

reports.title: Maroon population and communities
reports.description: Maroon (descendants of escaped enslaved people) population statistics and traditional communities, predominantly in the interior. Largest minority with elevated poverty incidence.
reports._notes: Core identity and social node. Maroons form roughly one-fifth of the national population and a large majority in several interior districts; poverty rates are markedly higher than the national average.

reports.title: Indigenous population and communities
reports.description: Indigenous population statistics and traditional territories, concentrated in the interior. Small national share but high local majorities and elevated poverty.
reports._notes: Complementary identity node. Continuously cited alongside Maroon communities in land-rights, poverty and service-delivery analysis.

reports.title: Labour force and employment
reports.description: Labour-force participation, employment and unemployment indicators. Gender gaps persist; skill shortages are a recurring constraint.
reports._notes: Lived labour market. Employment has recovered toward pre-pandemic levels but female participation remains lower and skill mismatches are cited as a binding constraint for the coming oil era.

reports.title: Education system — coverage and interior gaps
reports.description: Education enrolment, completion and quality indicators. National rates lag regional peers; interior schools face the most severe resource and outcome gaps.
reports._notes: Human-capital node. Secondary enrolment and completion are well below structural peers; interior (Maroon and Indigenous) communities experience the weakest school conditions and outcomes.
reports._url_evidence: Retrieved: MinOWC 'National Education Policy Suriname 2024-2031' (Aug 2024), containing NER/GER enrolment rates, graduation/drop-out/repeater data by district, and extensive analysis of interior (Sipaliwini) education gaps; listed on the Ministry of Education documents page on gov.sr.

reports.title: Health system — access and outcomes
reports.description: Public health-system access and outcome indicators. Coverage and quality gaps are largest in the interior.
reports._notes: Human-capital counterpart to education. Continuously cited for interior service-delivery challenges and for the need to convert future oil revenues into better health outcomes outside Paramaribo.
reports._url_evidence: Retrieved: ABS 'Sociale Statistieken' series page listing health tables - mortality and fertility indicators 2018-2020, disease prevalence and immunisation 2015-2021, health staff numbers 2018-2021, hospital beds by institution 2018-2022, and health expenditure summaries; no separate Ministry of Health statistics publication with a live link was found.

reports.title: Balance of Payments / External accounts
reports.description: Balance of payments and external-sector statistics. Dominated by gold and oil exports; capital account will be shaped by the large Block 58 investment.
reports._notes: External counterpart of the extractive economy. Gold and oil account for ~90% of merchandise exports; the forthcoming offshore project will dominate FDI and export volumes from the late 2020s.

reports.title: Public debt and IMF programme context
reports.description: Public-debt stock and the macroeconomic stabilisation programme context that followed the early-2020s crisis.
reports._notes: Sustainability and stabilisation node. High inflation, exchange-rate pressure and debt distress characterised the crisis years; an IMF-supported programme has framed subsequent policy.

reports.title: District Sipaliwini — largest interior district
reports.description: Largest district by area; predominantly Maroon and Indigenous population; among the weakest service-access indicators (electricity, water, internet, education).
reports._notes: Extreme interior node. Continuously cited in district-level service and poverty diagnostics as the clearest illustration of the coast–interior gap.

reports.title: Oil and mining fiscal revenues
reports.description: Fiscal revenues from onshore oil, gold and (prospectively) offshore oil. Current backbone of public finances; Block 58 expected to produce a step-change from ~2028.
reports._notes: Core fiscal-revenue node. Continuously cited in budget and sustainability analysis; the design of future oil-revenue management (including any sovereign fund) is a central policy debate.
reports._url_evidence: Retrieved: Staatsolie Media Center listing annual reports 2010-2025; the 2023 summary annual report (linked from it) states Staatsolie's contribution to the State of US$335m (36% of government revenues), incl. ~US$181m taxes and ~US$11m gold royalties from Newmont/Rosebel - the closest official publication series covering oil/mining fiscal revenues.

reports.title: Exchange rate / monetary conditions
reports.description: Exchange-rate and monetary-policy indicators. High inflation and exchange-rate pressure defined the early-2020s crisis; stabilisation remains ongoing.
reports._notes: Lived price and monetary signal. Continuously cited alongside inflation as the central stabilisation challenge of the post-crisis period.

reports.title: Merchandise trade statistics
reports.description: Exports and imports of goods. Export basket dominated by gold and oil; imports reflect consumption, intermediate goods and (prospectively) large project-related capital goods.
reports._notes: Primary high-frequency trade product. Gold and oil account for the large majority of export value.

reports.title: District Wanica — coastal peri-urban
reports.description: Coastal district adjacent to Paramaribo. Second major population concentration and peri-urban expansion area.
reports._notes: Completes the greater Paramaribo statistical geography. Continuously appears among the largest population districts.

reports.title: District Brokopondo — interior hydro and Maroon
reports.description: Interior district with major hydroelectric infrastructure and large Maroon population share. Intermediate between deep interior and coastal zones.
reports._notes: Interior energy and identity node. Completes the set of major interior districts alongside Sipaliwini.

reports.title: IMF-supported stabilisation programme
reports.description: IMF-supported macroeconomic stabilisation and reform programme that has framed fiscal, monetary and structural policy since the early-2020s crisis.
reports._notes: External policy-anchor node. Continuously cited as the framework for post-crisis stabilisation pending the arrival of offshore oil revenues.
reports._url_evidence: Retrieved: IMF's official Suriname country page, confirming the Fund relationship (last Article IV Board consultation 26 January 2026) and listing Article IV staff reports, financial position and transactions with the Fund.

reports.title: Agriculture, forestry and fisheries
reports.description: Agriculture, forestry and fisheries production and employment. Smaller share of GDP than mining but material for rural livelihoods.
reports._notes: Non-extractive primary sector. Continuously cited in diversification and rural-livelihood analysis.

reports.title: Electricity access and generation
reports.description: Electricity generation, access and reliability. National access is high on the coast; interior districts (especially Sipaliwini) have very low grid connection rates.
reports._notes: Basic-services node. Coastal access is relatively high; interior access is a defining gap (Sipaliwini grid connection often cited near 30%).
reports._url_evidence: Retrieved: ABS Environment Statistics series page; the 10th publication (Dec 2022) explicitly covers 'Electriciteit', the 9th (Mar 2021) covers 'Energie & Mineralen', and a dataset 'Consumption of Energy in KwH 2013-2017' is listed. EBS's own site was checked and has no generation/access statistics page.

reports.title: Staatsolie contributions to the State
reports.description: Taxes, dividends, royalties and related transfers from Staatsolie (and gold participations) to the central government. Material current fiscal contribution pending offshore first oil.
reports._notes: Operational fiscal link. Recent annual contributions on the order of hundreds of millions of USD (e.g. ~USD 400 m cited for 2025) form a large share of mineral revenues.

reports.title: Staatsolie financing for Block 58 equity
reports.description: Bond issuance and syndicated loan used by Staatsolie to fund its 20% participating interest in GranMorgu (order of USD 2 bn combined financing).
reports._notes: Financing counterpart of the state equity stake. Continuously cited in discussions of contingent public-sector exposure and of the cost of securing a larger share of future oil revenues.

reports.title: Non-mining / non-natural-resource GDP
reports.description: GDP excluding mining and oil extraction. Has shown more robust growth than the mineral sector in recent stabilisation years.
reports._notes: Analytical counterpart to headline GDP. Continuously cited as evidence of recovery outside the volatile mineral cycle; still small relative to the prospective oil step-change.

reports.title: District Nickerie — western agricultural
reports.description: Western coastal district with significant rice and agricultural activity. Secondary economic pole outside the greater Paramaribo area.
reports._notes: Coastal agricultural node. Completes the set of major districts beyond Paramaribo/Wanica and the deep interior.

reports.title: International reserves
reports.description: Stock of international reserve assets. Rebuilt from crisis lows; adequacy metrics have improved under the stabilisation programme.
reports._notes: External-buffer node. Continuously cited in exchange-rate and stabilisation analysis; levels remain sensitive to mineral export cycles and project-related import spikes.

reports.title: Rice production and exports
reports.description: Rice production and export statistics. Principal traditional agricultural export and rural livelihood activity on the western coast.
reports._notes: Traditional agro-export node. Continuously cited in non-mining diversification and rural-employment analysis.

reports.title: Energiebedrijven Suriname (EBS) — national power utility
reports.description: State-owned power utility with monopoly on distribution and retail. Operates transmission and distribution; depends heavily on generation from SPCS (Afobaka hydro + thermal) and other sources.
reports._notes: Core power-system node. Coastal grid access is relatively high; interior connection rates are low. Hydro variability (Afobaka reservoir levels) creates recurring supply risk and load-shedding threats.

reports.title: SPCS / Afobaka hydropower and thermal
reports.description: Staatsolie subsidiary that operates the Afobaka hydropower plant and associated thermal capacity. Supplies the large majority of electricity to the EPAR (Paramaribo-area) network.
reports._notes: Primary generation node. Continuously cited in power-security analysis; low reservoir levels periodically force reliance on expensive thermal and emergency rental capacity.

reports.title: Minimum wage
reports.description: Statutory national minimum hourly wage. Periodically adjusted; share of workers earning below the threshold is higher in the interior and among Maroon and Indigenous workers.
reports._notes: Labour-floor node. Continuously cited in poverty and informality analysis; enforcement and coverage gaps are largest outside the formal coastal economy.
reports._url_evidence: Retrieved: National Assembly page for the 'WET van 06 september 2019, houdende bepalingen over de vaststelling van het minimumloon (Wet Minimumloon)', S.B. 2019 no. 101, with PDF; the 2024 amending act (S.B. 2024 no. 31) was also verified on dna.sr.

reports.title: District Commewijne — eastern coastal
reports.description: Eastern coastal district adjacent to Paramaribo. Significant peri-urban and agricultural population.
reports._notes: Completes the greater Paramaribo coastal set alongside Wanica and Paramaribo itself.

reports.title: District Marowijne — eastern border
reports.description: Eastern border district with mixed coastal and interior characteristics; material Maroon population presence.
reports._notes: Eastern border node. Completes the set of major districts beyond the capital core and the deep western/southern interior.

reports.title: Labour informality
reports.description: Share of employed persons in informal employment (without social-security coverage). Structural feature of the labour market.
reports._notes: Lived labour structure. Roughly half of workers are classified as informal; informality is associated with higher probability of earnings below the minimum wage.

reports.title: Forestry and timber
reports.description: Forestry and timber production and export statistics. Non-mining primary sector linked to interior livelihoods and land-use debates.
reports._notes: Interior primary-sector node. Continuously cited in diversification and land-rights analysis alongside gold and agriculture.

reports.title: Savings and Stabilization Fund Suriname (SSFS)
reports.publisher: Government of Suriname / Ministry of Finance
reports.description: Sovereign savings and stabilization fund revamped by the 2024 SSFS Act. From 2026, all mineral revenues are to be deposited directly into the fund; annual budgets set a maximum withdrawal consistent with fiscal rules.
reports._notes: Central institutional node for the oil era. Designed to delink spending from volatile mineral revenues, accumulate assets, and finance the budget only within pre-set limits. Operationalization (investment policy, independent management, transparent reporting) is still incomplete as of mid-2026.
reports._url_evidence: Retrieved: National Assembly page for 'WET van 30 december 2024, houdende vaststelling van regels over het Spaar- en Stabilisatie Fonds Suriname (Wet Spaar- en Stabilisatie Fonds Suriname 2024)', Staatsblad 2024 no. 179, with PDF download.

reports.title: Public Financial Management Law 2024 — fiscal rules
reports.description: 2024 PFM (Comptabiliteitswet) legislation that embeds two binding fiscal rules: (i) a five-year target for public debt net of SSFS assets, and (ii) annual primary-expenditure ceilings consistent with that debt target.
reports._notes: Legal backbone of the post-crisis, pre-oil fiscal framework. Intended to prevent a premature spending surge when offshore revenues arrive and to force multi-year planning.
_referenced_by: IMF and rating-agency assessments of fiscal credibility
reports._url_evidence: Retrieved and read: the Comptabiliteitswet 2024, Wet van 30 december 2024, S.B. 2024 no. 178, hosted on the Government of Suriname's own site (gov.sr). Article 2 lid 2 establishes the two numeric fiscal rules the item describes - a ceiling on state debt at the end of the multi-year period net of Savings and Stabilisation Fund financial assets, and annual ceilings on primary expenditure consistent with that debt path. This is the law itself, not the 2026 amending bill that dna.sr surfaces.
reports._url_route: alternate official host - the law is published on gov.sr rather than dna.sr

reports.title: Offshore PSC fiscal terms (royalty, profit oil, tax)
reports.description: Production-sharing contract fiscal package: 6.25% royalty on gross production, profit-oil split, and 36% corporate income tax. Combined government take estimated in the 60–70% range (after costs) depending on price.
reports._notes: Contractual revenue-definition node. Continuously cited as the legal basis for the flow of royalty, profit oil and tax that will feed the SSFS once production begins.

reports.title: Medium-term fiscal framework (MTFF) / multi-year fiscal plan
reports.description: Requirement under the 2024 PFM law for a multi-year fiscal plan with annual primary-spending ceilings and a clear net-debt target, to be submitted with the budget (starting with 2026/2027).
reports._notes: Operational planning node. IMF assessments repeatedly stress that agreeing and publishing the five-year plan and expenditure limits is essential to make the fiscal rules credible before oil arrives.
reports._url_evidence: Retrieved: Ministry of Finance and Planning 'Financieel Jaarplan 2024' (29 Sep 2023), which sets out the Medium-Term Government Finance Framework (MTFF 2021-2027 / 2022-2027, tables 3.1.1-3.1.2), primary expenditure by ministry and debt-ratio path; linked from the ministry's documents page on gov.sr.

reports.title: Draft Budget Tables, Fiscal Year 2022/23
reports.publisher: Ministry of Finance and Planning, Republic of South Sudan
reports.description: South Sudan's FY2022/23 draft national budget book, downloaded directly from the Ministry of Finance and Planning's own site. Cover page: "Draft Budget Tables Fiscal Year 2022/23 Ministry of Finance and Planning Republic of South Sudan July 2022". Fiscal-policy narrative section states: "The Government will continue to provide budget in the form of annual grants to the State Government and block grants to the Budgetary Central government Bodies to provide flexibility, ownership and accountability in budget execution." The "Assumptions FY: 2021-22" table, under "Other Mandatory Expenditures", itemizes: "Transfer to Oil Prod. States (2%): 12,476,061,105" [SSP] and "Transfer to Oil Prod. Comm. (3%): 18,714,091,657" [SSP]. This confirms a state-transfer mechanism exists in current national budget policy, but it is a general, formula-based mechanism (oil-producing status, fixed percentages) rather than a schedule itemized by individually named state — no Central Equatoria-, Juba-, or county-specific figures appear anywhere in this document.
reports.cadence_note: Annual national budget document; this is the FY2022/23 edition.

reports.title: Appropriation Act 2023/2024
reports.publisher: Ministry of Finance and Planning, Republic of South Sudan
reports.description: South Sudan's national Appropriation Act for FY2023/2024, hosted on the Ministry of Finance and Planning's site. Section 2 (Definitions): "'Legislature' means the Constitutionally defined National Legislative Assembly and the Council of States", with "Council of States" appearing in Section 53's budget table as a funded line item (wages 4,648,569,882 SSP; goods/services 18,046,992,875 SSP; capital 4,956,723,686 SSP). IMPORTANT CAVEAT (documented so this is not mistaken for a subnational node in a future pass): the "Council of States" here is the upper chamber of the national Legislature (analogous to a Senate), not a subnational fiscal entity. The full document was searched for "State Government", "block grant", "transfer to state", and "conditional grant" — none of these phrases appear anywhere in the Act, and it contains no state-by-state or county-by-county appropriation schedule.
reports.cadence_note: Annual appropriation act; this is the FY2023/2024 edition.

This is a donor/PEFA-authored document, not a primary South Sudanese government document, and no subnational South Sudan state node exists in the corpus to link it to even if it were citable. No node or edge added.

The World Bank's "Western Equatoria State, South Sudan: Public Finance Management Assessment" (Report No. 78292-SS, May 31 2012) notes at indicator PI-10 that "The draft 2011 budget for WESG was available to the public when submitted to the State Legislative Assembly" but in-year execution reports and audited financial statements were not publicly available. This is the closest evidence found that a South Sudanese state government produces its own budget document at all, but it is World Bank-reported (not a verbatim primary excerpt), concerns Western Equatoria rather than Central Equatoria, predates the 2013-2018 civil war, and no South Sudan subnational-state node exists in the corpus. No node minted.

The CABRI (Collaborative Africa Budget Reform Initiative) South Sudan country profile (https://www.cabri-sbo.org/en/our-work/budgets-in-africa/countries/south-sudan) lists only national-level documents (2023 National Budget Plan, 2023 Financial Act, 2024 Compliance Audit Report) and no subnational entries at all — corroborating, not resolving, the structural gap already recorded above.

reports.title: Orçamento Geral do Estado para o ano económico de 2026 (Lei n.º 3/2026)
reports.publisher: Assembleia Nacional de São Tomé e Príncipe (Ministério das Finanças — Direcção do Orçamento)
reports.description: São Tomé and Príncipe's national state budget law for fiscal year 2026 (Lei n.º 3/2026), enacted by the Assembleia Nacional and published in Diário da República I Série, N.º 18 (23 March 2026). Table 6 ("Despesas Totais por Classificação Orgânica", sourced to the Ministério das Finanças' Direcção do Orçamento) itemizes multi-year expenditure by organic-classification code for all six São Tomé island district câmaras alongside the Príncipe regional government, e.g. the row "70.0.00-GRP 109 954,0 109 651,0 128 425,0 144 075,0 107 169..." through "76.0.00-CDMZ 10 950,0 14 623,7 27 966,0 32 168,0 19 966..." (columns: Execução 2022 / Execução 2023 / OGE 2024 / OGE 2025 / Pré-Orçamento 2026, figures in thousands of dobras). Code-to-name mapping (GRP = Governo Regional do Príncipe; CDAG = Câmara Distrital de Água Grande; CDCG = Câmara Distrital de Cantagalo; CDC = Câmara Distrital de Caué; CDLMB = Câmara Distrital de Lembá; CDLOBT = Câmara Distrital de Lobata; CDMZ = Câmara Distrital de Mé-Zóchi) is inferred from standard STP abbreviation convention rather than an explicit legend in the extracted text, but is corroborated by the same table's accompanying Table 8 prose, which independently names districts by percentage: "observa-se que 89% das despesas totais são de âmbito nacional, o que evidencia a abrangência das acções governamentais. Em seguida, destacam-se Água Grande com 3%, Região Autónoma do Príncipe com 3%, Mé-Zóchi com 1% e Lobata 1%, reflectindo a distribuição das despesas pelas diferentes regiões." Article 4 §2 establishes a recurring quarterly transfer mechanism grouping Príncipe and the district câmaras together under one legal regime: "As transferências previstas no OGE para a Região Autónoma do Príncipe (RAP) e Autarquias Locais (AL) são feitas por trimestre, proporcionalmente, de acordo com o valor aprovado, conforme a disponibilidade financeira, observando o tipificado no número 1." HOSTING CAVEAT: retrieved from cipstp.st (Centro de Integridade Pública de STP, a public-integrity NGO), not a .gov.st domain; the PDF's own title page and gazette metadata (Lei n.º 3/2026, Diário da República I Série N.º 18) identify it as a direct reproduction of the official gazette text, but the official host dre.gov.st returned a TLS certificate-hostname-mismatch error and could not be independently checked this round.
reports.cadence_note: Annual state budget law (Orçamento Geral do Estado), enacted yearly by the Assembleia Nacional; this edition covers fiscal year 2026 and also reports historical execution figures for 2022-2023 and approved budgets for 2024-2025.

reports.title: Constituição da República Democrática de São Tomé e Príncipe (Lei n.º 1/2003) — Título IX, Poder Regional e Local
reports.publisher: Assembleia Nacional de São Tomé e Príncipe
reports.description: São Tomé and Príncipe's Constitution (Lei n.º 1/2003), Título IX ("Órgãos do Poder Regional e Local"), supplies the constitutional basis for both Príncipe's regional autonomy and the six-district câmara system referenced throughout the OGE 2026 budget law. Artigo 136.º ("Funções"), §3, states: "Os órgãos do poder regional e local dispõem de finanças e património próprios, de acordo com a lei." [Regional and local power bodies have their own finances and assets, in accordance with the law] — the constitutional "own finances" clause covering both tiers, leaving the specific transfer mechanism to ordinary law (supplied, per existing corpus node st-principe-lei10-2022, by Lei n.º 16/92, and for the annual budget cycle by st-oge-2026's Article 4). Artigo 139.º ("Órgãos distritais") defines the district government structure: "A organização das autarquias locais em cada Distrito compreende uma Assembleia Distrital eleita e com poderes deliberativos e um órgão executivo colegial, denominado Câmara Distrital." Artigo 142.º ("Câmara Distrital") further specifies: "1. A Câmara Distrital, constituída por um presidente e vereadores, é um órgão executivo colegial do distrito, eleita de entre os membros de cada Assembleia Distrital. 2. A Câmara Distrital é responsável politicamente perante a Assembleia Distrital e pode ser destituída a todo o tempo, nos termos da lei." The Constitution itself does not enumerate the six district names; that enumeration appears only in ordinary legislation (the OGE 2026 budget table, st-oge-2026).
reports.cadence_note: One-off foundational constitutional instrument.

reports.title: Decreto Legislativo Regional n.º 02/2024 (Orçamento Regional da Região Autónoma do Príncipe para 2024)
reports.publisher: Assembleia Legislativa Regional da Região Autónoma do Príncipe / Governo Regional do Príncipe
reports.region: São Tomé and Príncipe — Região Autónoma do Príncipe
reports.description: The Príncipe Autonomous Region's own regional budget decree for fiscal year 2024, approved by the Assembleia Legislativa Regional on 28 February 2024 and published 16 April 2024, hosted on principe.gov.st (the regional government's own official site). Its preamble explicitly ties the regional budget to the national state budget's approval: "Na sequência da aprovação pela Assembleia Nacional do Orçamento Geral do Estado para o ano económico 2024 e a alteração das receitas e despesas afectas à Região Autónoma do Príncipe." Article 2 §1(b) specifies the resulting transfer line item as STD 128.425.000,00 under "Transferências de Tesouro Nacional." reports.title: Industrial Product Price Index (IPPI)
reports.description: Monthly measure of price change for major commodities sold by manufacturers operating in Canada, record 2318, produced by the Prices Division alongside the Consumer Price Index. Prices are collected at the factory gate, so they are what the producer receives rather than what a purchaser pays: record 2318 states they 'exclude all indirect taxes, such as sales taxes, customs duties and tariffs as this money does not go to the factors of production', and exclude common-carrier transport and retail or wholesale distribution beyond the gate. That is the whole reason the accounts need it as well as the CPI — the supply and use tables are built at basic prices, and the CPI measures purchasers' prices. The IPPI is the deflator the Canadian accounts actually run on: it is named in 64 rows of the monthly GDP by industry source table against the CPI's 27, and the input-output deflation guide calls it 'the main data source of deflators for manufactured goods'. Record 2318 states the role in its own words: 'the IPPI series supports the Canadian System of Macro-Economic Accounts (CSMA), where it is used in the calculation of real Gross Domestic Product (GDP).' It replaced the Industry Selling Price Index in the early 1980s.
reports.cadence_note: Monthly, reference period month. Two lags worth knowing before this node is used for timing. Collection: 'For most products included in the IPPI, the collection process occurs over a three-week period starting during the third week of the reference month.' Revision: 'price indexes remain subject to revision for six months after publication of a given month's data', so any dependent reading a recent month is reading a provisional number. The weighting structure moves on a far slower clock than the index — 'The entire weighting scheme for the IPPI is generally revised every 5 years' — which is what the reference period on the edge to the supply and use tables records.

release_schedule.note: Listed on the calendar as 'Industrial product and raw materials price indexes' — the IPPI and the RMPI are one release.

dependencies.basis: The monthly programme's industry-by-industry source table, 'National monthly gross domestic product by industry, summary of Methods and data sources' (2021), names the IPPI by title and by IMDB record number in 64 separate rows. Representative row, NAICS 3111 Animal food manufacturing, under 'Gross output': 'Sales and inventory change in constant prices, Monthly Survey of Manufacturing, Record no (number). 2101. Industrial product price indexes, Record no (number). 2318.' Record 2318 is the IPPI. `uses_data_from` follows the type already taken for statcan-gdp-monthly -> statcan-cpi, which rests on the identical evidence in the identical document. WORTH STATING PLAINLY: this is the best-evidenced deflator edge in the Canadian corpus and it was the last one built. The same table names the CPI in 27 rows and SEPH in 37, and both of those became edges two sessions before this one — the IPPI was invisible only because nobody had grepped for it. Note also that record 1301's own IMDB page never mentions the IPPI at all; the release-level disclosure lives entirely in this attached table, which is the disclosure asymmetry doctrine operating within a single statistical programme.
dependencies.evidence_quote: Sales and inventory change in constant prices, Monthly Survey of Manufacturing, Record no (number). 2101. Industrial product price indexes, Record no (number). 2318.

dependencies.basis: Catalogue 15F0077GIE, 'A Guide to Deflating the Input-Output Accounts: Sources and Methods' (2001), which record 1301 cites as the description of the double-deflation method used to produce constant-price GDP by industry. Under the heading 'Sources of deflators', unhedged: 'The main data source of deflators for manufactured goods is the Industrial Product Price Indexes (IPPI) produced by Statistics Canada's Prices Division. Prior to 1981, deflators were based on Industry Selling Price Indexes (ISPI).' Earlier in the same chapter, on why basic-price deflation is possible where purchaser-price deflation is not: 'the commodity price information collected by the Prices Division to compile industry product price indexes can be used to construct deflators for values at basic prices. These Industrial Product Price Indexes (IPPI), aggregated where necessary to the input-output classification, constitute the main source of deflators for manufactured commodities.' Both passages verified verbatim against the PDF. `methodology_depends_on` matches the type taken for statcan-sut -> statcan-cpi from the same document. ONE HEDGE, STATED, AND IT IS THE ONLY ONE: the guide is a 2001 edition marked ARCHIVED, twenty-five years old, and it remains the document record 1301 points at for this method. The 'can be used' softness that qualifies the CPI edge does not apply here — the 'Sources of deflators' sentence says 'is'.
dependencies.evidence_quote: The main data source of deflators for manufactured goods is the Industrial Product Price Indexes (IPPI) produced by Statistics Canada's Prices Division. Prior to 1981, deflators were based on Industry Selling Price Indexes (ISPI).

dependencies.basis: The reverse direction, and the graph's second mutual pair. Record 2318, under Estimation: 'For the IPPI, commodity and industry weights are derived from a combination of the 2019 Supply and Use Tables that closely reflect actual economic transactions by industry and the sales of goods manufactured by companies as reported for the 2019 ASML.' The same section adds that the industry indexes are 'aggregated to the level required for the input-output tables and the measurement of Gross Domestic Product', so the tables set the aggregation structure as well as the weights. Admissible under the V0.10 mutual-partner rule on its own terms: each direction is stated by a different document in its own words, each carries its own evidence_url, and the two are asymmetric in kind rather than restatements of one relationship — the tables take the IPPI as a price measure, the IPPI takes the tables as a weighting frame. `relationship_type` records the asymmetry as the rule requires: `methodology_depends_on` outbound from the tables against `uses_data_from` here, because the SUT figures are a direct numerical input to the weights rather than a method the IPPI follows. THE MECHANISM IS NOT SIMULTANEOUS AND THAT MATTERS FOR READING THE CYCLE: the 2019 tables weight today's index, and today's index deflates a later vintage of the tables. Nothing circular happens in any single calculation; the loop closes only across vintages, five years apart.

reference_period.stated_as: 'The entire weighting scheme for the IPPI is generally revised every 5 years.' The weights in force are derived from the 2019 Supply and Use Tables and from the 2019 ASML, so the window is a single calendar reference year and the reading recurs roughly once every five. Record 2318 adds an unusual note of intent — 'In the future, we will explore increasing the frequency to every two years' — which is a stated plan and not a rate, so it is not in the numbers.

dependencies.evidence_quote: For the IPPI, commodity and industry weights are derived from a combination of the 2019 Supply and Use Tables that closely reflect actual economic transactions by industry and the sales of goods manufactured by companies as reported for the 2019 ASML.

dependencies.basis: Record 2318, under Estimation: 'The second set of indexes covers the total commodity output of individual industries. These reflect the sales of goods manufactured in 2019 in each industry. The industry indexes are classified according to the NAICS 2022v1, aggregated to the level required for the input-output tables and the measurement of Gross Domestic Product.' And under Target population: 'the industry universe corresponds to the North American Industry Classification System (NAICS).' Same type as the five NAICS edges already in the graph, which rest on the same kind of statement — a classification the release is compiled against rather than a figure it reads.

'Another statistical agency' is agency-level attribution with the agency left out — weaker even than H.15's 'Source: U.S. Treasury', which at least named the department. The same section quantifies how much of the index this covers: 'Extraction of data from other sources (10%)' by weight. So a tenth of a headline national price index comes from somewhere the release does not say, and this is a `no-document` finding rather than a research gap: the search is complete and the answer is that the document declines. THE BLOCK IS LIFTED AND THE NODE IS THE NEXT OBVIOUS PIECE OF WORK, with statcan-national-accounts and statcan-sut as its documented members and six citing documents in hand.

Not a dependency and recorded so it is not proposed as one. Record 2318, Imputation: 'Because petroleum data is unavailable at the beginning of the month, it is estimated using ARIMA GARCH models and later revised with respondent data prior to the release.' A statistical model applied to the programme's own missing observations is internal method, not an external input — the same category as X-12-ARIMA seasonal adjustment in record 1301. Worth a line because a graph about where numbers come from will keep meeting sentences of this shape, and a model is not a source.

reports.title: Canadian System of Macroeconomic Accounts
reports.description: The overarching accounting framework Statistics Canada operates under for macroeconomic statistics -- the umbrella that the quarterly income-and-expenditure accounts (statcan-national-accounts, IMDB record 1901), monthly GDP by industry (statcan-gdp-monthly), the Supply and Use Tables (statcan-sut) and the National Balance Sheet Accounts all sit inside, per the User Guide's own chapter structure and per record 1901's language describing the annual benchmarks as arising 'through the construction of annual supply and use tables' within this system. Minted as a node in its own right 2026-08-08 because two federal fiscal-transfer regulations (SOR/2007-303, both the Equalization and Territorial Formula Financing divisions) name the framework itself -- not a specific release -- as the thing a statutory wage/salary term is 'determined... for the purpose of': 'as determined by Statistics Canada for the purpose of its System of Macroeconomic Accounts'. Thomas's ruling (2026-08-08, Open-Questions-2026-08-08-sweep.docx Q1): frameworks and legislative instruments a regulation is built on are worth a node even with no cadence of their own -- 'its sole role is broadcasting and that needs represented.' No releases_per_year: this is an evergreen framework, not a periodic release, the same shape as the one-off foundational instruments already in the corpus.

reports.title: Supply, Use and Input-Output Tables
reports.description: The annual benchmark of the Canadian System of Macroeconomic Accounts. The supply and use tables trace the production of products by domestic industries, combined with imports, through their use as intermediate inputs or as final consumption, investment or exports, and yield gross value added by industry; the symmetric industry-by-industry input-output tables are derived from them. Record 1401's own description states the tables 'can be used to calculate economy-wide gross domestic product (GDP) either directly, by summing value added over the industries, or indirectly, by summing to the economy-wide cost of primary inputs (income-based GDP) or by computing the grand total of the flow of products into final use categories (expenditure-based GDP) - the link to the national income and expenditure accounts.' Both the monthly GDP by industry programme and the quarterly income and expenditure accounts are projections off this benchmark, which is the actual shape of the Canadian accounts and was not representable in this graph until now.
reports.cadence_note: Annual, reference period calendar year, but with an unusually long lag: record 1401 states the tables 'are available about two and half years after the end of the reference year; this is because of the delay in obtaining the needed source data and by the complex nature of producing such a detailed account.' The programme also releases derived products on separate dates — the 2026 release schedule lists April 15 for the input-output tables, May 4 for value added in exports and June 16 for the economic impact of wireless telecommunications carriers — so releases_per_year 1 counts the benchmark tables and not the satellite products.

entries.covers: 2025 reference year Supply, Use and Input-Output Tables (national symmetric input-output tables)

release_schedule.note: Statistics Canada's IMDB page for SDDS 1401 states supply/use and input-output tables are annual and 'available about two and half years after the end of the reference year' due to data-collection lag. Observed national releases: 2023 reference-year data released 2025-04-14, and 2024 reference-year data released 2026-04-15 (both via The Daily / table pid 3610008401, catalogue 15-207-X). This gives a consistent mid-April annual pattern for the most recent two cycles, implying the 2025 reference-year release would land around April 2027. Earlier years (2017-2022) show more variable timing (June-July, and some Nov/Dec releases), and there is a separate, later-lagged provincial/territorial supply-and-use table release that has landed in November in recent years (e.g. 2025-11-13 for 2022 provincial data) - so the overall SDDS 1401 program has more than one sub-release per year even though releases_per_year=1 on file; treat the April date as the primary/national release this corpus field likely tracks.

dependencies.basis: Record 1301 states the anchoring three separate ways in its own words. Under Estimation: 'The monthly estimates are benchmarked to annually chained Fisher volume indexes of GDP obtained from the constant-price supply and use tables.' Under Data accuracy: 'GDP by industry depends on the Supply and Use tables to which it is anchored', and 'as the monthly GDP by industry program relies on the annual estimates of real GDP obtained from the Supply and Use tables, the quality of these estimates has a direct influence on the quality of the monthly GDP measures.' Record 1401 says the same from the other side: 'two industry-based programs - one producing the country's current monthly GDP figures (record no. 1301), the other annual provincial-territorial estimates (record no. 1303) have been set up. These two programs, which can be viewed as extensions of the supply and use tables, use a set of indicators to project the GDP by industry benchmarks from the supply and use tables'. `calculated_from` because the monthly figure is literally a projection of a benchmark drawn from these tables, not merely informed by them — and note the release identifies the dependent by record number, which is the strongest cross-reference in the StatCan corpus so far.
dependencies.evidence_quote: The monthly estimates are benchmarked to annually chained Fisher volume indexes of GDP obtained from the constant-price supply and use tables.

dependencies.basis: Record 1901, under Estimation: 'The National Gross Domestic Product (GDP) by Income and by Expenditure Accounts are estimated by taking the most complete and high quality data sources available to establish annual benchmark estimates. ... The annual benchmarks for GDP by the income approach and by the expenditure approach are generated through the construction of annual supply and use tables which balance the supply of each product in the economy against its use. These tables present the most complete and accurate depiction of Canadian economic activity.' The same record's Revisions section adds that statistical revisions incorporate 'the annual benchmarking process of the supply and use tables'. This is the edge that makes the V0.10 deletion of statcan-national-accounts -> statcan-gdp-monthly legible rather than merely correct: the quarterly and monthly programmes do not read each other, they are two projections off this common annual benchmark.
dependencies.evidence_quote: The National Gross Domestic Product (GDP) by Income and by Expenditure Accounts are estimated by taking the most complete and high quality data sources available to establish annual benchmark estimates. ... The annual benchmarks for GDP by the income approach and by the expenditure approach are generated through the construction of annual supply and use tables which balance the supply of each product in the economy against its use. These tables present the most complete and accurate depiction of Canadian economic activity.

dependencies.basis: Catalogue 15F0077GIE, 'A Guide to Deflating the Input-Output Accounts: Sources and Methods' (2001), which record 1301 cites as the description of the double-deflation method used to produce constant-price GDP by industry. Chapter 2, in the passage on trade margins: 'Consumer price indexes can be used to deflate the purchaser value of commodities sold for personal expenditure. Similarly, industry product price indexes are used to deflate the basic values of the same commodities. This has made it possible to calculate the trade margin for commodities bought for personal expenditure as a residual using both of these observed prices.' `methodology_depends_on` rather than `uses_data_from` because this document is the accounts' deflation methodology and the index is named as the price measure the method takes, which is the case the type comment describes. ONE HEDGE REMAINS, AND ONE WAS RETIRED IN V0.11. Retired: the 'can be used' softness above is not the document's last word on the CPI. Four sentences later in the same passage, unhedged and read while verifying the IPPI quotations, the guide states the mechanism outright: 'The total trade margin at constant prices is calculated as the difference between the purchaser value, deflated with the appropriate Consumer Price Index (CPI), and the sum of the basic value and the ...'. 'Deflated with' is a statement of what deflates what, which is exactly what the hedged sentence was recorded as lacking, so this edge is stronger than V0.10 believed and was under-rated by a first reading that stopped at the first mention. Still standing: the guide is a 2001 edition marked ARCHIVED — it remains the document record 1301 points at for this method, but it is twenty-five years old and a later methodology note may supersede it.
dependencies.evidence_quote: The total trade margin at constant prices is calculated as the difference between the purchaser value, deflated with the appropriate Consumer Price Index (CPI), and the sum of the basic value and the ...

dependencies.basis: The reverse of statcan-national-accounts -> statcan-sut, and taken deliberately under the V0.10 decision that a node may be a mutual definitional partner. Record 1401, Quality evaluation: 'The input-output framework is validated for accuracy, coherence and overall reasonableness. The major components of the framework, such as the income and expenditure-based GDP components are reconciled to the national and provincial-territorial income and expenditure accounts.' Record 1901 states the converse in its own Estimation section: 'The annual benchmarks for GDP by the income approach and by the expenditure approach are generated through the construction of annual supply and use tables which balance the supply of each product in the economy against its use.' Neither statement is a mistake and neither supersedes the other — annual benchmarking is an iterative balancing process in which each side constrains the other, which is what the accounts mean by coherence. The pair is asymmetric in strength and the `relationship_type` records that: 1901 discloses the SUT as the source of its benchmark levels (`calculated_from`), while 1401 describes reconciliation as a validation step rather than an input (`methodology_depends_on`), so the cycle is not symmetric in weight and does not assert that the two are interchangeable.
dependencies.evidence_quote: The input-output framework is validated for accuracy, coherence and overall reasonableness. The major components of the framework, such as the income and expenditure-based GDP components are reconciled to the national and provincial-territorial income and expenditure accounts.

The mutual-definitional-partner question was then decided in the affirmative — see the decision in REPORTS.md — and both edges now exist. What made it safe is the V0.8 proportional-retention rule, and the argument is worth stating because it is the reason the objection above no longer bites: every node with outgoing edges keeps exactly 50% of its own rank regardless of how many edges it has or how strongly they are typed, so two nodes pointing at each other each pass on half and retain half. A mutual pair therefore converges instead of inflating, and cannot pump rank into itself the way a self-retaining sink could under the pre-V0.8 fixed retention. reports.title: Primary Insurance Amount (PIA) Formula and Bend Points
reports.publisher: Social Security Administration, Office of the Chief Actuary
reports.description: Annual automatic determination of the Primary Insurance Amount formula bend points used to convert a worker's Average Indexed Monthly Earnings (AIME) into a Social Security retirement, disability or survivor benefit. The bend points are wage-indexed each year by the ratio of the National Average Wage Index two years prior to the 1977 AWI value. Published by the Office of the Chief Actuary alongside the other October automatic determinations.

entries.covers: PIA bend points for workers first eligible in 2027

release_schedule.rule: By November 1 of each year, SSA must publish the national average wage index for the preceding year and the formula for computing the Primary Insurance Amount (PIA) — including the bend points — for workers who first become eligible for benefits or die in the following year (Social Security Act section 215(a)(1)(D)). In practice the determination is published in the Federal Register as part of the annual "Cost-of-Living Increase and Other Determinations" notice (e.g., the 2026 bend points, $1,286 and $7,749, were published November 3, 2025, document 2025-19763).
release_schedule.note: Statutory deadline is November 1; actual Federal Register publication has historically landed within a few days after (e.g., Nov 3, 2025 for the 2026 bend points), so the entry window reflects that typical lag. The ssa.gov/oact/cola/piaformula.html page itself is updated once the new bend points are determined and is not on a fixed publication calendar independent of this statutory process.

reports.title: Financial Accounts of the United States (Z.1)
reports.publisher: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System
reports.description: Quarterly release presenting the flow of funds, balance sheets and integrated macroeconomic accounts for the United States, covering financial assets and liabilities of every institutional sector. Depository institution sector data are aggregated from the quarterly FFIEC Call Reports. Since the June 2026 release, Z.1 tables are numbered using System of National Accounts sector and instrument codes.

release_schedule.rule: Data are typically released during the second week of March, June, September, and December.
release_schedule.note: Federal Reserve's own release-dates page states the general timing rule; the most recent confirmed dated release was June 11, 2026 (2026:Q1). No specific date for the September 2026 release has been posted yet as of 2026-08-11, so the September/December 2026 entries are computed from the stated 'second week' rule rather than taken from a posted calendar.

dependencies.basis: SSA's PIA page shows the bend points are computed directly from the Average Wage Index series: 'Computation of bend points for 2026: First bend point $180 times 69,846.57 divided by 9,779.44 equals $1,285.59, which rounds to $1,286', where 69,846.57 is the AWI for 2024 and 9,779.44 the AWI for 1977. The page links explicitly to the 'Average wage indices' series.

SSA 'Application of COLA to a Retirement Benefit': 'Each Social Security benefit is based on a "primary insurance amount," or PIA. The PIA in turn is directly related to the primary beneficiary's earnings through a benefit formula. It is the PIA that is increased by the COLA, with the result truncated to the next lower dime.' The page links directly to the PIA formula page. So the PIA carried forward each year is the prior PIA escalated by the annual COLA.

reference_period.stated_as: 'It is the PIA that is increased by the COLA', carried forward each year with the COLA effective for December.

Not resolved this session; a 2025/26-dated primary source (a budget speech or Ministry circular) would settle it.

reports.publisher: Central Statistical Office, Ministry of Economic Planning & Development, Kingdom of Eswatini
reports.description: UPDATE 2026-08-13 (AF/G.23, cross-report methodology enrichment + new SACU HCPI input edge): the March 2026 edition (report dated 'CONSUMER PRICE INDEX (CPI) REPORT MARCH 2026', release date 15 April 2026) confirms in its Foreword that 'For over half a century, the Central Statistical Office (CSO) has been compiling the Consumer Price Index (CPI) for the Kingdom of Eswatini. The CPI is an economic indicator which is primarily used to calculate national inflation rate figures as well as the Harmonized Consumer Price Indices (HCPI) for both COMESA and the SADC regions,' and separately acknowledges 'the continuous technical support received from the International Monetary Fund (IMF), the financial support from the Central Bank of Eswatini.' The same edition states 'The country uses the Laspeyres type of index formula to compile the CPI' -- an unresolved discrepancy against this entry's own geometric-Lowe formula quote below (drawn from a different, February 2026 edition); both are quoted as found without adjudicating which is the currently governing formula. Eswatini's CPI is also now confirmed as a named per-country input line to the SACU-published Harmonised Consumer Price Index bulletin (new node sz-sacu-hcpi-2019, see src/data/research/sz-g23-municipal.json) via a dedicated uses_data_from edge. Original entry follows: Eswatini's official monthly Consumer Price Index release. VERIFIED DIRECTLY this session via the February 2026 report (released 17 March 2026): base period 'June 2020 = 100'; weights 'based on data from the 2016/17 Household Income and Expenditure Survey (HIES)'; classification 'according to the Classification of Individual Consumption according to purpose (COICOP)'; a two-stage formula -- 'the lower level or elementary index... is calculated as a geometric mean of price changes' and 'the upper-level index is a geometric Lowe index -- the weighted geometric average of elementary indices'. Among the branch's most completely documented CPI methodologies so far, comparable in depth to Botswana's and Tanzania's.
