release_schedule.note: Deadline is set by statute/DCED form instructions, not a publisher release calendar. Cities file by March 1; Boroughs and Townships (the large majority of PA municipalities) file by April 1 — the April 1 date is used as the representative next occurrence since the 2026-04-01 deadline has already passed relative to today (2026-08-11).

reports.title: Connecticut Public Act 152 of 1959 — abolition of county government
reports.description: The act that ended county government in Connecticut. Since 1960 the state's eight counties "exist only as geographical regions, without their own independent government" — the functions they held, from jails and courthouses to weights and measures, went to the state or to municipalities.

reports.title: Change to County-Equivalents in the State of Connecticut
reports.publisher: US Office of Management and Budget
reports.description: The 2022 Federal Register notice adopting Connecticut's nine planning regions as county-equivalent units for federal statistics, on the ground that the counties "have not served as functional governmental and administrative entities since county government in the state was abolished in 1960". The most interesting single document in the county-tier work: a geography that stopped existing in 1960 kept being reported on for sixty-two years, and this is the instrument that finally stopped it.

reports.title: Massachusetts General Laws Chapter 34B — abolition of county government
reports.description: The chapter abolishing seven county governments between 1997 and 2000 — Middlesex, Hampden, Worcester, Hampshire, Essex, Berkshire and, separately, Franklin — and transferring their functions, employees, assets and liabilities to the Commonwealth. Six counties keep their governments. Included as the partial case beside Connecticut's complete one, and carrying an unusual trigger: abolition comes early if the commissioner of revenue certifies a default on county debt.

reports.title: Texas Local Government Code Chapter 231 — county zoning authority
reports.description: The answer to a question left open in the previous pass. Texas counties have no general zoning power; Chapter 231 grants it only in named places and for named purposes — parts of Padre Island, land around certain lakes, areas near military installations. The absence of a general grant is the structural reason the Texas county tier is so crowded with independent districts.

dependencies.basis: Education Code §42238.02(d)(2): the grade span adjusted base grants "shall be adjusted by the percentage change in the annual average value of the Implicit Price Deflator for State and Local Government Purchases of Goods and Services for the United States, as published by the United States Department of Commerce for the 12-month period ending in the third quarter of the prior fiscal year. This percentage change shall be determined using the latest data available as of May 10 of the preceding fiscal year compared with the annual average value of the same deflator for the 12-month period ending in the third quarter of the second preceding fiscal year." The published series is BEA NIPA Table 1.1.9 line 26, account code A829RD. Open across two research rounds and closed here: the statute was always clear, and what was missing was which table the deflator actually lives in.

reference_period.stated_as: The 12 months ending in the third quarter of the prior fiscal year against the same window a year earlier, both read as of a fixed May 10 date — so the number is frozen two months before the fiscal year it governs begins.

dependencies.evidence_quote: shall be adjusted by the percentage change in the annual average value of the Implicit Price Deflator for State and Local Government Purchases of Goods and Services for the United States, as published by the United States Department of Commerce for the 12-month period ending in the third quarter of

dependencies.basis: The association reports the mechanism directly: "Beginning in January 2006, counties' Medicaid cost contributions were capped based on 2005 expenditures and indexed to a growth rate of 3.5 percent in 2006, 3.25 percent in 2007, and 3 percent per year thereafter." The State Comptroller's own county Medicaid analysis carries the same figures. The report is the standing published account of what the cap costs and saves counties each year.

The code sets both what a township may levy and what it must report. §3205(a) provides that "The board of supervisors may by resolution levy taxes upon all real property within the township made taxable for township purposes, as ascertained by the last adjusted valuation for county purposes, for the purposes and at the rates specified in this section", with fire apparatus "not exceeding 3 mills" and ambulance and emergency medical services "not exceeding 0.5 mill". The code separately requires the township auditors to complete their settlement before April 1 and the secretary to publish concise financial information by April 15, alongside the state filing.

The levy provision reads a roll the township does not produce: taxes are levied on property "as ascertained by the last adjusted valuation for county purposes". Assessment in Pennsylvania is a county function under the Consolidated County Assessment Law at 53 Pa.C.S. Chapter 88 — so a township's tax base is set entirely by the county above it, and the township tier has no assessment machinery of its own at all.

reference_period.stated_as: The last adjusted county valuation in force when the township levies.

dependencies.basis: The notice gives the abolition as its reason for acting: the planning regions are adopted as county-equivalents because Connecticut's counties "have not served as functional governmental and administrative entities since county government in the state was abolished in 1960". Sixty-two years between the government ending and the statistical geography following it.

The notice directs the change into named products: the Census Bureau will "adopt the State's nine planning regions as county-equivalent geographic units for purposes of collecting, tabulating, and disseminating statistical data", implemented "internally in 2022, with public data and geospatial products reflecting the change beginning in late 2022. By 2024, all Census Bureau operations and publications." The American Community Survey is named first among the affected programmes.

The notice names "the intercensal Population Estimates Program (PEP)" among the programmes that must re-base onto the planning regions. A county-level estimate for Connecticut published after the transition is an estimate for a different geography than one published before it, which is the kind of discontinuity a graph of dependencies ought to record.

The notice names the "Small Area Income and Poverty Estimates (SAIPE) Program" among the affected products, alongside the Economic Census and County Business Patterns. SAIPE county estimates drive Title I education allocations, so the geography change reaches money.

The county association handout lists the narrow matters on which Texas counties may act by ordinance — subdivision regulation, road and drainage construction, sexually oriented businesses, septic systems, certain flood plain development, and airport zoning — against home rule cities, which "have the constitutional power to adopt any ordinance not in conflict with the constitution or the general laws of the state". Chapter 231 is where the enumerated zoning grants sit, and they are geographic: parts of Padre Island, land around named lakes, areas near military installations.

_dropped.why: Chased hard and refuted. The previous research asserted that Houston's charter defines a "Designated Index" as the CPI-U for the Houston-Galveston-Brazoria metropolitan area. Neither of two City bond Official Statements uses the term "Designated Index" or names any metropolitan CPI; both say only "inflation". A search for the phrase against Houston charter and revenue-cap sources found no instance anywhere. The term appears to be an invention and has been kept out of the corpus. What the Official Statements do confirm is the fiscal 2005 base, the cumulative inflation-plus-population adjustment, the 4.5 percent alternative and the $90 million public safety addition — which is why the two Houston cap edges cite the City's bond disclosure for the formula and the Finance Department budget for the series it reads.

A negative finding that survived a deliberate attempt to break it. No federal allocation formula was found that reads the *count* of local governments as a term — formula factors recur as population, poverty, per capita income, tax effort, housing age and acreage, never a count of units. Even Payments in Lieu of Taxes, which depends on the Census classification of a "unit of general local government", uses acreage and population as its numeric inputs. The closest candidate is the Census Bureau's own internal use of the universe as a benchmark and sampling frame for the annual finance and employment surveys, which is exactly the frame-and-classification use the claim excludes. Recorded as "not refuted" rather than proven, because a negative of this shape cannot be proven by search.

One detail of the cap could not be confirmed, filed as an observation because a caveat has to annotate an edge that exists and this one does not. The research this came from described the 2006-2014 trend factors as non-compounded, and no source reachable states that. The available phrasing ("3 percent of additional growth was permitted") is consistent with a simple base-applied increment but does not establish it. Immaterial to the live mechanism, since the trend factors stopped operating when growth was frozen at 2015 levels, but recorded so nobody later treats the compounding question as settled.

Kept as an island deliberately. Massachusetts abolished seven county governments and kept six, and §4 transferred jails, registries of deeds and courthouses to the Commonwealth — so the abolished counties' reporting obligations moved rather than stopped. Which Commonwealth series absorbed them was not established, and until it is there is no edge to draw. Franklin County's separate 1997 abolition and Suffolk's coterminous status with Boston were both left unverified rather than asserted.

The fourteen-mill general purposes cap is stated in a township supervisors' handbook citing §3205, and the per-purpose caps for fire and ambulance were quoted from a primary reprint. The subsection itself could not be rendered from a primary source: the General Assembly's per-section viewer is robots-blocked and every full-code PDF found truncates before the relevant article. The operative levy clause quoted in the edge above comes from a 2024 amending act that reprints it, which is why the edge cites that act rather than the code.

_dropped.edge: ct-county-abolition-1959 -> a successor county financial series
_dropped.why: The clean answer to the question the corpus was actually asking, and it is two-layered. County *government* financial reporting in Connecticut stopped in 1960 and never acquired a successor — there is no entity to report, and the Census of Governments records no county governments in the state. County *geography* statistical reporting carried on for another sixty-two years on legacy boundaries and was then re-based onto the nine planning regions. So an abolished tier does not produce migrated financial reports; it produces a statistical geography that outlives the government by six decades.

_slice: The county tier — California realignment and the Harris County district layer
_note: Counties had been present in this corpus only as the place a city sits. This pass treats the county as a government tier in its own right, on both sides of the American comparison, and the two sides turn out to solve the same problem in opposite directions. California pushed health, welfare and public safety down to counties in two realignments, 1991 and 2011, and funds them with dedicated shares of the state sales tax and vehicle licence fees — so a Californian county is largely financed by Sacramento against formulas Sacramento writes. Texas gives counties almost no ordinance power at all and instead lets services be constituted as separate districts that levy their own property tax: flood control, hospital, emergency services, community college, port. Harris County's Assessor-Collector collects for seventy separate taxing entities. The sharpest finding is a negative one. California indexes an extraordinary amount — five different price indexes at last count — but indexes almost none of what it sends to counties. The 1991 Realignment base is a ratchet against 1991-92 percentages; its growth account references a September 1991 report; the county share of in-home supportive services escalates at a flat 4 percent named in statute; and the Proposition 172 within-county split is measured against 1993-94 property tax losses. Only the county-level Proposition 172 ratio reads anything current. A state that legislates against indexes for wages, rents, taxes and welfare grants declines to do so for the money it sends its own counties.

reports.title: Counties Annual Report (County Financial Transactions Report)
reports.description: The annual compilation of revenue, expenditure, fund balance, debt and staffing reported by all 58 California counties under Government Code §§12463 and 53891 — the county companion to the Cities Annual Report. Since 2014 it has been published as open data rather than a bound volume, which is a quiet but real change in what "published" means.

Code §12463(b). The most recent statutory deadline (Nov 1, 2025, covering FY2024-25) has already passed relative to today (2026-08-11), so the next occurrence is Nov 1, 2026, covering FY2025-26. The compiled data is published on the open-data platform bythenumbers.sco.ca.gov rather than as a single static document/PDF, but the statutory publication deadline governs its timing.

The 1991 settlement that moved a large block of health and welfare responsibility from the state to the counties, and the money with it.

No specific day-of-month is specified in statute; since FY2013-14 the statute delegates scheduling authority to the Department of Finance (deposits made "pursuant to a schedule provided by the Department of Finance").

No page publishes a dated release calendar; the underlying cadence is governed by statute (monthly Controller deposits per WIC 17600.15(b)), consistent with the corpus's existing releases_per_year=12. Exact day-of-month deposit dates are set administratively by the Department of Finance and were not found published as a public calendar.

California's official statutory-reports tracking system (agencyreports.ca.gov, entry for this report) records this Controller reconciliation report as required 'Annually' with a recurring due date of December 31, and lists explicit due dates for FY reconciliations from 12/31/2013 through 12/31/2036, most recently 12/31/2025 (already passed as of 2026-08-11).

Code §30025 as authority and lists a consistent December 31 recurring due date through 2036. The statute itself specifies a September 30 county documentation deadline but does not spell out the exact December 31 day for the Controller's report in the text I could access.

reports.title: Constitutional Basis of County Government

reports.description: A structural context document, filed as a Texas House committee handout, setting out that Texas counties hold only powers the Legislature expressly grants and have severely limited ordinance authority — unlike home rule cities, which may adopt any ordinance not in conflict with state law. reports.title: Port of Houston Authority Annual Comprehensive Financial Report
reports.description: The calendar-year financial report of the port authority. Structurally odd and worth having for exactly that reason: the Authority is a primary government and explicitly not a component unit of the county or of any city, yet Harris County Commissioners Court levies an ad valorem tax on its behalf and the county Assessor-Collector bills and collects it, with the proceeds funding general obligation debt service only.

reports.title: Toll Road Enterprise Fund of Harris County — basic financial statements
reports.description: The contrast case in the Texas district layer: the toll road authority is a department and enterprise fund of the county rather than an independent taxing unit, and drew 90.8 percent of its revenue from tolls in fiscal 2024. It levies no tax of its own, though legacy tax bonds remain secured by a pledge of the county's unlimited taxing power — so the contrast is "no own levy", not "no tax nexus".

reports.title: Houston Community College System approved budget
reports.region: Harris County and Fort Bend County, Texas
reports.description: The annual budget of a junior college district, which in Texas is a taxing unit in its own right — the only post-secondary body anywhere in this corpus that levies a property tax. Ad valorem taxes were 52 percent of budgeted revenue in fiscal 2024, at $0.092231 per $100 on $281.6 billion of certified value drawn from two separate appraisal districts.

release_schedule.note: No published budget calendar or statutory adoption date was found on HCC's site. Observed pattern: the Board of Trustees has approved the upcoming fiscal year's operating budget in late June in each of the last two documented cycles — FY2025 budget approved 2024-06-26 and FY2026 budget approved 2025-06-25 (fiscal year runs Sept 1–Aug 31). The FY2027 budget approval (expected around June 2026) could not be directly confirmed via search, so the projected next entry is for the FY2028 budget (~June 2027), based on the observed pattern.

reports.title: Harris County Emergency Services District annual financial report
reports.description: The audited annual report of an emergency services district — independent taxing units under Health and Safety Code chapter 775 that fund fire and ambulance service. Because Harris County exceeds three million people, §775.0825 requires the audit by July 1 and filing with the clerk of Commissioners Court within thirty days. Modelled on District No. 9 as the retrievable instance of a class.

entries.covers: FY2026 annual audit/financial report for each Harris County Emergency Services District

release_schedule.rule: A district shall prepare on or before July 1 of each year an audit of the district's fiscal accounts and records. (This section, Tex. Health & Safety Code § 775.0825, applies only to a district located wholly in a county with a population of more than three million — i.e., Harris County ESDs, as distinct from § 775.082's June 1 deadline for ESDs in less populous counties.) A copy of the audit must then be filed with the clerk of the county commissioners court within 30 days after the board receives it.
release_schedule.note: The July 1, 2026 deadline for this cycle has already passed as of the reference date (2026-08-11), so the next occurrence is July 1, 2027. Harris County has ~60+ separate Emergency Services Districts (ESD 1, ESD 9, ESD 11, ESD 14, ESD 15, ESD 17, ESD 46, ESD 75, ESD 80, etc.), each governed by this same statutory deadline and each publishing its own audit independently — there is no single unified 'Harris County ESD' report.

dependencies.basis: Government Code §30052(a) makes the allocation a pure share of measured retail activity: the accounts are "continuously appropriated, without regard to fiscal years, to the Controller for allocation to each qualified county in proportion to its share of the total taxable sales in all qualified counties during the most recent calendar year for which sales have been reported." A county's public safety money therefore rises and falls with how much is bought in it.

reference_period.stated_as: The most recent calendar year for which taxable sales have been reported; the ratio is refreshed annually and applied to monthly receipts.

dependencies.evidence_quote: continuously appropriated, without regard to fiscal years, to the Controller for allocation to each qualified county in proportion to its share of the total taxable sales in all qualified counties during the most recent calendar year for which sales have been reported.

dependencies.basis: Revenue and Taxation Code §97.70 defines each entity's vehicle license fee adjustment amount for 2005-06 and every year after as the prior year's amount multiplied by "the percentage change from the prior fiscal year to the current fiscal year in gross taxable assessed valuation" within that entity's jurisdiction, with the county auditor computing and certifying the figure for the county and each city under §97.70(c)(5). The gross taxable assessed valuation comes off the county assessor's roll — so a payment named for vehicles is in fact a function of property value.

reference_period.stated_as: The change in gross taxable assessed valuation between two fiscal years, each measured on the January 1 lien date; certification due June 30.

dependencies.basis: The Controller's county reporting instructions state that "Pursuant to Government Code section 12463 ... the data used for the financial transactions report come from audited financial statements, if available", and instruct counties that reported amounts should agree with what they report in their own annual comprehensive financial report for the year. The Controller's compilation is therefore downstream of every county's audited statements.

reference_period.stated_as: The county fiscal year just closed; filings due within seven months of year end.

dependencies.basis: The same instructions direct counties to the Controller's Accounting Standards and Procedures for Counties manual, which "conforms to Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (GAAP) as prescribed by the Governmental Accounting Standards Board (GASB)", and prescribe modified accrual for governmental funds and full accrual for proprietary and fiduciary funds.
dependencies.evidence_quote: conforms to Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (GAAP) as prescribed by the Governmental Accounting Standards Board (GASB)

dependencies.basis: Government Code §30029.05 provides that Local Revenue Fund 2011 money "shall be allocated ... pursuant to schedules developed by the Department of Finance in consultation with the California State Association of Counties", and that the Controller "shall allocate these funds pursuant to the base allocation schedule provided by the Department of Finance for that fiscal year". §30029.07 applies the same mechanism to the growth account. The Governor's Budget item for 2011 State-Local Realignment is the Department's published statement of those amounts.

Welfare and Institutions Code §17606.20(b)(5) provides that general growth allocations from the Sales Tax Growth Account "shall be determined based on schedules developed by the Department of Finance" in consultation with the county associations. The Department's published statement is the Governor's Budget item for 1991 State-Local Realignment, which sets out the sales tax, vehicle license fee and growth accounts and records that they are continuously appropriated for allocation to local governments according to formula.

The Tax Office states that "When the certified appraisal roll is received from the Harris Central Appraisal District, the property values are loaded into the Tax Office's internally developed computer system", and that the office "maintains approximately 1.5 million tax accounts and collects property taxes for 70 taxing entities including Harris County." Tax Code §26.01(a) supplies the mechanism: "By July 25, the chief appraiser shall prepare and certify to the assessor for each taxing unit participating in the district that part of the appraisal roll for the district that lists the property taxable by the unit."

reference_period.stated_as: Values as of the January 1 appraisal date, certified by July 25; the 2025 worksheets were signed on 1 August 2025.

dependencies.basis: The published summary carries the caption "Truth in Taxation Summary Provided in accordance with Texas Property Tax Code, § 26.16", and the per-jurisdiction worksheets state that "Tax Code Section 26.04(c) requires an officer or employee designated by the governing body to calculate the no-new-revenue (NNR) tax rate and voter-approval tax rate for the taxing unit."

The District's own rate calculation worksheet states that "The calculation process starts after the chief appraiser delivers to the taxing unit the certified appraisal roll and the estimated values of properties under protest", with the total current year taxable value taken from that roll. The Harris County Tax Assessor-Collector signs it, certifying she "accurately calculated the tax rates using values that are the same as the values shown in the taxing unit's certified appraisal roll."

reference_period.stated_as: January 1 appraisal date; worksheet signed 1 August 2025 for the 2025 rate.

dependencies.basis: The District sets its rate through the same no-new-revenue and voter-approval framework as every other Texas taxing unit; the adoption notice carries the statutory comparison language, "THE TAX RATE WILL EFFECTIVELY BE RAISED BY 3.49 PERCENT".

The District's statements record that "On January 1, at the time of assessment, an enforceable lien is attached to the property for property taxes", and refer to subsequent adjustments to the tax rolls. Its rate calculation worksheet, filed under "Harris County Hospital District dba Harris Health", is built from the certified appraisal roll and signed by the county Assessor-Collector; Commissioners Court adopted a 2025 rate of $0.18761 per $100.

reference_period.stated_as: Lien attaches on January 1 at the time of assessment.

dependencies.basis: The statements record the division of labour plainly: "The Harris County Commissioners' Court approves the System's tax rate and annual operating and capital budget", and "The taxes are collected by the Harris County Tax Assessor-Collector and are remitted to the System as received." A hospital district that neither sets nor collects its own tax.

The hospital district's statements record that "The System is a component unit of Harris County, Texas (legally separate from Harris County, Texas), since the members of the System's governing board are appointed by the Harris County Commissioners' Court", so the district is consolidated into the county's reporting entity.

The Authority's report states that "Property is appraised, and a lien on such property becomes enforceable, as of January 1, subject to certain procedures", and that "Property taxes are generally levied in October or November for the year in which assessed." Its rate calculation worksheet, filed under "Port of Houston Authority", is computed from the certified appraisal roll and signed by the county Assessor-Collector.

reference_period.stated_as: Appraisal and lien as of January 1; levy in October or November.

dependencies.basis: The Authority states that "Debt service on Port Houston outstanding tax bonds is funded entirely from ad valorem taxes levied by the Harris County Commissioners Court on behalf of Port Houston", and that "Taxes are invoiced and collected by the Harris County Tax Assessor-Collector, which charges a fee for those services." It is nonetheless not a component unit — no county or city "exercises financial control over the Authority" — which makes it a body taxed for but not owned by the county.

The toll road statements record that "The Authority is a department and fund of the County and is included in the County's financial statements." Unlike the hospital district, this is not a component unit consolidated in — it is part of the county outright, and the distinction is exactly why one levies a tax and the other does not.

The college's budget builds ad valorem tax revenue — 52 percent of budgeted revenue, $205.7 million — on certified values from the Harris County and Fort Bend County appraisal districts: "Taxable values totaled $281.6B, which is a 10.2% increase compared to prior year certified values", at an adopted rate of $0.092231 per $100.

The college publishes a no-new-revenue rate and a voter-approval rate like any other taxing unit, noting that "The 86th Texas Legislature modified the manner in which the voter-approval tax rate is calculated to limit the rate of growth of property taxes in the state", and that the calculation uses July estimated values from the counties pending certification.

reference_period.stated_as: July estimated values, superseded by the certified roll.

dependencies.basis: District No. 9's audited report states that "All property values and exempt status, if any, are determined by the appraisal district", and the rate calculation worksheets for the county's emergency services districts are computed from the certified appraisal roll and signed by the county Assessor-Collector.

reference_period.stated_as: January 1 appraisal date.

dependencies.basis: Health and Safety Code §775.074 provides that "The board shall annually impose an ad valorem tax on all real and personal property located in the district" and must certify that rate "to the county tax assessor-collector, who is the assessor-collector for the district". District No. 9 records paying the county Assessor-Collector $164,267 for assessment and collection services in one year.

_dropped.why: A negative finding worth as much as any edge here. The 1991 Realignment base reads nothing: Welfare and Institutions Code §17604 fixes 1991-92 base-year percentages of the vehicle license fee account county by county (Los Angeles 37.26 percent, San Francisco 7.15, Orange 5.43) and then directs the Controller to deposit "until the deposits equal the amounts that were allocated ... in the prior fiscal year". The growth allocation is no better — §17606.10 references "the percentage of total state resources received in the 1990-91 fiscal year" and a report dated September 1991. A transfer of several billion dollars a year runs on a ratchet against a thirty-five-year-old snapshot, and names no population estimate, price index or current series at all.

_dropped.edge: in-home supportive services county maintenance of effort -> a price index
_dropped.why: Checked specifically because California indexes so much else, and the answer is no. Welfare and Institutions Code §12306.16 provides that "Beginning on July 1, 2020, and annually thereafter, the rebased County IHSS MOE from the previous year shall be adjusted by an inflation factor of 4 percent" — a flat statutory number, not a measured one. The pre-2019 version conditioned a 5 or 7 percent factor on whether realignment revenues grew, which is a revenue test, still not a price index. So the county share of in-home care escalates at a rate the Legislature named once.

Only the county-level split reads a current series. Government Code §§30054-30055 allocate the within-county share to cities on their proportionate 1993-94 property tax loss from the second phase of the education revenue augmentation shift, reduced by a one-time 1993-94 transport account receipt, with everything unallocated going to the county — and cities that received no property tax or did not exist in 1980 are ineligible outright. So one half of this transfer is a live measurement and the other half is a photograph of 1993.

Checked and refused, because it is the obvious guess. The Necessities Index drives the CalWORKs grant level under Welfare and Institutions Code §11453, which is already an edge in the corpus, but no county allocation reads it. §17600.15 provides only that the child poverty subaccount deposits "equal the amounts that were deposited in the prior fiscal year", and §17600.50 allocates on 1991 historical amounts. The index sets what a family receives, not what a county receives.

The District publishes separate audited statements at a stable, predictably named path under the County Auditor's site, but that site's robots.txt disallows the entire directory the reports live in, so a compliant fetcher gets nothing. Its own site, hcfcd.org, publishes no financial documents at all. Every claim above is therefore evidenced from the tax rate worksheets and adoption notices instead. Publishes, but not readable.

The disclosure channel is split and only half of it is addressable. Rate documents are excellent — every district's worksheet sits at a predictable URL on the Assessor-Collector's site. Audited financials, required by §775.0825 to be filed with the clerk of Commissioners Court, surface only as agenda attachments with opaque identifiers and no per-district path. This is the emergency services district version of the problem already recorded for municipal utility districts, and it is the same shape: the tax is public, the accounts are not.

No college document names the Harris County Assessor-Collector as its collector, and the college's own posted rate worksheet now returns a 404. It also spans two appraisal districts, so the collection arrangement may not be uniform across its territory. Plausible and uncited.

_slice: US federal policy indexation — the rules that turn statistical releases into money
_status: Swept 2026-08-09 as part of the corpus-wide _dropped sweep (Tier 3; see planning/dropped-sweep-scoping_2026-08-08.md, which flagged this file's fed-h15 entry as live and urgent — a correctness bug, not just a missed lead, since V0.9's deletion of fed-h15's only edge left it dropping from every build). Minted treasury-daily-yield-curve and wired fed-h15 -> treasury-daily-yield-curve, closing that entry. The other seven _dropped entries were re-read and found already correctly settled as deliberate scope/evidence decisions (two unpublishable-source, one denied, one no-document, two deferred-for-scope-balance, one wrong-target) — none re-opened.
_note: This slice is about the rules that convert a statistical release into a payment, and about the survey machinery underneath the headline numbers. The shape that emerged is that the US does not have one inflation index driving policy — it has at least four, and which one applies to you is an artefact of when your programme was legislated. Social Security benefits move on the CPI-W, third quarter to third quarter, under a 1972 statute. The federal poverty guidelines move on the CPI-U, annual average to annual average, under a 1981 statute — and they move on it twice, because Census already inflates the poverty thresholds by CPI-U before HHS inflates the published thresholds forward again. Tax brackets move on the C-CPI-U, twelve months ending August 31, under the 2017 act, an index that runs about 0.2 points a year slower and is still being revised for ten months after the value the IRS is required to use is fixed. And the Federal Reserve's 2 percent target is defined on none of these — it is the BEA's PCE price index, which is itself largely a reweighting of the same BLS price quotes onto national-accounts expenditure weights. The other structural fact worth recording is that the Social Security system is indexed on both sides but to different things: benefits to prices via the CPI-W, the taxable wage base and the PIA bend points to wages via SSA's own national average wage index. When wages and prices diverge, the programme's finances move in ways neither index alone predicts. On the survey side, the CPS cannot produce a population level at all; it produces rates, and the levels come from Census population estimates, which are a carry-forward of the decennial count. That is why the January Employment Situation carries a discontinuity every year that has nothing to do with the labour market.

reports.title: National Average Wage Index (AWI)
reports.publisher: US Social Security Administration, Office of the Chief Actuary
reports.description: Annual index of average wages tabulated by SSA from wages subject to federal income tax plus contributions to deferred compensation plans. It is the wage-side counterpart to the CPI in the Social Security system: it indexes a worker's lifetime earnings when their initial benefit is computed, and it drives the taxable maximum, the earnings test exempt amounts, the PIA bend points and the quarter-of-coverage amount. Published roughly a year in arrears — the index for a calendar year is announced in October of the following year.
reports.cadence_note: Announced each October alongside the COLA, for the calendar year two years prior to the year the indexed amounts take effect.

release_schedule.rule: SSA must publish the national average wage index for the prior calendar year by November 1 of each year (Social Security Act section 215(a)(1)(D), 42 U.S.C. 415(a)(1)(D)); in practice SSA has published it in the Federal Register in the notice titled 'Cost-of-Living Increase and Other Determinations for [year]' in mid-to-late October each year (e.g., Oct 22, 2021; Oct 24, 2022; Oct 23, 2023; Oct 25, 2024).
release_schedule.note: The SSA AWI.html page itself lists the most recent figure (currently the 2024 index, 69,846.57) but does not itself state a publication schedule. The publication deadline comes from the annual Federal Register 'Cost-of-Living Increase and Other Determinations' notice, which explicitly cites the November 1 statutory deadline for publishing the prior year's national average wage index. Actual publication has historically occurred a few days before the Nov 1 deadline (per past Federal Register notice dates).

reports.title: OASDI Contribution and Benefit Base (Social Security taxable maximum)
reports.publisher: US Social Security Administration, Office of the Chief Actuary
reports.description: The annual ceiling on earnings subject to the Social Security portion of payroll tax, and the ceiling on earnings credited toward benefits. Announced each October in the same release as the COLA — but indexed to wages, not prices, which is why it can rise in a year when the COLA is small and vice versa. Published in the Federal Register as an automatic determination under section 230 of the Social Security Act.

entries.covers: 2024 contribution and benefit base announced with COLA press release
2025 contribution and benefit base announced with COLA press release
2026 contribution and benefit base ($184,500) announced with COLA press release
2027 contribution and benefit base, expected to be announced alongside the annual COLA press release

release_schedule.note: The cbb.html page itself states only that the base changes each year with the national average wage index, but gives no announcement date. In practice SSA has consistently announced the new contribution and benefit base for the following year in the same October press release as the annual COLA (e.g. 'Social Security Announces 2.8 Percent Benefit Increase for 2026', released 2025-10-24, which also states the 2026 base of $184,500). Observed announcement dates cluster in mid-to-late October: 2023-10-12, 2024-10-10, 2025-10-24. BLS has already scheduled release of the September 2026 CPI (which anchors the COLA determination) for 2026-10-14, so the 2027 COLA/benefit-base announcement is expected around that date, with SSA's own press release typically following within days.

reports.title: Current Population Survey (CPS)
reports.publisher: US Census Bureau and US Bureau of Labor Statistics
reports.description: The monthly household survey of about 60,000 eligible households, collected by the Census Bureau and estimated by BLS. It is the sole source of the official unemployment rate and of every labour force measure broken down by age, sex, race, education or reason for unemployment. On average one CPS respondent stands for about 2,500 people, so the survey cannot produce a level on its own — it produces a rate, and the level comes from population controls supplied by Census.

entries.covers: August 2026 Employment Situation (CPS household survey data)
September 2026 Employment Situation (CPS household survey data)
October 2026 Employment Situation (CPS household survey data)
November 2026 Employment Situation (CPS household survey data)

release_schedule.note: The Current Population Survey (CPS) is the household survey component of BLS's monthly 'Employment Situation' news release, published on the BLS Schedule of Releases page. CPS microdata/tables (bls.gov/cps/tables.htm and census.gov/programs-surveys/cps.html) are released on the same monthly cadence tied to the Employment Situation release. Dates are subject to change; BLS has in the past shifted this schedule due to government shutdowns (e.g., a notice on bls.gov/cps/notices/2026/ references a March 6, 2026 release date for February 2026 data due to a population control revision).

reports.title: Population Estimates Program (Vintage Estimates)
reports.description: Annual estimates of the resident population for the nation, states and counties, produced between decennial censuses. Each vintage starts from the most recent decennial census count and carries it forward with administrative records on births, deaths and net international migration. Distinct from the decennial census itself: the census is a count, this is a model built on top of the count, and it is the model rather than the count that most federal programmes and surveys actually use year to year.
reports.cadence_note: A new vintage is released each December for the nation and states, with county and sub-county detail following through the following spring.

release_schedule.note: Stated target is 'December' for the first release, but the Vintage 2025 national release actually slipped to Jan 27, 2026 — treat month-level dates as plan, not guarantee.

reports.title: Annual Update of the HHS Poverty Guidelines
reports.publisher: US Department of Health and Human Services, Office of the Assistant Secretary for Planning and Evaluation
reports.description: The federal poverty level, published each January in the Federal Register as a simple table of income by household size. It is not a measurement — it is an administrative simplification of the Census Bureau's poverty thresholds, inflated forward by the CPI-U and then rounded so the interval between family sizes is uniform. Medicaid, ACA premium subsidies, SNAP, Head Start and dozens of other programmes set eligibility as a percentage multiple of it.
reports.cadence_note: Published mid-January each year, effective on the date of publication unless an administering programme specifies otherwise.

entries.covers: 2024 Annual Update of the HHS Poverty Guidelines
2025 Annual Update of the HHS Poverty Guidelines
2026 Annual Update of the HHS Poverty Guidelines
2027 Annual Update of the HHS Poverty Guidelines (projected)

release_schedule.note: Section 673(2) of the Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act (OBRA) of 1981 requires HHS to update the poverty guidelines 'at least annually,' adjusted by the CPI-U, but the statute sets no specific calendar date. In practice, HHS/ASPE has published the update in the Federal Register in mid-January every year (e.g., 2024-01-17, 2025-01-17, 2026-01-15), consistent with the existing cadence_note. The 2027 date below is a projection based on that observed pattern, not a confirmed calendar date.

reports.title: Census Bureau Poverty Thresholds (Income and Poverty in the United States)
reports.description: The official statistical poverty measure: a matrix of thresholds by family size, number of children and (for one- and two-person units) age of householder, used to count how many Americans are in poverty. Published each September for the prior calendar year, using income data from the CPS Annual Social and Economic Supplement. The thresholds are a statistical instrument; the HHS guidelines are the administrative simplification of them.

entries.covers: 2025 poverty thresholds, released alongside Income, Poverty, and Health Insurance Coverage in the United States: 2025 (CPS ASEC)

release_schedule.note: Census Bureau's media advisory sets Tuesday, September 15, 2026 as the release date for 2025 Income, Poverty and Health Insurance statistics from the CPS ASEC, which is when the Bureau's poverty thresholds table for 2025 is published (in the P60 series report and the historical-poverty-thresholds.html data tables). Poverty thresholds are typically released once a year, in September, alongside the annual Income/Poverty/Health Insurance report; a preliminary weighted-average threshold estimate is sometimes posted earlier (a 'Preliminary Estimate of Weighted Average Poverty Threshold for 2025' appears on the thresholds landing page, last revised Jan 15, 2026), but the citable dated release is the September CPS ASEC report.

reports.title: Chained Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (C-CPI-U)
reports.description: A superlative price index built from the same price quotes as the CPI-U but using a Tornqvist formula with expenditure weights from both the current and the comparison period, so it captures consumers substituting between categories as relative prices change. It therefore rises more slowly than the CPI-U. Published monthly alongside the CPI, but initially as an estimate: values are revised twice and only become final about a year later, which is why the tax code pins the values used to those published as of the initial August release.
reports.cadence_note: Released with the monthly CPI news release, but each month's value is initial and subject to three interim revisions, with final data posted 10 to 12 months later.

entries.covers: Initial C-CPI-U for July 2026, released with the CPI-U news release

release_schedule.note: The 'Initial' C-CPI-U estimate is published monthly in the same news release as the regular CPI-U (confirming releases_per_year=12). Per BLS (chained-cpi-introduction.htm), each Initial monthly value is later revised to an 'Interim' estimate the following February, and to a 'Final' value in February two years after the reference year, so historical C-CPI-U figures for a given month are revised twice on a fixed February cadence even though the initial monthly release follows the standard CPI calendar.

reports.title: Annual Inflation Adjustments Revenue Procedure (Rev. Proc. 2025-32 and successors)
reports.description: The revenue procedure issued each autumn that sets the dollar figures for the following tax year: rate bracket thresholds, the standard deduction, the AMT exemption, the earned income credit, the estate tax exclusion, HSA and FSA limits and dozens of other provisions. Since the 2017 tax act the escalator is the chained CPI rather than the CPI-U, which slows bracket growth relative to the pre-2018 rule and quietly raises revenue over time.
reports.cadence_note: Normally issued in October or November for the following tax year; the 2026 figures were reissued as Rev. Proc. 2025-32 after the July 2025 tax act changed the underlying provisions.

entries.covers: Tax Year 2026 inflation adjustments (Rev. Proc. 2025-32, IR-2025-102)
Tax Year 2027 inflation adjustments (expected successor Revenue Procedure)

release_schedule.note: The IRS has no statutory or published-calendar date for this Revenue Procedure; it is an internal annual practice. Over the last several cycles the news release/Rev. Proc. announcing the following year's inflation-adjusted figures has consistently landed in October or (occasionally) early November. The TY2026 edition (Rev. Proc. 2025-32) was released Oct. 9, 2025 as IR-2025-102, and was itself a reissue after the July 2025 'One, Big, Beautiful Bill' changed underlying provisions (per the existing cadence_note). Based on the observed Oct/Nov pattern, the TY2027 successor is expected to be released in the Oct-Nov 2026 window; no exact date has been announced yet as of 2026-08-11.

reports.title: Daily Treasury Par Yield Curve Rates
reports.description: The Treasury's daily par yield curve for its own securities, from which Constant Maturity Treasury (CMT) rates at specific maturities are read directly. Treasury's own FAQ: 'CMT yields are read directly from the Treasury's daily par yield curve, which is derived from indicative closing bid market price quotations on Treasury securities.' Minted 2026-08-09 (sweep session, Tier-3 item, us-federal-policy.json) to close a `no-node-yet` lead that was flagged urgent: deleting `fed-h15 -> fed-fomc-statement` in V0.9 had left the Fed's H.15 release with no surviving edge, meaning it dropped from the graph on every build. H.15's own footnotes 9 and 10 read 'Source: U.S. Treasury' for its Treasury nominal and inflation-indexed constant maturity series, describing those yields as 'interpolated by the U.S. Treasury from the daily yield curve' — this node is that source.
reports.cadence_note: Every business day — the corpus's own convention for daily releases, matching fed-h15's own cadence_note ('Every business day.').

entries.covers: Next business-day update of Daily Treasury Par Yield Curve Rates

release_schedule.rule: Treasury's Daily Par Yield Curve Rates are updated each business day, using closing market bid yields on actively traded Treasury securities as reflected in indicative, bid-side market quotations obtained by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York at approximately 3:30 PM each business day.
release_schedule.note: This is not a calendar of discrete editions but a continuously updated daily series published on every US Treasury market business day (excludes weekends and federal holidays when bond markets are closed). The next occurrence listed is simply the next business day after 2026-08-11 (Tuesday), i.e. Wednesday 2026-08-12; this pattern repeats on essentially every subsequent business day.

dependencies.basis: SSA states the statutory formula outright: 'The Social Security Act specifies a formula for determining each COLA. According to the formula, COLAs are based on increases in the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W). CPI-Ws are calculated on a monthly basis by the Bureau of Labor Statistics. A COLA effective for December of the current year is equal to the percentage increase (if any) in the CPI-W from the average for the third quarter of the current year to the average for the third quarter of the last year in which a COLA became effective.' The arithmetic is shown in full: the 2.8 percent COLA effective December 2025 is (317.265 - 308.729) / 308.729 x 100, using the July, August and September CPI-W values for 2024 and 2025. Note the index is CPI-W, a subpopulation index for urban wage earners and clerical workers, not the headline CPI-U.

reference_period.stated_as: 'the percentage increase (if any) in the CPI-W from the average for the third quarter of the current year to the average for the third quarter of the last year in which a COLA became effective'.

dependencies.evidence_quote: The Social Security Act specifies a formula for determining each COLA. According to the formula, COLAs are based on increases in the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W). CPI-Ws are calculated on a monthly basis by the Bureau of Labor Statistics. A COLA effective for December of the current year is equal to the percentage increase (if any) in the CPI-W from the average for the third quarter of the current year to the average for the third quarter of the last year in which a COLA became effective.

dependencies.basis: SSA lists the amounts driven by the wage index and puts the taxable maximum first: 'We use the average wage indexing series to update several amounts that are important to the operation of Social Security's Old-Age, Survivors, and Disability Insurance (OASDI) program. — OASDI contribution and benefit base (also known as the taxable maximum); Retirement earnings test exempt amounts; Formulas for a primary insurance amount and maximum family benefits; Amount of earnings needed to earn a quarter of coverage.' This is the interesting structural fact about the Social Security system: benefits are indexed to prices, the tax base is indexed to wages, and the two indices diverge.
dependencies.evidence_quote: We use the average wage indexing series to update several amounts that are important to the operation of Social Security's Old-Age, Survivors, and Disability Insurance (OASDI) program. — OASDI contribution and benefit base (also known as the taxable maximum); Retirement earnings test exempt amounts; Formulas for a primary insurance amount and maximum family benefits; Amount of earnings needed to earn a quarter of coverage.

dependencies.basis: The Handbook of Methods is unambiguous that the survey cannot produce population levels by itself: 'Population controls are independent estimates of the population that are used to weight the CPS sample results so that estimates reflect the civilian noninstitutional population ages 16 and older. The Census Bureau develops the CPS population controls, which are based on decennial census population counts, supplemented with birth and death data and estimates of net international migration. The Census Bureau reviews and adjusts the population estimates every year. BLS introduces the Census Bureau's annual population control adjustments into CPS estimates for January.' This is why the January Employment Situation carries a break in the household series each year — the level jumps by whatever the new vintage says, independent of anything that happened in the labour market.

reference_period.stated_as: 'BLS introduces the Census Bureau's annual population control adjustments into CPS estimates for January.'

dependencies.evidence_quote: Population controls are independent estimates of the population that are used to weight the CPS sample results so that estimates reflect the civilian noninstitutional population ages 16 and older. The Census Bureau develops the CPS population controls, which are based on decennial census population counts, supplemented with birth and death data and estimates of net international migration. The Census Bureau reviews and adjusts the population estimates every year. BLS introduces the Census Bureau's annual population control adjustments into CPS estimates for January.

dependencies.basis: The population controls are 'based on decennial census population counts, supplemented with birth and death data and estimates of net international migration' — the estimates programme is a carry-forward of the decennial base, which is why a census undercount or overcount propagates into every intercensal year until the next census resets it.
dependencies.evidence_quote: based on decennial census population counts, supplemented with birth and death data and estimates of net international migration

dependencies.basis: The Employment Situation news release is two surveys stapled together. The household half — the unemployment rate, the participation rate, and all demographic detail — is the CPS. BLS: 'When the Census Bureau's processing activities are completed, the microdata file is securely transferred to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) for estimation of labor force statistics.' The establishment half (payroll employment) is the CES, already linked to QCEW elsewhere in the graph.
dependencies.evidence_quote: When the Census Bureau's processing activities are completed, the microdata file is securely transferred to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) for estimation of labor force statistics.

dependencies.basis: The statute names the index: 'Section 673(2) of the Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act (OBRA) of 1981 (42 U.S.C. 9902(2)) requires the Secretary of the Department of Health and Human Services to update the poverty guidelines at least annually, adjusting them on the basis of the Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U). ... As required by law, this update is accomplished by increasing the latest published Census Bureau poverty thresholds by the applicable percentage change in the Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U). The guidelines in this 2026 notice reflect the 2.63 percent price increase between calendar years 2024 and 2025.' Note this is CPI-U, annual average to annual average — a different index and a different reference period from the CPI-W third-quarter comparison that drives the Social Security COLA.

reference_period.stated_as: 'the applicable percentage change in the Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U)' between calendar-year averages.

dependencies.evidence_quote: As required by law, this update is accomplished by increasing the latest published Census Bureau poverty thresholds by the applicable percentage change in the Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U).

dependencies.basis: The guidelines are not an independent measure — they are the Census thresholds inflated and smoothed: 'The poverty guidelines issued here are a simplified version of the poverty thresholds that the Census Bureau uses to prepare its estimates of the number of individuals and families in poverty. ... this update is accomplished by increasing the latest published Census Bureau poverty thresholds by the applicable percentage change in the CPI-U. ... The poverty guidelines continue to be derived from the Census Bureau's current official poverty thresholds; they are not derived from the Census Bureau's Supplemental Poverty Measure (SPM).' The notice even states the guidelines are 'roughly equal to the poverty thresholds for calendar year 2025, which the Census Bureau expects to publish in final form in September 2026' — the administrative number arrives eight months before the statistical number it approximates.
dependencies.evidence_quote: As required by law, this update is accomplished by increasing the latest published Census Bureau poverty thresholds by the applicable percentage change in the Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U).

dependencies.basis: The Census Bureau's own methodology page labels the published threshold table 'Poverty Thresholds by Size of Family and Number of Related Children Under 18 Years — Source: Current Population Survey (CPS)'. The threshold matrix is carried forward by CPI-U, but the income distribution it is applied to, and the official count of people in poverty, come from the CPS Annual Social and Economic Supplement.
dependencies.evidence_quote: Table Poverty Thresholds Poverty Thresholds by Size of Family and Number of Related Children Under 18 Years Source: Current Population Survey (CPS)

dependencies.basis: 'The official poverty thresholds do not vary geographically, but they are updated for inflation using the Consumer Price Index (CPI-U)... Thresholds are updated annually for inflation using the Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U).' Worth noting the doubling-up: the thresholds are CPI-indexed, and then HHS indexes the published thresholds forward by CPI again to get the guidelines, so the CPI enters the eligibility rule for Medicaid twice, a year apart.
dependencies.evidence_quote: The official poverty thresholds do not vary geographically, but they are updated for inflation using the Consumer Price Index (CPI-U)... Thresholds are updated annually for inflation using the Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U).

dependencies.basis: Rev. Proc. 2025-32 says the figures 'are generally determined by reference to § 1(f)', and 26 U.S.C. § 1(f) names the index and the reference period exactly: '(3)(A) The cost-of-living adjustment for any calendar year is the percentage (if any) by which (i) the C-CPI-U for the preceding calendar year, exceeds (ii) the CPI for calendar year 2016, multiplied by the amount determined under subparagraph (B).' '(6)(A) The term "C-CPI-U" means the Chained Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (as published by the Bureau of Labor Statistics of the Department of Labor). The values ... shall be the latest values so published as of the date on which such Bureau publishes the initial value of the Chained Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers for the month of August for the preceding calendar year.' '(6)(B) The C-CPI-U for any calendar year is the average of the C-CPI-U as of the close of the 12-month period ending on August 31 of such calendar year.' The August cut-off is why the IRS can publish next year's brackets in October, and the freeze on 'latest values as of' the initial August release is how the statute copes with the fact that the chained index is revised for a year after first publication.

reference_period.stated_as: 'The C-CPI-U for any calendar year is the average of the C-CPI-U as of the close of the 12-month period ending on August 31 of such calendar year' — 26 U.S.C. s.1(f)(6)(B).

dependencies.evidence_quote: (3)(A) The cost-of-living adjustment for any calendar year is the percentage (if any) by which (i) the C-CPI-U for the preceding calendar year, exceeds (ii) the CPI for calendar year 2016, multiplied by the amount determined under subparagraph (B).

dependencies.basis: The chained index is not a separate collection — it is the CPI's own price quotes reaggregated. BLS: 'all three of the CPI indexes are built in two stages. In the first stage, prices for each of the 7,776 item-area combinations (243 item categories X 32 geographic areas) are averaged together to form 7,776 basic indexes... The geometric mean estimator is used in the C-CPI-U in the same item categories in which it is used in the CPI-U and CPI-W. In the second stage... It is at this second stage where the C-CPI-U is different from the CPI-U and CPI-W. The use of a superlative formula for upper-level aggregation... is designed to address consumer substitution across item categories.' BLS also confirms the policy use: 'Since 2017, the C-CPI-U has been used to adjust Federal tax brackets for inflation.' The average gap is about 0.2 percentage points a year, which compounds.
dependencies.evidence_quote: all three of the CPI indexes are built in two stages. In the first stage, prices for each of the 7,776 item-area combinations (243 item categories X 32 geographic areas) are averaged together to form 7,776 basic indexes... The geometric mean estimator is used in the C-CPI-U in the same item categories in which it is used in the CPI-U and CPI-W. In the second stage... It is at this second stage where the C-CPI-U is different from the CPI-U and CPI-W. The use of a superlative formula for upper-level aggregation... is designed to address consumer substitution across item categories.

dependencies.basis: NIPA Handbook Chapter 5 lists the CPI among the principal inputs — 'The following are among the principal source data used for the PCE estimates: BEA's Benchmark Input-Output (I-O) Accounts... the Census Bureau's Annual Retail Trade Survey, Service Annual Survey, Quarterly Services Survey, and Monthly Retail Trade Survey; and the Bureau of Labor Statistics' Consumer Price Indexes (CPIs)' — and then explains the mechanism: 'The estimates of quantities purchased, or real spending, for most of the detailed PCE categories are prepared by deflation. In this method, the quantities are calculated by dividing the current-dollar value of the component by an appropriate price index... For most PCE categories, the closest matching price index is a consumer price index or indexes.' Tables 5.A and 5.B name the specific CPI series component by component (CPI for new cars, CPI for used cars and trucks, CPI for food at home, and so on). The Fed's preferred inflation gauge is therefore largely a reweighting of BLS price quotes onto national-accounts expenditure weights.
dependencies.evidence_quote: The estimates of quantities purchased, or real spending, for most of the detailed PCE categories are prepared by deflation. In this method, the quantities are calculated by dividing the current-dollar value of the component by an appropriate price index... For most PCE categories, the closest matching price index is a consumer price index or indexes.

dependencies.basis: The FOMC's Statement on Longer-Run Goals and Monetary Policy Strategy, reaffirmed effective January 27, 2026, names the series that defines the target: 'The Committee reaffirms its judgment that inflation at the rate of 2 percent, as measured by the annual change in the price index for personal consumption expenditures, is most consistent over the longer run with the Federal Reserve's statutory maximum employment and price stability mandates.' The 2 percent goal is not defined on the CPI — a distinction that matters because the two indexes routinely differ by several tenths.
dependencies.evidence_quote: The Committee reaffirms its judgment that inflation at the rate of 2 percent, as measured by the annual change in the price index for personal consumption expenditures, is most consistent over the longer run with the Federal Reserve's statutory maximum employment and price stability mandates.

dependencies.basis: The Summary of Economic Projections reports each participant's projection of inflation as the percent change in the PCE price index and in the core PCE price index, precisely because the FOMC's longer-run goal is stated as '2 percent, as measured by the annual change in the price index for personal consumption expenditures'. The projection variable is defined by the statement of goals, so the SEP inherits BEA's index by construction.
dependencies.evidence_quote: 2 percent, as measured by the annual change in the price index for personal consumption expenditures

dependencies.basis: H.15's own footnotes 9 and 10 both read 'Source: U.S. Treasury' for the Treasury nominal and inflation-indexed constant maturity series, and the release describes those yields as 'interpolated by the U.S. Treasury from the daily yield curve'. Treasury's own FAQ confirms the mechanism: 'CMT yields are read directly from the Treasury's daily par yield curve, which is derived from indicative closing bid market price quotations on Treasury securities.' This reconnects fed-h15 to the graph after V0.9's deletion of fed-h15 -> fed-fomc-statement left it with no surviving edge.
dependencies.evidence_quote: CMT yields are read directly from the Treasury's daily par yield curve, which is derived from indicative closing bid market price quotations on Treasury securities.

_dropped.why: SSA states the AWI is derived from 'annual wage data we tabulated. The wage data are based on wages subject to Federal income taxes and contributions to deferred compensation plans.' That is an administrative tabulation of W-2 and Schedule SE records, not a published statistical release with a cadence, so there is no node to point at. Same category as the QCEW-versus-UI-records problem: the ultimate source is a tax file, not a report.

Deliberately not created. The federal minimum wage is set by statute at $7.25 and has no indexation provision at all — it has not moved since 2009. The absence of an edge is the finding, but a node with no dependencies and no cadence is noise in a dependency graph. Several states do index their minimums to the CPI; that would be a state-level slice.

SSA's latest COLA page states that 'Federal SSI payment levels will also increase by 2.8 percent effective for payments made for January 2026', so SSI rides the same determination. Not given its own node because it would be a near-duplicate of ssa-cola with the same driver and the same announcement date; the same is true of the retirement earnings test exempt amounts and the quarter-of-coverage amount on the wage-index side. If the graph later wants programme-level granularity these are the obvious four to add.

NIPA Handbook Chapter 5 names the Census Bureau's Annual Retail Trade Survey, Service Annual Survey, Quarterly Services Survey and Monthly Retail Trade Survey as principal source data for the current-dollar PCE estimates — better documented than most edges in this file. Left out only because it is expenditure-side plumbing rather than policy indexation, and adding four Census economic surveys would unbalance the slice. Clearly real; worth a future pass.

The ACA premium tax credit under section 36B is computed from household income as a percentage of the federal poverty line, so the IRS revenue procedure's 36B tables do interact with the HHS guidelines. But the revenue procedure sets the applicable percentage table rather than the poverty line itself, and the linkage runs through the tax return rather than through the revenue procedure's inflation adjustments. Not clean enough to assert on the evidence read.

Deleted in V0.9, and the seed edge's premise turned out to be false rather than merely unevidenced. The basis claimed H.15 'reports the current federal funds target range set by the FOMC alongside observed market rates'. It does not: the H.15 release carries no target-range series at all. Its only federal funds line is 'Federal funds (effective)', and footnote 1 states that since March 1 2016 the EFFR 'is a volume-weighted median of transaction-level data collected from depository institutions in the Report of Selected Money Market Rates (FR 2420)'. So H.15's fed funds number is built from an administrative reporting form, not from the FOMC's announcement — the same shape as FR 2644 behind H.8, and unpublishable for the same reason. Checked against the release of 2026-07-28.

Deleted in V0.9. The seed basis hedged in its own wording — 'CPI inflation is referenced as context even though the target is PCE-based' — and V0.8 had already flagged that an edge whose reasoning hedges is not one to go hunting for a URL to justify. The Committee's longer-run goals statement names PCE inflation, and the documented edge fed-fomc-statement -> bea-pce already carries that relationship with evidence. Nothing states the FOMC Statement takes the CPI as an input, so what remained was a plausible-looking link with a documented sibling doing the real work.
